Volume 1 of Preacher is exactly what I would expect from Ennis and not in a good way. Volume 1 of Preacher introduces the reader to the world of Jesse Custer. Jesse is a preacher in the small town of Annville, Texas. He's had a bit of a crisis of faith after dealing with a less than desirable flock when the unholy combination of angel and demon known as Genesis comes crashing into his life (and head). Jesse's church goes up in flames, along with the entire town and the remnants of his life. Genesis is an odd creature. It's immensely powerful but lacks a will of its own so essentially it gives Jesse knowledge (that he can't tap into yet) about God and Heaven as well as the ability to speak the Word of God such that all who hear must obey. Heaven isn't exactly happy about Genesis' escape and subsequent possession of Jesse and they send the Saint of Killers, an unstoppable gunman, to separate Genesis from Jesse by death if necessary. Along with his former lover Tulip and his best friend (and vampire) Cassidy, Jesse plans to track down God and use the Word to find out exactly what's going on. I'll be the first to admit that I'm not an Ennis fan. I find him tolerable when he's writing stories like Punisher or Dredd which are meant to be gory and non-stop violence but I find him virtually un-readable the rest of the time. What always gets me about Ennis is his complete inability to be subtle. Reading one of his stories is like trying to have a conversation with a psychopath. It's just one hundred percent crudity, profanity and balls to the wall mania that it gets both exhausting and tiresome really quickly. What is basically an interesting story is completely subsumed by Ennis' inability to do anything but leave the dial cranked to 11 and left me feeling unsatisfied. Volume 1 introduces the story but quickly gets overwhelmed by the intensely puerile character of Arseface ('cause a teen who fails spectacularly in killing himself a la Kurt Cobain and ends up hideously ugly is just hilarious). Preacher has a very "classic Western in the real world" feel to it so if that appeals to you and you don't mind Ennis' style, it's worth reading the series. Just don't expect much from the first volume. I'm not saying Preacher is unreadable (unlike The Boys, Volume 1: The Name of the Game), but this volume just didn't do it for me. If you're alright with an intensely violent, crude and profane story that pushes all boundaries, you might like it better than I did. Full series review: here

10:00 a.m. : The principal of Opportunity, Alabama's high school finishes her speech, welcoming the entire student body to a new semester and encouraging them to excel and achieve. 10:02 a.m. : The students get up to leave the auditorium for their next class. 10:03: The auditorium doors won't open. 10:05: Someone starts shooting. Told over the span of 54 harrowing minutes from four different perspectives, terror reigns as one student's calculated revenge turns into the ultimate game of survival. This Is Where It Ends is tense, explosive, shocking, and heartbreaking. The way this book is written is striking. The reader is shot between different points of view, inside the auditorium, outside, way from the school, and back in so fast it's like time isn't passing. Because it isn't, not quite. So many things happen during these 54 minutes. So many thoughts, worries, fears, tears, hopes. So many tears cried. So few words spoken aloud for fear of being the next victim. For not wanting any of it to be true. But it is. We only get glimpses of the characters, who they are in those moments and what they're thinking about, who they're worried about. That's all we get. Which is okay for me. That's what I expected. Of course, I do still wonder what might've happened next, what questions would've been asked in the days to come. Who would've survived and who would've been lost, physically or mentally. It's very likely that this is the most frightening book I've read in the last few years. It comes from the news events of the last few years, the increase in gun violence, the immediacy that social media has brought to events like shootings and riots and press conferences. This story feels so honest, so real. And it's sad that I'm not surprised by how real it feels. How easy it was to believe that, yes, this could absolutely be a real shooting at a read high school in America. That is what scares me. It's hard to talk about this book objectively. I think it's safe to say that this isn't the kind of book I generally read, a hard-hitting, realistic YA. Did I like it? I'm not sure. Would I recommend it? Yes. This book is sad and surprising and full of terror and fear, but it's one of those frighteningly honest stories that I think people should read. The writing was good, but the central conflicts just turned me off - romances where the main obstacle to Hero & Heroine getting together is lack of communication drive me batty, also lack of trust, and I cannot help but feel edgy and tense when so much of the attraction between a man and woman is of the "he's so bad and he treats me awfully, but I know he's good deep inside and I'm sure I can change him!" sort. These tropes tread brutally close to the language of victim / abuser, and the titular Rogue of this story goes far beyond alpha male bad boy, traveling deep into Inconsiderate Scumbag territory. I love a tale of childhood crush turning into adult affair, but the execution of this was too painful. MacLean made it clear she was working on a sort of Greek mythical tale mimicking Hades and Persephone, as the too-perfect Penelope descends into the dark abyss of Michael Bourne's pit of sin, but even Persephone got to feast on pomegranate seeds and visit her mom for six months of the year. This poor chick is living on a starvation diet of crumbs of affection and occasional bouts of sexy times interspersed with lots of being abandoned like yesterday's cold potatoes for what feels like 80% of the book. The inevitable turn --Hero realizes that Heroine is in fact his entire reason for living and that he's been a total chump-- is such a heavy swing of the emotional pendulum in the other direction that it reads as fake and excessively syrupy, like something soap opera stars would be embarrassed to watch due to the over the top declarations of undying love and addict-level worship. Again, it's a real shame so much of this was uncomfortable and awkward for me because the author's craft is considerable - she knows how to write dialogue and steamy scenes, she can move things along and her period detail is good, but too many hang ups stopped me from doing much beyond trudging grouchily to the finish line. Alas!

I just didn't want to re-read everything I had already read in the Calloway Sisters' spinoffs. I'm just not a big fan of rereading the same story from an alternate POV. My favorite couple is Rose and Connor. I happen to be one of the few who relates to Rose, and one of the many who thinks Connor is her dream guy. I adore and appreciate Lily and Lo's relationship. Their love is epic, and I admire that. However, their immaturity is not as endearing to me, nor is their science fiction comic book obsession. Review: Protagonists: Alyssa Ana'Raisa, crown princess of the Fells, has been fighting in the war against Arden since she was a lytling, but she wants to do much more than just defend her borders. She wants to make Gerard Montaigne sweat and for his thanes to find warring with the Fells to be too costly. She wants to invade Arden and show Montaigne the might of the Fells. Halston Matalon knows the king is gunning for him. As the son of one of Arden's thanes, and one particularly against the war at that, Hal knows that he could lose his life as a message to his father. Breon d'Tarvos travels with a group of performers, but when a commission to woo a pretty girlie with music turns south, he's on the run and without much of a place to go. All three of these protagonists are amazing. I mean, never once did I feel that a certain character got the short end of the stick. They all have compelling personal plotlines that entangle in a fascinating way. Oh, and the best part is there's a fourth POV, and it's someone we met in book 1, but I won't ruin the surprise. Romance: So, there's really only one romance in this story and I loved it so much more than the first book. While I understand why the insta-love in the first book happened the way it did, I still wasn't too keen on it, but luckily in this story, we don't get anything close to an insta-love. While the romance between Alyssa and Hal isn't exactly slow burning, it's still rife with complications and feels realistic and very much in character for both these characters. Best of all the romance is pretty swoon worthy. I can't wait to see where Chima takes these characters since we didn't get all too much of a romance in this book and there is most assuredly more to explore with this relationship. World Building: So I knew before venturing into this book that this series was going to be very different than series I've read in the past. Imagine if you will mixing a companion novel series and a more traditional series and you'd have this series. Unlike the previous book this story isn't told from the POV of Ash, instead, the clock gets turned back a bit and we see some of the events that happened in Flamecaster from other characters perspectives and we get to see some events that we really only heard about in the previous book. The central mystery of this entire series is the magemark mystery and while we do get some more clues as to what the magemarks are and why certain individuals have them, there is still far more to learn about them and by this point, I need to know. It's like an itch I can't scratch and while I'm a bit pacified for now I can't wait to see how things unfold in the next installment. One of the things about this series that I find very interesting is that in both this book and Flamecaster, the stories start out making the reader believe that Arden and/or Montaigne are the "Big Bad(s)" of this series, however, the real threat comes from across the seas and in this story we get to see more from Empress Celestine and learn more about her plans for the Seven Realms. Predictability: So, I'm going to level with you, and I feel like I've done this a lot lately, but I was sort of spoiled on a plot point that happened at the very end of this book, but while it sort of was the entire basis for the cliffhanger, it didn't impede my enjoyment of this book at all. As for the things I wasn't spoiled for, since this does turn back the clock a bit there are things that happen that I knew would happen thanks to the first book, and honestly, there were quite a few twists that I was able to predict, though luckily they were smaller twists. The larger ones still managed to surprise me and suck me deeper and deeper into the story. Ending: Like I said this story ends with a cliffhanger and the wait for the next book is going to kill me, I know it. The cliffhanger ending isn't all that bad, it's more what this story didn't reveal that has me chomping at the bit for book three. The final climax of this book was fantastic, I mean the edge of your seat, white-knuckle gripping the arms of your chair fantastic. Even though I already knew what would happen there were other details that I didn't know and that made this ending all the more exciting. We see the ending from a couple of perspectives and honestly, the final words in this book left me breathless and pretty much internally holding out "gimmie" hands for book three! Rating: I knew going into this book that I was going to love it and it did not disappoint, I only wish that I had read it sooner as I had planned on. I can't wait to read the next installment in the series and I hope to be able to read it early, and trust me if I get that chance I will read it early this time!

I read this after I'd seen the movie, but that was about six months ago. I didn't really remember what happened once Katniss went into the arena again, so that was all interesting -- although many things came back to me as I was reading. I enjoyed Katniss as a character just as much in this second book as I did in the first. The big appeal for me in both books is how Katniss writes about herself. For me, it rings very true. I believe in her as a person, as a human being, as a girl in her late teens. I believe in the world she lives in. President Snow is too much a comic-book villain (and President Coin the same), but Katniss and her characterizations of Peeta, Haymitch, and some of the others seem spot-on to me. Everyone who likes these books says they are a quick read, and that makes them sound light and fluffy. I don't agree. They are by no means heavy -- but they have a decent amount of depth to them, especially in Katniss's complex feelings toward Peeta. There's also a subtle message about the effects of violence, which I like. I don't think the author could have gone much further than she has without making the books a drag (and less popular) -- but there is an undercurrent here of how Katniss has been changed by having been used by the Capitol as their reality-TV star and by having been forced to kill other human beings for them.

I know a lot of people complain about how some authors are breaking up their work into smaller bits to sell them off individually and make more money. As long as that's clear before I spend any money, I don't mind it . and if the first book is free, I actually like the idea because it gives me a chance to see if it's worth spending money on the rest of the book. In the case of Identity, I decided it's not. Identity is book 1 of a 4 part series titled Eyes Wide Open (you can buy the subsequent "episodes" separately or buy the entire book together). The only reason I downloaded this one was because it was free and it looked kind of interest (my interest threshold for free books is much lower than it is for paid ones). Sometimes I leave Amazon to read the reviews on Goodreads because I like the format better. I must not have in this case because I had no idea this was labeled as "Christian Fiction." None of those elements come up in the first episode, but according to other reviewers, it becomes pretty clear in the last one. Had I known that beforehand, I never would have downloaded it. Just not my thing. However, that has nothing to do with my low rating of this book (or, rather, piece of a book). I just thought it was worth pointing out. Ted Dekker is a NYT bestselling author. I really hope his other books are leaps and bounds above this one. Of course, "bestseller" does not always (or often, really) indicate "best written". The writing isn't bad, per se; it just isn't that good. The descriptions are overdone and the dialogue is flat. As for the story itself . I can suspend disbelief for a lot of things. My favorite genres are sci-fi and fantasy. But there were just too many bits here that defied logic and I can't get past them. (Spoilers hidden below) --- The two main characters, Christy and Austin both come from an orphanage and both suffer from amnesia. Neither one knows anything about their families (Austin doesn't particularly care, but Christy does). Christy receives $2000/month from a trust fund . um, wouldn't that mean someone knows who her parents are and wouldn't it make the most sense to press the orphanage for answers? --- Christy gets trapped in the basement of a hospital. She has a cell phone with minimal battery left. Instead of using it to call someone, she pretty much kills the rest of the battery by using the flashlight app, so by the time she does use it to call Austin, it dies. --- Austin is awaiting results from an MRI. When he gets the call from the doctor's office, he's told he can come in right away or in two weeks. Seriously? He couldn't schedule at least a phone call with his doctor to discuss his results? --- After Christy becomes trapped in the psych ward and she finds out that they "think" she's Alice, the missing patient, they send her to a shrink to "ask her some questions." It's a total psych intake and I can't imagine that someone would sit there and allow a stranger holding her against her will to ask the questions the shrink asked. Then after they tell her that she is indeed Alice, she starts to question her own sanity, thinking that maybe she is and that everything else is a delusion. (I didn't read the book, so maybe it really is, which would account for the other issues, but assuming it's not, I have trouble believing someone would question their sanity that quickly, even if that person clearly has other unresolved psychological issues.) The book is also painfully predictable. As soon as Christy passed the crazy lady in the hall, it was obvious that she was in psych ward . and with her wearing a patient's shirt, well, duh, she's going to be "mistaken" for a patient. Obviously, her necklace and cell phone would be gone before she could prove herself. The second Austin decides to check it out, well he obviously takes the cell phone and necklace. He oversees something he shouldn't in the psych ward (of which we're already questioning the legitimacy and ethics), so boom, he's going to be a patient too. As they're trying to escape (a description that just seems to go and on and on), it's obvious they're not going to get out (where would the rest of the story be? and the staff all seem fairly confident that no one can get out). I'm kind of interested in spoilers for the rest of the book, just to see where this was going . as I keep reading that it has a rather Christian-y end to it and I'm curious. If I ever see the last book for free, I might grab it. Otherwise, if someone care to, please spoil away! I've seen people rave about Ted Dekker, so I was hoping to find another author to follow, but it seems he is just not for me. (It always seems easier to write long negative reviews than long positive ones . I'm going to work on that.)

his being my first novel written by Jennifer, I am pleasantly surprised. At first, I was skeptical because of the backlash that followed the novel's initial description. Apparently, people thought the description was offensive which made me hesitant about reading it. Since I got the book, I decided to give it a try. The book is not offensive at all. In fact, the book is a beautiful example of accepting who you are and how two unlike people can support each other. Jennifer Niven did an astounding job creating the story. The book will be a great read for young adults because it teaches many important lessons. One lesson that it taught is that nothing can stop you from living your life. Libby is an example of this lesson because she manages to move on after the loss of her mother and her accident. Libby loses weight and returns to school despite her fears. She overcomes the bullying and focuses on herself. Another lesson is self-love. Libby embraces her body and understands the effort that was taken in order for her to lose the weight. Also, Libby stands in front of everyone in a bikini to show people that she is wanted and that she is beautiful. Finally, Jennifer teaches that you cannot use your faults to justify your bad decisions. Through Jack, it is shown that you cannot use your weaknesses as reasons for your mistakes. Eventually, you have to take responsibility for yourself. Despite the many positive messages in the book, there are other aspects of the book that I liked. The main aspect that I found enjoyable was that Jennifer was able to successfully make readers understand what the characters were going through. Her constant emphasis on how someone with face blindness viewed the world made it easier to understand Jack's situation. Also, we are able to understand Libby better with flashbacks to her mom's death and the accident. Another thing that I enjoyed was Jennifer's writing style. The novel was easy and fun to read. The use of lists in the novel showed readers the characters' thoughts. Finally, I loved Jack. His situation was interesting to read about. Also, his point of view was captivating. In all honesty, he is the character that I feel made the book so great. I believe that Jennifer focuses more on Jack rather than the rest of the characters. Despite greatly enjoying most of the book, there were a few things that I disliked. The major issue that I had with the book was that, besides Jack, the characters seemed flat. Some characters seemed hard to relate to. Another thing that I disliked was the slightly forced chemistry between Jack and Libby. They do not appear to be a romantic relationship but rather a friendship. Their feelings felt rushed and not established well. Overall, the book was very fun and interesting to read. I believe that this book is a positive read. Jennifer teaches many important lessons in the story.

2.5 / 5 stars rating This review is also posted at http://readingnookandcranny.blogspot.... I have still yet to be blown away by Aimee Carter. It seems she is just another author in the vast array of young adult writers out there. Though her fundamental plots are often unique, the execution of them throughout her series has been so far tired and cliched. Queen is no exception. While it wraps up the series well, the ending for the rebellion was a bit predictable, and the romance was a little too heavy considering the dire situation they are all facing. Granted, I now realize this series is published by Harlequin Teen, so of course it's going to have a strong dose of romance. Unfortunately, the romance in Queen seems to come at the cost of the plot. Kitty (still a terrible name for the main character) is limping along with the Blackcoats, trying to find a way to prove that Prime Minister Daxton is not who he says he is and to overthrow his power. They struggle at every turn to make a mark and find a foothold for the rebellion, and yet there is still an emphasis on this love triangle between Kitty, Benjy, and Knox. I don't think it would be so bad, except there is no real chemistry between any of them at all, so it makes it that much more glaringly out of place. Overall, I think this series fails to deliver on expectations I started with in Pawn. For such a crazy dystopian and an unique world and idea, the possibilities were endless. And while there is a bit of suspense and excitement through the series, it's heavily weighed on by other issues that aren't quite as gripping. So while I bought Pawn and got an ARC copy of Captive, I probably won't add Queen to my collection to complete the series in my personal library.

This book turned me off from the very beginning. I often found my attention wandering while reading and had to force myself back to it. If I had to guess why I was turned off initially (acknowledging that humans are bad at introspection), I would say that the following three things contributed initially: (1) The prelude began with a description of a ship taking off and a "Mind" detaching from it, with reference to things I as a reader didn't yet have the context to understand. Perhaps I was in a bad mood (or just lazy), but this irritated me and, pathetically, I want to know about people and not the actions of single ships in space that I don't yet care or know anything about. (2) The first chapter felt like an overwrought attempt to impress the reader with the lengths the author was willing to go to gross you or create an action-packed scene. (3) The treatment of women in the first few chapters was incredibly sexist and that pissed me off. Only female characters' physical appearance seemed to be noted, the first female character the protagonist interacted with was described as a strong woman yet he wanted to "rustle her hair and pinch her cheeks" (I'm paraphrasing), and the second female character introduced was immediately evaluated by the protagonist in a sexual manner (including stating that he just couldn't see her as a woman, although later he slept with her), and so on and so forth. Nothing endeared the main character to me and I just. didn't. care. When the action first picked up in the book, I didn't care who lived or died. When the book got crazy gory (I'm referring to the cannibalism ), it felt gratuitous and no plot advancement was achieved (although I will say that it made the book more interesting). The "Damage Games" made the book become more interesting to me, but ultimately there seemed to be no point to it other than to illustrate the characters' indifference to the loss of human life. I became more interested toward the end when the action really began to heat up, but "interested" is about it. I still didn't care and there was no payoff at the end that made the book worth it. However, about the ending, I will say that... killing off everyone but Balveda was very satisfying. I would have been disappointed if somehow it all worked out happily and nicely. I thought perhaps Horza would be the only one left, but I thought it was well done to kill him off. Honestly, I never liked Horza. The way he used his abilities as a Changer to get out of situations could be interesting, but again "interesting" did not equate "caring" for me. Throughout reading Consider Phlebas I thought that it would make a good movie. Action-packed, visually shocking scenes... Stuff that I feel goes well in a movie, but that I personally am not drawn to in books. In books I want character development and emotion, and all I thought about Horza was that he could be kind of a maladaptively single-minded dick. I think the anthropomorphized drone Unaha-Closp was my favorite part of the book. To sum it up, my main problem with this book is that I didn't feel invested in the characters or the story. Perhaps it is a unique interaction between me as a reader and the book itself; maybe I read it at the wrong time. I like it when books evoke some emotion, positive or negative (ideally, both), in me, and this one just didn't do it for me. Even the scenes that were supposed to be gory and disgusting had no impact on me. Am I that desensitized to violence? Yet I just finished re-watching all of Breaking Bad and there is so much non-graphic (and also graphic) violence in that show that elicits a huge reaction from me, and not just because it's visual. I think it's because I *care* about the characters that I react, and I just didn't care about the characters or events in Consider Phlebas. And now I feel like a broken record, so I'll end here.

See more of my reviews on my blog the Book Deviant Why even have a summary? One thing I hate the most is when the summary promises something, and the book doesn't deliver. Intrigue? Nope. Mystery? Aha, what mystery? "Bloody events"? Unless you count the decapitated mouse head, then no. This book was a huge disappointment. Besides skipping over everything that was promised in the summary, I found nothing at all interesting or new. Nothing original-just another retelling of Alice in Wonderland, taking the oh-so-unique idea of delving into the Queen of Hearts's past. I have to admit, this is the first one I actually read, but after this one, I don't think I'll be reading another. Instead of mystery, we get constant complaining from Dinah. Instead of "bloody events", we get a severed mouse's head and more complaining. That's literally all this book was. Dinah complaining about one thing or another, whining, whining, and, yes, more whining. I don't even know what the mystery was supposed to be. There was one thing that pointed to there being a problem, and Dinah used her 'super-sense': "I can't explain it, but I need to find her. Faina. This note wasn't sent in malice, I can feel it." One-sided characters None of the characters were interesting. None of the characters were reminiscent of the White Rabbit or the Mad Hatter-in fact, the character that was called the Mad Hatter was basically a small child. He was described as small, and acted like a child, and I don't see how that can be considered 'mad'. The romance between Wardley and Dinah was just so awkward. Dinah was obsessed with him, while he just 'wanted to be friends'. Not only did I have to read through her unwanted advances towards him, but I also had to read how she kept doing it over and over again. And don't even get me started on her father and Cheshire. one and a half stars - Overall? This book was a huge disappointment. I found a few things interesting, but of what I did find interesting, they were brushed aside within a paragraph. The writing was somewhat decent, but that's all I could really stand about this book. The characters were just cardboard cut-outs, some of which were obviously put in place only to get killed. Would I Recommend? Probably not. This was my first Alice in Wonderland retelling that I've read, and I was ultimately, hugely, disappointed. Overall, it's completely up to you whether or whether not you read this book. But, in my opinion, find a different retelling.

Meatier than the first one, and a little nastier. Enjoyed thoroughly. So far it seems to me like the two Cormoran Strike books are intensely concerned with appearances. Vanity, perception and presentation of self. Celebrity and reputation in the main mystery plot, yes, but also in more insidious, more prosaic ways in the background subplots that I actually found myself enjoying more by the end. Strike is terribly perceptive about people, about the way they like to show themselves, but he seems almost an unreliable narrator when it comes to himself. He stands out, effortlessly cool, masculine, authentic compared to the suburban, social climbing mileu he spends so much being contemptous of. But the text itself has just a little more sympathy for these characters - his fussy, well-meaning sister and self-awarely spoiled brother, Robin's jealous fiancee, the p3ublisher he takes up with and dumps - and the gap gets interesting. Strike makes more sense to me here, with that context. He's proudly aloof of his famous father, but there's a jealousy there too. His willingness to use people and throw them out of his life when he's done. The shade of longing for his old army life - discipline and his own authority, rather than cameraderie or sense of purpose of whatever. His ex - who seemed like a bit of a drama queen in the first book, but basically ok - is revealed here as an utter piece of work, thoroughly selfish, gratuitously cruel and snobby to boot. It rather raises the question - what kind of man would have that as the grand, torrid love afair of his life?

***Review posted on The Eater of Books! blog*** Dream A Little Dream by Kerstin Gier Book One of the Silver Trilogy Publisher: Henry Holt and Co. (BYR) Publication Date: April 14, 2015 Rating: 4 stars Source: ARC sent by the publisher Summary (from Goodreads): Mysterious doors with lizard-head knobs. Talking stone statues. A crazy girl with a hatchet. Yep, Liv's dreams have been pretty weird lately. Especially this one where she's in a graveyard at night, watching four boys perform dark magic rituals. The really weird thing is that Liv recognizes the boys in her dream. They're classmates from her new school in London, the school where's she's starting over because her mom has moved them to a new country (again). But they seem to know things about her in real life that they couldn't possibly know, which is mystifying. Then again, Liv could never resist a good mystery. What I Liked: Kerstin Gier does it again! I wish all of her books could be picked up by USA publishers, because I've been quite in love with her books since Ruby Red was published in the United States, in 2011. The Ruby Red trilogy is one of my favorite series of all time! In this new series, Liv is leaving one place for another, but her new home has some... interesting people to it. Her and her younger sister, Mia, are constantly traveling and moving, as their mother is a professor (their father is as well, but the parents are divorced). The girls show up in London, and the first person their mother introduces them to? Surprise - her boyfriend! Whom she will be marrying, and Liv and Mia will being moving in to his house. Liv's soon-to-be stepbrother, is a strange, quite one, and her soon-to-be-stepsister is pushy and a bit rude, and her soon-to-be-stepfather is old and just a bother in general. Attending school means meeting new people, and Liv immediately meets Grayson's friends - Arthur, Jasper, and Henry. Things get weird when Liv starts dreaming, and the four boys are in her dreams. Or she's in theirs. When they want her to join their strange dream group, Liv is skeptical, but she joins. But perhaps things aren't so plausible - perhaps things are much more sinister than they appear... One thing that strikes me in all of Gier's books is the humor. I love how funny Liv's voice is, how Gier makes Liv a tiny bit awkward, a lot sweet, and a bit sarcastic, in a funny way. This book is hilarious, even if there are parts that are very serious, and borderline scary. I liked Liv. She has a distinct voice, and it's so great to watch the story unfold from her perspective. She likes logic and science, and likes to figure things out. She joins the boys and their bizarre rituals, but mostly she wants to help them, and wants to prove to herself that demons aren't real. See, the boys tried to summon a demon who will grant their hearts' desire. On Halloween. Wild. I like the boys. There are four of them, one of them being the stepbrother (Grayson), the other three being his friends. They're all described as super good-looking, like shampoo commercial guys. Each has their own personality. Jasper is very rambunctious, and doesn't really take things seriously. Grayson is a bit protective. Arthur... he's an odd one (and you'll see why, at the end of this book). Henry is the mysterious and brooding one, but he's also very sweet. Another thing that I really liked about this book is the sister-sister relationship! Usually, the younger sister is SO ANNOYING, and I dislike her a lot (like, genuinely dislike her, not dislike her as the kid sister). Mia is about five years younger, but she's mature for her age, yet fun like a child should be. I liked her a lot, which surprised me. The story is quite interesting and goes by very quickly. I was really strapped for time this week (soooo many exams and papers and research), but I finished this one faster than I expected. I love how Gier writes - her writing is beautiful, but also very easy to read and pay attention to. Seriously, anyone could read her books, translated or not, and know her writing style and voice. There IS romance in this book! Check out my Swoon Thursday post from yesterday (March 12th) if you want a little insight on the romance. The love interest is pretty swoony, and he's more than a love interest - he plays quite pivotal roles in the book. No love triangle, and while Liv becomes infatuated with the love interest pretty quickly, I wouldn't call it insta-love. More like insta-interest. There are no declarations of love or serious feelings, so no insta-love. The romance is really sweet, but also very subtle and a bit in the background compared to the story. The story was intriguing and almost scary at some points! Dreams are beautiful and scary places. I didn't see the climax coming - and it occurs pretty late, around 90% of the book. But I couldn't stop reading. This book wraps up pretty nicely, but in a way that you KNOW there will be more books (hence, the Silver Trilogy). No cliffhanger though, yay! What I Did Not Like: Nothing in particular - I might have wanted a little more from the romance, but I know how Gier writes in the romance into the story of her books, and it's always very slow and subtle. Which is cool, I'm fine with that. Would I Recommend It: Yes! Great paranormal/fantasy read, set in the contemporary world. This one was fun and easy and quick, and not to mention lush in details and gorgeous in writing. And the cover is pretty great! I liked the original USA cover, but this new cover is spectacular. In any case, I'd recommend any Gier book I've read (now four), this one included! Rating: 4 stars. I'll definitely be reading book two as soon as I can get my hands on it! Noooow, please! I wonder if there are editions in Spanish (bilingual for the win!)... I'll buy one of those, if I have to!

Also, I get that she can't be expected to be happy about her husband's illegitimate child, but her flippant remark about "swatting" Soo-Lin when she gets back, if Elgy hasn't managed to run her off REALLY bothered me. Like it or not, he's got a responsibility now to another child; whatever the circumstances of conception, it's certainly not the baby's fault. Surely even self-centered bipolar genius Bernadette can see that. I could go on (and on) but I won't. It does have occasional bad language throughout the book.

While I did not really rate Twilight, this novel was a step worse again. The story is incredibly slow, focusing on angsty internal monologues rather than advancing any kind of plot. Although there was the occasional moment that sparked my interest, such as the meeting with the Volturi and Bella's famous cliff dive, these were quickly lost and forgotten in the midst the mire of Bella's lamentations. Her first person narrative really hampered the story as she was not present for most of the events and thus all the excitement had to be related back to her by a third party, removing any tension. The three main characters - Bella, Edward and Jacob - were all also utterly detestable. Bella was a particularly weak female lead, proving that she could not function in any way without a man, but the two male leads were equally as frustrating - both behaving thoroughly selfishly and treating her as little more than a possession. Finally, and this is a very personal gripe, I also found the numerous references to Romeo and Juliet to be incredibly heavy handed and lacking in any subtlety. A reference is only really effective if you don't have to hammer it home. All in all, I felt this novel really suffered from the absence of the rest of the Cullens and really hope that the next book picks up again now that they have been returned to the story.

I also thought the concept of the Innkeepers turned out to be just a cool concept and was so overshadowed by a bunch of other crap that by the end I didn't even care anymore. I was barely listening. Someone made out. There was a fight. Probably another mention of someone's sweet pectorals. The end. Three Dark Crowns is a very boring novel. I'm just going to say that. Book Synopsis In every generation on the island of Fennbirn, a set of triplets is born--three queens, all equal heirs to the crown and each possessor of a coveted magic. Mirabella is a fierce elemental, able to spark hungry flames or vicious storms at the snap of her fingers. Katharine is a poisoner, one who can ingest the deadliest poisons without so much as a stomachache. Arsinoe, a naturalist, is said to have the ability to bloom the reddest rose and control the fiercest of lions. But becoming the Queen Crowned isn't solely a matter of royal birth. Each sister has to fight for it. And it's not just a game of win or lose...it's life or death. The night the sisters turn sixteen, the battle begins. The last queen standing gets the crown. I REALLY, REALLY almost stop reading this book. It started off really slow, and you barely got an introduction into the world. You were just thrust into this entirely new universe, and you get nothing from it. at all. Three Dark Crowns features three triplet queens, all sisters, who have to fight for the throne to the death. Arsinoe is supposed to be a naturalist (and useless), Katharine, the youngest, is a poisoner with a horrible stomach, and Mirabella is an elemental, who breaks the ground and dances in fire(what have her parents taught her????). By far, Mirabella is the strongest and no one expects the other two to win. The novel also features some other minor characters, Jules, Arisone's best friend who flits around killing bears and being upset at Joseph, who basically is cheating on her with the enemy. Elizabeth is technically Mirabella's torture shard and the rest are so unimportant. Three Dark Crowns has a very interesting plot, don't get me wrong. But the first seven eighths of this book are so boring. They're about the queens walking around getting dressed and having ultimate love problems. The novel just progresses so slowly, and there is barely any action that anyone cares about. It's not as interesting as everything makes it out to be and it hurts so bad. The plot is essentially dead. "It was only a joke, Mia," says Bree gently. "Of course I do not wish that. No one really wishes to be queen." It's kind of ironic with these quotes in that MIRABELLA DOESN'T WANT TO KILL HER SISTERS. IF I SPOILED IT THEN I SAVED YOU A YEAR OF FALLING ASLEEP AT THE WHEEL. This book made me cringe so much and it's unbearably horrid. Overall Rating: 1.2/5 stars

A very immersive and atmospheric Lovecraftian sci fi, with an ethereal narrative that doesn't intercede a strict boundary between surrealism, post modernism, adventure, horror and suspense. Area X is a Visitation Zone, an Arkham 'blasted heath', somewhere along the tropical coast line, presumably in America; For its obfuscating transitional alien ecology, the area is demarcated for exploration, by a shadow (non)government agency called Southern Reach (VanderMeer's Wayland Yutani). Our narrative follows the 12th expedition to The Tower, by a team of 4 members, all women, who are identified by their respective roles- a biologist, a psychologist, a surveyor and an anthropologist. What we read in its entirety, are survey notes by the Biologist - an after incident relic, with obvious missing information. The setting of this novel is similar to the classic premise of Lovecraft's A Mountain of Madness or its space cousin Randezvous with Rama, where a group of individuals are exploring the unexplainable; or Jacob's Ladder if you consider the character centric limbo. But here, VanderMeer's after event narrative doesn't trust the readers, nor can it be trusted absolutely. If you are invested in clear cut explanations and conventional character developments, this book is going to disappoint you colossally. Our Biologist is an unreliable narrator, exploring a House of Leaves, too strange for her brain cells to intercept. The narrative won't let you identify with any of the characters, except for the biologist, who in turn is openly critical towards the readers. A man might need a name, but clearly these women don't. In its Hard Boiled Wonderland treatment, none of the characters are addressed by their names, not even among themselves, like they have already detached their personal attachments for the higher purpose of Area X happenings. I found author's philosophy eerily similar to that of Strugatsky Brother's Roadside Picnic - explorers investigating stuffs they can't or will ever possibly comprehend, like cats and dogs trying to make sense of leftovers from a picnic. For its 'plot far bigger than the characters' treatment, I found the biologist monologue genuinely heartfelt, almost in lines with that of Chiang's Story of Your Life. The digressions in her monologue, the seemingly gratuitous past life side quests, in course of reading, added to the mega narrative confusion, often making sense. VanderMeer's writing was well crafted, layered and well-engineered with fragmentation, anxiety and growing paranoia. The log entries were prosaic yet poignant, and kept definitive character traits of the biologist, from the adjectives she use, to her working explanations of Area X. Permanence, I believe, was the biggest luxury in Area X, for all the five characters (including biologist's husband), well within their ulterior motives, were found to be perpetually transitioning throughout their progress in survey. Their perception of the alien environment was shaky (the tower? the tunnel? ), with memory vacuums created by psychological suggestions. The Area X in itself was full of radically different ecosystems in overlap, constantly rearranging themselves, and the map, the equipments and sponsoring organization were severe misdirections to even begin with. A great chunk of the novel felt like playing Alan Wake, or Silent Hill, or like binge watching first season of Lost. The unfathomable environment and writing kept me on the edge like reading Then There Were None for the first time. * I received a free copy on goodreads first reads for review* You don't realise how language actually interferes with communication until you don't have it, how it gets in the way like an over dominant sense. I was continually amazed at the level of complexity and emotion that Lily King was able to fit into a mere 250 page novel. And, true to her quote at the top of this review, reading between the lines at what was left unsaid revealed far more about the characters than their own musings and anthropological discoveries. Euphoria is about the relationships formed between three anthropologists studying river tribes in New Guinea during the early 1930's. Nell, the American, and most well known of the three, having published a rather controversial book regarding the sexual lives of tribal children. She never really states it, but we get the picture that she suffers abuse at the hands of her husband, Australian anthropologist Fen, who seems desperate to right the balance of his perceived power in their relationship by making a discovery that will eclipse the scholarly achievements of his wife. Add to this, Andrew Bankston, a British anthropologist and erstwhile suicide attempter, who latches onto the couple in the hopes that they can possibly save him from his misery. Of course, they may also be his ultimate undoing, which makes this book such a tension filled pleasure to read. The tribes in which the characters settle and assimilate are colorful and fascinating and King draws them in such a way that we feel like scientists of sorts just reading and observing their customs and interactions with each other and with the main characters. I felt like King gave them just enough "screen" time to make them a vital part of the story without letting them overtake the spotlight on the relationships between Nell, Fen, and Bankston. This book also made me realize that we readers are all anthropologists of a sorts. Studying and observing human life through the lens of literature. Not a bad sort of profession in my opinion.

The sequel is always the hardest part of a trilogy, I guess. Whereas the first book in a series is building an entire universe, introducing characters and creating suspense, the second book is mostly about developing themes and leading up to the final conclusion and ultimate finale that will occur in the third book. Sequels are hard because they are 'fillers'. They do not create suspense, they prolong it. Which is perhaps why "Catching Fire" is my least favorite in the Hunger Games series. It is still good, it is still incredibly fast-paced and completely consuming - but it fades a bit in comparison to both "The Hunger Games" and "Mockingjay". Personally, I never really liked the idea of the return to the arena, of Katniss and Peeta in yet another round of the Hunger Games. It is an extremely bold choice for any author to repeat their own pattern so deliberately, and while I think Collins avoids the worst repetitions, I have always skimmed through the pages of training and prepping for the arena, as I've already grasped the concept of that so clearly in the first book. "Catching Fire" introduces a beautiful variety of characters and I especially like Finnick as a new addition to the series. I adore the relationship between Katniss and Peeta, and they share some really touching moments that almost ripped my heart out. They cling to each other in their desperation, and I cling to them throughout the pages, as they're the only source of hope the book can offer its reader. My only complaint in Collins' characterization is Katniss' sudden weakness in the arena. It feels out of character for her. It feels wrong. Overall, I think "Catching Fire" does a worthy job in leading the series forward to its finale. It has some minor flaws, little parts that I disagree with, a hint of repetition and a poor writing style (did you notice all the question marks?! ), but the book is still impossible to put down or let go of. Once you've read "The Hunger Games", you will experience an insatiable hunger, an extreme degree of reading fever that will haunt you until you've finished the trilogy. Your heart will race and your eyes will never tire. You will devour every word as fast as you possibly can.

I'm giving Daughter of Smoke and Bone a 3 1/2 star rating. There were parts of the story I found undeniably attractive. The imagery and descriptions were well done. The characters were strong. The writing style was good. I really liked the novel, but I did have a couple of issues which is why it's a 3 1/2 star for me instead of a 5. Seventeen year old Karou is attending a fine arts school in Prague. She's trying desperately to get away from her ex and keep her life a secret from everyone - because she has to. The catch is that Karou was raised by 4 chimera beings = not quite human. She goes on missions for the man (?) who's been like a father-figure to her her entire life; strange missions hunting for teeth. She's trained in fighting and been to plenty of black markets around the world. She has a necklace that can grant small wishes and she knows around 20 different languages. Needless to say, not quite your typical teenage experience. While on one of these missions, she encounters an angel; someone that tires to kill her; an enemy. From there, she starts to uncover secrets that Brimstone (her father figure) has been keeping not only about where he's from, but about who she is. The blurb to this book is incredibly misleading. An angel and demon falling in love? Not quite. This shouldn't dis-sway anyone from reading the novel in and of itself though. I actually loved the fact that the book wasn't at all what I expected it to be. The author breaks the story down into something incredibly basic: war. It's about prejudices and people brought up to hate their enemy - who that is exactly depending completely on which race you are. It's about starting to overcome those per-conceived notions, hoping for peace, and eventually falling in love with someone you never dreamed you would. And especially with war going on today, I think most people can relate well to the feeling Laini Taylor portrays about war, hate, death, destruction, bonds, and mercy in the mist of life-time enemies. I loved that aspect of the novel. That it could so accurately pinpoint some of the feelings war leaves behind was truly something to be commended for. A quote that struck me was: "It is a condition of monsters that they do not perceive themselves as such. The dragon, you know, hunkered in the village devouring maidens, heard the townsfolk cry 'Monster!' and looked behind him'" - which is nothing if not true. Villains never perceive themselves to be villains; they all believe they're doing the right thing. It's hard to see a foe's point of view, hard to see them for anything other than monsters. They tend to feel the same way though about you. I loved that this book lets you see 2 characters lives intersecting, and both realizing that the other isn't as evil as they had imagined. I loved loved loved Akiva (our love interest). He's a tortured soul, broken in grief. Then he meets Karou. Although they don't get off to the best of starts (trying to kill someone really isn't the gentlemanly way to approach a girl, after all), they feel pulled to each other. It does get kind of insta-lovey, but in the context of the story and finding out what we do about Karou, it makes sense. He's a hardened soldier with other-worldly beauty and a killer of the chimera, no mercy given. He's closed off and has dead eyes. Karou knocks him out of that and throughout the story, you can really see how much he loves her and is willing to sacrifice for her. He even puts his life in her hands when he tells her something unforgivable he's done to her. So now that I've gone over several things I loved, let me mention why my rating is 3 1/2 stars instead of 5. Maybe I'm just jaded but whenever creature-like beings, half human, half animal are described (like the chimera in this book), I always get flashbacks of the Chronicles of Narnia. I mean I love the idea but I feel like C.S. Lewis beat everyone to it and to describe anything similar is just...well, disappointing. It feels like cheating to me, although others may not have the same feelings about that as I do. Towards the end of the novel, Karou finds out exactly who/what she is. And, while I believe that to an extent, some of it was necessary, the last 100+ pages of the book are completely about the past. To me, a flashback here and there is completely fine but I felt like this information was dumped on me in one setting. During the ENTIRE book Karou is shrouded in mystery, even, she doesn't know exactly who she is. Then, in the last 100 pages, we get every detail about her history, how she came to be here, love interests, everything. It was just too much dumping. It was interesting but it drug a little bit for me in places and I was getting impatient for the author to go back to the present. That was the biggest let down for me. It was dump, then end of book one. However, I will say that that last couple pages (back to the present) dropped a big bombshell that I didn't see coming. Because of it, it was left on a bit of a cliffhanger, making me anxious to read book 2. Finally, although I liked Karou's character, I did not love her or always relate to her. I can't pinpoint exactly what made me feel that way. She's lonely, and she feels like she's missing part of herself (the void isn't filled by needing a boyfriend thank goodness, like some other books). My heart goes out to her at certain places but like I said, I didn't fall in love with her like I want to for hero's/heroine's of books.

When this book showed up on NetGalley, I was quite excited because the premise sounds so unique--not your typical YA murder mystery! I'm a major sucker for a contemporary with a slightly paranormal twist (because let's be honest--Vee's sliding is not exactly normal). Vee can't really control who she slides into--it has to do with that person leaving some kind of emotional imprint on an object that Vee touches. When she slides into a killer, the stakes are immediately raised because not only did Sophie not kill herself as everyone suspects, but Vee knows the killer somehow, even if she can't figure out how. The characters in this novel were very well done. I immensely enjoyed Vee, even though I really wanted to just give her a little shove when she didn't tell Rollins the truth. She's a really tough chick and I liked that she was a little out there with her pink hair and "narcolepsy." She's also hiding a lot of pain that those around her can't/don't really know about and I thought that it made her character have a lot of depth. I thought that Ms. Hathaway also did a really good job making her side characters interesting and dynamic, especially with Vee's family. I thought her sister and father had a lot more to them than you could see at first glance. Maddie is a lot less of the shallow girl she seems at first, and her father obviously has a lot of pain and secrets that he's hiding. As for the mystery, well, I had a pretty good idea what was up fairly early on, but that didn't stop me from enjoying every aspect of the story. I think even after you figure out what's going on there's still a lot of learn about the motivations and it would be hard to guess where she's really taking the story. The writing is very well-done--succinct and smooth with a realistic storyline. Overall, I think Jill Hathaway's debut Slide welcomes her perfectly into the world of YA literature and she'll be an author to look for in the future. If you're looking for a quick YA mystery to read, I wouldn't hesitate to recommend this book to you and I think it's one worthy of reading and quite possibly adorning your bookshelf.

This Song Will Save Your Life tells a story of a young girl named Elise who has been drowned by her issues and insecurities of having no friends and never fitting in. This caused her to change and reinvent herself into someone like them, but her attempts were unsuccessful. Driven by frustration and sorrow, she thinks of a better way of solving her problems. And with that, she ends up with an even more scarring life experience to carry on her shoulders. But fate stepped in as she accidentally stumbles into the best underground party in the world that made her experience new things, and eventually changed her life This book tackles not only the usual inequalities of the hierarchical high school world, but also issues about bullying and it's severe effects to those who people involved. We've heard that a few time before, but what makes this book a stand out for me is that Elise, although she wants to become like everybody else, refuses to listen to the kind of music popular today. It's the one thing she's not willing to let go or change. That was the beam of light in the darkness that surrounds Elise, which became even brighter when she discovers her love for DJing. Speaking of Elise, there were times that I really had been exasperated with her behavior and her choices. Maybe because I have never felt what she felt, but still, I got irked sometimes. But most of the times, I do get why she acts that way. So for the most part, Leila Sales has created relatable Elise. The other characters, especially Vicks and Mel, were pretty awesome as well. They were their own, exploding with personality and individuality. But I don't want to talk about Char, or Pippa, or Emily. The other characters felt like small extras in a big film due. For the plot, it was okay. I still have mixed feelings for it. I liked it in general, but I'm not sure if I liked some of the little things that happened on the sidelines. I am still a little skeptical with the ending because of what happened to Elise at school, what happened to Alex, or even Pippa or Char. There were a lot of loose ends that I feel were essential for Elise's characters growth, and even for the satisfaction of the readers. But all in all Leila Sales has delivered something good. A good coming-of-age stories for those who feel like they don't belong. Plus, the title and cover is amazing!

"Terror. The black crow of panic was perched on her shoulder." That line? That's when I knew this book was going to be so excruciatingly bad it would round the corner and become good for all the wrong reasons. The black crow of panic? Only a short way in I knew this is going to be one of those books where, no matter how I hate them and hate myself for reading them, I'm going to compulsively work through the entire series because I have to see how ridiculous it gets. Thank goodness I already have a GoodReads shelf called "car wrecks I have to look at". The "its so bad its almost good" feeling abates halfway through the book as you experience a bit of burnout, but if you choose to focus on how OTT it all is- how ridiculous the premise and how poor the execution - you'll get back to enjoying the awfulness. The gaping plot holes... the continuity errors... the unending too-stupid-to-live behaviour from both the heroine and (how unusual) the hero... the heavy use of cliches... the formulaic PNR characters... the unappetising and unbelievable sexual chemistry... This book should be used in a Lit class to illustrate just how terrible a book can be and still be readable, just as long as it isn't too offensive or too insulting to the reader. It's dullness and blandness works in its favour and the best thing I can say about the book, overall, is that I finished it. Yes, the end was rushed and disappointingly weak and disconnected from the rest of the book's pace and "plot". Pretty much what you'd expect, really. A few gems that I have to share: Cliche: "Smart idea. So you're like the canary in the coal mine. If you go down, your leader knows there's danger. " (First you resort to a cliche, then you feel the need to explain what it means. Wow.) Too Stupid To Live: "Kelly had opened her mouth to offer to watch Neva when she looked at the other woman's face. Glazed eyes and all, Neva's focus was only on Macario. She wanted the pack leader. Alpha girl hadn't scared her off. Kelly closed her mouth." (Thus abandoning her emotionally vulnerable & recently traumatised friend to an entire werewolf pack they've met a few minutes beforehand and the aggressive experienced alpha female werewolf who has laid a prior claim to Macario.) Plot: "Everything depends on me and my freaking flute." (Despite an entire page of dialogue discussing how the opposite was true.... and then she proceeds to find a series of excuses for not having said flute at the ready anyway.) Pure Wtfuckery: "Ty sat on the couch eating his meal. He wore a clean pair of jeans. She had a brief but intense underwear moment. Was he wearing any?"

3.5 stars I received a free digital copy from the author/publisher via Netgalley in exchange for an honest review Portia White has always been in the shadow of her smarter, prettier twin Alex until one day something odd happens and Portia finds herself transported to Ancient Egypt where she finds out she has the magic power of Heka. When Portia realises Alex and another girl Selene have also been transported, they must figure out what's going on and how to get home. From the get go, i just really liked Portia and I think I really connected with her doubts in her self belief and self worth and her new struggles to connect with her twin and best friend when they suddenly want different things. I feel like Portia had some really great character development in this book and I really saw her grow as she came into her powers and really became a leader for Alex and Selene in a way she had never been before. I didn't really like Alex and the obsession with 'twinning' and I actually just wanted her to get lost most of the time (would have totally preferred her to have just stayed in the other world). I liked Portia's older sister relationship with Selene and how they protected each other, it was lovely to read and unlike Alex, I liked Selene who also had some great character development throughout. There were some bits abut the Heka and the Star that I think at one point went over my head so at times, I was a bit confused about what was going on but I think it might have been cause I was slightly ill when reading so my attention probably wavered a bit at that point. I really loved Portia's relationship with Merenptah/Seti. I thought they seemed to have a genuine chemistry and especially the second time they meet there is just so much chemistry, I was begging them to kiss! I thought the second last chapter ended really abruptly and I would have liked it to have been wrapped up a little bit better. I am presuming there's going to be another book coming out in this series/trilogy and will definitely be reading!

This story is so captivating and spot on it's scary. It shows a perfect outline what the world could become if technology develops past a certain level and everything is perfectly controlled by officials. In an environment that guarantees health, safety and security as long as you play by the rules, would you dare to question the establishment? Would you accept that everything is determined for you? Where you live, whom you love, the moment you die? For us it's hard to imagine to be taken away the most precious thing we have, our free will and the possibility to choose. And then to finally realise that there are options, just that you're never allowed to pick one because it's done for you. I can't even consider a world where there are only a hundred poems to read, one hundred songs and so on. And it makes me wonder: If it was me, would I speak up? Would I dare to be brave? It's easy to say of course from your safe reading cushion, but is it really? And that's the best quality of this book. It makes you wonder. As a former student of literature I adored the way Dylan Thomas was woven into the story, especially this poem. Let the artist read his masterpiece to you, it is amazing, the perfect villanelle and in general a wonderful poem. Do not go gentle into that good night read by Dylan Thomas. And now I can hardly wait for Crossed. Run, don't walk, to get this book if you haven't already.

Actual Rating: 3.5 Stars Depending on where you began this story... As much as I love this book, and the rest of the series, I can't help thinking that I wanted more from The Raven King. Don't get me wrong; I loved most of the book, and am satisfied with the ending. As always, I adored Stiefvater's writing, which is so poetic and fluent and metaphorical and enchanting, and I loved the characters and their relationships. However, I also felt that there were lots of loose ends that needed to be tied up. One of the things I didn't like about this book was the lack of Noah. I wasn't expecting a miracle for him (but was hoping for one) and I felt as though he was forgotten by everyone. I know that Maggie did this to show that the living have to move on from death and continue with their lives, but we didn't even get a mention of him in the epilogue. I don't like the idea that his four best friends didn't mourn him or notice he was gone - which probably isn't the case at all. I wished we had seen the effect of his absence in everyone's lives, but all in all Noah deserved better. Another thing I had a problem with was Henry. I really liked his character individually, but I felt as though he had replaced Noah in the group. I was also hoping that Gansey's story would end differently. It was very predictable that he wouldn't stay dead, but that didn't stop me from crying my eyes out, and I didn't want him to die for good, but, I just wanted more from this. It's hard to explain and I don't fault Maggie for this. Another thing I can't accept is that Glendower is dead. How? There were meant to be three sleepers, and only two were found (unless Artemis counts as one but I don't think so). Since the first book, I thought that Gansey was Glendower, so I can't fathom how he had been dead for years. The epilogue: I loved it but it was far to short. I wanted to see everyone together again, talking, but instead we have them all going their separate ways. I wanted another Gansey POV. Will everyone still be friends in the future? Did they talk about Noah? Did the Gray man and Maura get their happy ending? Is Blue still cursed? SO MANY QUESTIONS!! What I did like about The Raven King was Adam and Ronan's relationship. These two deserve so much happiness and I am so thrilled at how their relationship evolved. I also loved Blue and Ronan's relationship, which I feel is very unappreciated. These two are absolute gold together. They have come so far and every little bit of banter between them is perfect. In my opinion, The Raven King is a lot darker than the others in the series, and I loved how Maggie can write about Gansey hearing the bees, for example, and it can be far more thrilling and heart-pounding than an action sequence in other novels. Overall I enjoyed this book very very much and I would DEFINITELY recommend this series to everyone. The Raven Cycle is one of the best series I've ever read. ** spoiler alert ** I have to say, I'm pleasantly surprised. I avoided reading this series for years. Honestly, I just didn't think that I would enjoy them. Historical books for me are either a hit or a miss and the last few that I had read, had been big misses for me. Once, I finally broke down and got The Luxe from my local library, I actually couldn't wait to start reading it. There was something about it that was all of a sudden calling my name and I ended up skipping it ahead of some books and starting it before schedule (lol). And I couldn't put it down.... Oh, what a tangled web of lies, deceit, gossip and heartbreak Anna Godbersen has weaved for us within this book. I actually had to but the book aside at one point and make a list. I put all the names of the main characters and connected them to: who loved who, who was backstabbing who, etc., just so that I could keep everything straight. The Luxe is told from 5 different POV's. 4 girls and 1 boy. And while I have read a book told in 5 different POV's before and found it rather confusing, Anna did it in a way that it was absolutely essential to the story, to be told by all of them. Each character is so destintely different from one another, that there is no way to get them confused (or be confused about whose POV you are currently residing in). While I didn't really enjoy the character of Elizabeth, she was just way to weak willed for me throughout most of the book, she did finally win some credit for herself after what she did at the end (even if I did see it coming from practically the beginning of the book). Penelope played a good scorned lover, but there is no love lost for me on her. The same for Lina, who was just a back stabbing lady, who couldn't be happy with what she had, she wanted it all and more. My favorite female in this book by far would have to be the little sister, Diana. She was full of life and not afraid to try and life her life the way she wanted it, despite what other may have thought of her (she reminded me a lot of myself). I hope to get more depth with Henry's character, but for now he is just floating down the middle for me, I neither love nor hate his character. I must also give Anna props on doing her research, because I couldn't really find anything out of place that made me feel like I wasn't back in time. Like I wasn't in 1899, because from the very first page, I felt like I was traveling back to the past and experiencing these ladies lifes as they struggled to overcome everything and have the world at their beck and call. I already have Rumors (got it from the library today) waiting on myself to be read, to see what happens next in this exciting series. Who will back stab who next? Who will try to ruin who next? Who will fall in love with who next? Will Elizabeth be found? I can't wait to find out. The joys of a library book. Crazy how people feel they must write in a book that doesn't belong to them. LOL.

1.5/5 -- "...it was like her daddy always said--sometimes you get what you want, but mostly you get what you get." Well, we got what we got. This review contains spoilers. I delayed writing a review for this. I was disappointed, and I didn't want to talk about it. The story within Sleeping Beauties is muddy, tiring, and boring. By about the 250-page mark, I just wanted to get through it. It's a book about a plague, but there's no thrill or suspense. There's a surplus of characters, and they're mostly flat. The narration did nothing to help the situation, either. Let's start with that. There is no distinct voice. It does not read like a Stephen King novel. People wanted a Stephen King novel. His charming, even seductive, style is absent. I was prepared for this to an extent. He was working with another writer, after all. However, his collaboration with Owen diluted Stephen's writing to a point of monotony and paralysis. Like I said, it doesn't read like a King novel--it reads like some poor sap's attempt to mimic a King novel, and he failed. Anyone familiar with SK will recognize the writing as distinctly non-King. It doesn't sound anywhere close to his style. Owen cannot emulate his father even when he writes with him. He needs to break away and hone his own voice. The characters are copious and uninteresting. There is very little depth. The main antagonist is annoying and vague. Many criticize the villain in Doctor Sleep for similar reasons, but Rose the Hat is Iago compared to Evie. If you're going to create an illusive, enigmatic villain, you have to make up for her reticence with something else. Evie had nothing else. If you give us a 700-page novel with dozens of characters, make us care about some of them, whether they're good, bad, or both. If there's no interest in them, we surely don't give a rip about what they do. And in the story, of course, from these dull ranks, cadres form to fight one another. I won't call any of them a ka-tet, as they don't deserve that title. Usually when forces converge to fight at the height of a story, you know who you're rooting for. Not here. I didn't care. Simply put, there's an overflow of characters who aren't sufficiently fleshed out, which usually isn't a problem for a King novel--The Stand is the best evidence. In that book, for just one example, King devotes a single page to a man who loses his whole family and then runs until he dies. He was never mentioned again, but it added to the story, and I actually felt for the guy. I didn't care--Have I said that enough?--what happened to anyone in Sleeping Beauties. The meager connections to the characters that are offered turn out to be flimsy, like strings of wet, moldy yarn. Everything in this book has been done by SK before, only much better in those past examples. It's as if we're always looking at these townsfolk from the outside. Reading this book is like walking through a low fog, deceptive and almost familiar, like a dream you've had many times before. But, this time, when the dream returns, you're in your sickbed, parched and woozy, desiring nothing but to wake and be well and shake your head of that pestering dream. Stephen knows how to suck us right into the hearts and minds of his creations, and does so subtly; before we know it, very quickly, often before we realize it. That does not happen here. Not even close. From the interview with Stephen and Owen, it appears that the latter probably wrote most of this stuff. I appreciate the message he tries to pack into the mess. Women are given the chance to start a new world without men. Well, without any of the current men--we do have some pregnancies in Our Place. Everyone tries to decide the fate of the women who have gone over, as well as those remaining in our world. Owen clearly wanted to address the concept of individualism and identity in relation to a person's sex, and how that goes on in a society. Particularly, the rights of women and choice. Well, good for you, man. But, next time, leave your dad out of it. We read his books for fun. This book isn't fun at all.

I wish there was a 4 1/2 star category, because that's what I'd give this funny and entertaining story. It's about a man who can be perceived as simply highly scientific, intelligent, detail-oriented but who actually has Asperger's syndrome. This author has completely captured the personality of this character in the most delightful way, and the reader can't help but cheer for him and cringe over his social errors even while understanding why he makes them. Rosie is the perfect fit for him, a young woman who would like to know the identity of her biological father. Since the narrator, Don Tillman, is a geneticist, he's perfectly equipped to help. Rosie comes with her own baggage, and the fact that she has trouble trusting men makes Don, someone who hasn't the slightest notion how to tell a lie, a perfect fit for her, too. At the same time it's almost hard to imagine that it'll work out--the obstacles are set up so well in this perfectly structured story. Since most of the books on my shelf are clean reads, Christian stories, I wanted to add that the language in this is unnecessarily bad, but if you can overlook that this is a very entertaining story. And even though Don is an atheist and the author mustn't be aware there is a growing number of Christians who believe Creation began billions of years ago, the conclusion reached on Claudia's behalf about the importance of marital fidelity was most welcome.

Now my Divergent journey is officially complete. This was actually a pretty good behind the scenes alternate perspective collection -- it was definitely interesting to see the pre-Divergent stuff happening and beginning to happen in Dauntless through Four's perspective, limited though it might have been.
