This review of mine sort of summarizes the book, certainly a big spoiler, I must warn you (: Caleb Becker has just been released from jail, and he longs for that moment to come. But Margaret Armstrong doesn't. She wishes he would stay in jail until she escapes to Spain to study. Afterall, he was the person whom went to jail as he was the person responsible for knocking her down with a car, causing the problem in her knee. Or so she thought. Margaret, also known as Maggie, had crush on Caleb before she had the accident with him. They had been next door neighbours, and Maggie was best friends with his sister, Leah. But he was dating Kendra, someone Maggie felt was not worthy of Caleb. On the night of the accident, Maggie told Caleb then Kendra had been cheating on him with his best friend, Brian. During that same time, Maggie confessed to him, telling him that she's the true one for him, and told him to stop believing Kendra. But Caleb refused to listen. I mean, of course. He even told Maggie off for 'talking bad' about his girlfriend. Then they meet again, for the first time after Caleb had been released. It was at Paradise Park, and Maggie had been shocked to see him there. She wasn't ready for it, not at all. When she tried to stand to get away from him, she stumbled and he automatically tried to help her up. But she jerked him away. After all, she wasn't over that accident yet. He caused her to become that state, and she wanted him to know that. She just didn't understand that the fact had been imprinted in him, and she didn't need to remind him almost everytime. [ IMO: At this part of the story, I felt that Margaret might have been a little childish towards the situation of facing Caleb. But afterall, I have never been knocked down by anyone so my unfeelingness may be because of that. But it was seriously meaningless to want Caleb to "repay his debt towards her". He had his punishment, and he was willing to apologize. Maggie was a little unreasonable, but still. ] A letter arrives for Maggie, and that same letter dashed any hopes of her leaving Paradise for Spain. The scholarship had been revoked because she applied for an athelic one, and seeing that she had not been active for the past year, she was 'disqualified'. It was upseting, because she really wanted to escape Caleb and everything that made her the loser she was. Then she had a job opportunity, to work for Mrs Reynolds as her companion. She had been working well at Mrs Reynolds, until Caleb comes to the house for the community service program. Maggie falls onto the ground when she sees Caleb, and refuses to be helped up by him. [IMO: It was supposed to be natural of Maggie to react that way, but I felt irritated at this point of time. Caleb may have knocked her down before, but Margaret Armstrong was a little too cowardy. A little too stiff. ] She said some harsh things to him, and then told him what to do. It was silent, but I guess both liked it that way. When Margaret realizes she has to work with Caleb for another few weeks while he builts the Gazebo, she freaks out. Like seriously. She runs, hides, and cries. [IMO: all the acts of a coward.] There are her thoughts about how she tried forgiving Caleb but failed, and how she felt glad about his misery. But finally she allows him to stay, the condition being, 1. He can't tell others, and 2. She ignores him, and he should do the same. Caleb agrees, willing to do anything to get out of the shit he was in. But then something happens [IMO: something that kinda changes Maggie's opinion of Caleb, and things change for the better, so I'm only going to have good things to say from here~ ] Vic Medonia was picking a fight with Caleb and dragged Maggie in somehow. Caleb protected Maggie, and Magge really appreciated it. But things weren't that good for Caleb yet. Tristan, Drew, Brian and himself go to Tristan's house for a guys Sunday afternoon together, with the "no chicks allowed" rule. But Tristan's mother was the stereotypical kind of mother, who wanted her son to not hang out with the ex-convict friend. After being 'chased' out of the house, Brian confessed to Caleb about seeing Kendra even before the accident with Maggie happened. [ IMO: Brian was sort of a wimp to me, and I never really liked him.] Caleb wants to end it with Kendra, but she turns up, and leaks to him that she knows his secret. So he gave in to her, letting himself get controlled. Sometime after, Maggie receives a call from her dad, and it made her cry because her dad obviously didn't give a damn about what happened in her life. She called Caleb, and they met. One thing led to the other and they kissed. Yeah, surprisingly, they kissed. That changed everything, awakening Maggies feelings for Caleb once again. Caleb got Maggie to play tennis again somehow, even though it was only ten balls, it was better than nothing. Vic tests Caleb patience once again, by messing with Maggie, and Caleb beats Vic in the wrestling competition to vent his anger. Then the secret Caleb had been hiding was told: Leah was the one who had knocked Maggie down. [ If you don't remember, Leah is Caleb's twin sister. ] There comes a situation where Maggie overheard Caleb lying to Kendra that he loves Kendra, not Maggie. Caleb had no choice, because he was being controlled by Kendra as she knew what happened that night. Maggie stormed off, thinking Caleb had played her. Caleb was told by Damon that Maggie had called and told Damon that Caleb was harassing her. He was angry, and when Maggie finds him, he kisses her hard, trying to scare her. When Caleb reaches home, he gets faced by his pathetic family. His parents don't believe him- his mother acting like nothing was wrong in the first place, trying to continue pretending everything's perfect. And his dad, gosh. His dad was a perfect example of a coward, a chicken. And damn, I really detested his father. And. His sister was a zombie. I pitied Caleb, I really did. It was unfair for him. It wasn't even his fault in the first place. So he packed and left the house. Maggie recalls that Leah had been the one driving. She finally recalled. Because she had been too afraid to remember the accident. She finds him and tries to get him to stay, but his mind was set on leaving, so she let him. The last words she say to him - "the red hen has flown the coop". But in the end, he never told her the truth about who really knocked her down. Leaving Paradise was a book I read that I didnt like at first, unfortunately. But as it progressed, I started to fancy the plot and it's characters. They developed well and it was indeed interesting for me. I have always loved Simone Elkeles writings, and this book just prove my point. It may not be as exciting as "Perfect Chemistry" or "Rules of Attraction", but it's certainly a book you would want to read finish when you start.

4.5 stars A feel good ending seems to be a trend in Sarah Dessen's books, and I hope that's something that continues as I work through her back list. Lock and Key was another solid offering from the author, bringing so many emotions to the surface. I love idea that for Ruby, who's had a tough time of it, there's hope waiting just around the corner. It was always just Ruby and her mom trying to make ends meet, but when her mother disappears, Ruby decides to go it alone. When her landlords finally catch on to the fact that Ruby's been abandoned, social services steps in and reunites her with Cora, the older sister she hasn't seen in years. I absolutely loved the dynamic between Ruby and Cora, from the past, to the present, to what would come. It's clear there's apprehension on both sides, fostered unknowingly (to them) by their mother. It doesn't help that Ruby already has a hard time trusting, and sliding into her new life and perceived expectations wasn't easy. There was a great cast of secondary characters in this book, but my favorite was Cora's husband, Jamie. I love how he took to Ruby immediately, almost oblivious to how discomforted she felt and plopping her right into their home as if she'd always been there. He was a genuinely good guy, and I think he was a big reason why Cora and Ruby were able to find their way to being a family again. Ruby's hot neighbor, Nate, was her opposite in every way. While she was always waiting for the other shoe to drop, Nate liked to see the positive in things. It never occurs to Ruby that Nate's life might not be that great until she inadvertently overhears a conversation with his father. Ruby's inner struggle with what to do about Nate and his father was the perfect addition to the story. She goes back and forth between doing what she thinks is right, and what she wishes would have been done when her plight had been discovered. And again, like in Just Listen, the heroine's life didn't revolve around this boy; he was just another facet of her life. Gervaise, the middle school genius, Olivia, the friend that sort of wasn't, and Harriet and Reggie rounded out these colorful secondary characters, and they were fun to read about. They were all given a lot of depth without overwhelming the story, and I feel like they were a vehicle to the author showing us how in tune Ruby was to the people around her. Even with her own problems, she never missed a beat with those she (even begrudgingly) cared about. I loved the significance of the title, Lock and Key, and how it came to mean something different to Ruby as time went on. I also enjoyed the school project that was a backdrop of sorts to this story as Ruby tries to define what 'family' really is. I listened to the audio version of this book, and I enjoyed it very much. The narrator had great intonation and really brought the characters to life. I did have to adjust the speed a bit, but that doesn't bother me, as it's something I usually have to do. Not everything was wrapped up in a pretty little package in this story, and I liked that, especially given the characters ages. Overall, I thought this was a wonderful story of finding yourself where you least expect it, and how sometimes it pays to give something a chance. I think Sarah Dessen was a great choice to hold myself to my goal of adding more YA to my reading schedule. Below is a list of the books I hope to read from her this year. If there are any you think should be moved up the list, let me know. Like every reader, I'm always on a quest for the next great book! This review was originally posted at Badass Book Reviews.

this could have been so good. i don't rightly know how to rate this because it had some real strong moments which were alas mixed with very disappointing authorial choices. very strong beginning, interesting characters. love owen. i really appreciate characters who grapple with serious issues, and i like personal growth and happy endings for people with a lot stacked against them. loved nick's sister june; what a force of nature, and what a wonderful way to open a door for owen to come out of his own, sad, self-limited life. there was some really good stuff in there about disability, and how difficult it can be to handle sensibly even for people of good will. it looked like a great 5-star story. but then nick dropped his bomb shell. and my opinion of him went through the floor. not because of the bomb itself, but because of the timing. sorry; not negotiable. this is something you talk about before getting intimate. and completely unnecessary to the plot. because nick's fears? make sense. even though we now know a lot more than we did in the 80s (though i wonder whether marie sexton does; there was some weird conflation going on). it stretches believability because nick's a vet and has medical knowledge, but sure, his irrational mind might still not have caught up with his reason. but then what the hell is he doing with owen? one of the tropes i do not ever buy in romance is that we're slaves to our overwhelming sex drives. no. we're not. if we were, that would be a great excuse for rape and all sorts of other atrocities. we can damn well control ourselves. if nick really cared about owen, he would have controlled himself. he would have talked instead of getting physical and then blowing cold all the time. so in one swell foop marie sexton made me dislike one of the main characters in a romance. that's a death knell. everything from then on was a mess. and it overshadowed how much i liked owen and june. owen's mother -- there's a tough thing to assess in a short romance. to the people who thought her unbelievable per se: oh, i wish. that's my mother right there. and my father (minus the same back story). contrary to owen i dumped the lot of them at 17, but i know too many people who put up with utterly cruel and despicable parents all their lives, so i can't blame owen for not manning up sooner. if you've never met someone like that, consider yourself lucky, but also sheltered. yet in the context of this romance, i agree she was probably too much. it wasn't necessary to paint her this black; she could have crippled owen's self-esteem without being so relentless. i generally don't like pure good/evil characters; they're just not very interesting. the ending -- what the heck? was that supposed to be a pun? dear marie, did you want me to dislike owen as well? what did regina ever do to him? she didn't ask to star in his -- wholly inappropriate and misguided -- fantasies. did he ever even correct her when she got his name wrong? no, that ending was a total miss. usually such solid writers who i basically had on auto-buy, but this series is not making me happy. after reading 6 of the books in this series i am thinking riptide needs a much stronger editor. yeah, i know, none of these small publishing houses can actually afford a good editor, one of those cranky, chain-smoking, NYC types with a massive red pen and an unerring nose for turning the so-so into something shiny.

In this golden age of young adult literature, there are two distinctive audiences: the young people the books are intended to be read by, and the older generation who, perhaps beguiled by the excellence of the sub genre over the past couple of decades, have continued to read YA well into adulthood. I am one of these. When I read a YA novel, I try to evaluate it on two levels: would I have enjoyed it as a kid reader, and do I enjoy it now? There have been a number of books that meet the first criteria while being problematical for the second. This is not one of those books. I can see my teenage self reading this book by the light of the streetlamp down the street, well after my parents had gone to bed, because I couldn't stand to stop until I reached the finish. Magic! History! History of places not usually written about! Mythology! A pirate ship! A girl navigating the pirate ship! A girl who feels like an outsider in her own family -- her own troubled family -- who has her own goals and enough smarts to go after them. And of course a cute guy or two, who do not overwhelm the story. The adult me appreciated the vivid depictions of different cultures during various points in history, especially when overlaid with a palimpsest of mythological possibilities. I was fascinated by the glimpse of Hawaii in the 1880s, even knowing that the kingdom was doomed thanks to the greed of American entrepreneurs. The author demonstrates the cost without hammering the point home, all while keeping the action brisk, and the threats real. Nix Song, half-Hawaiian daughter of an American man who discovered he could navigate to other times and places if he had the right maps, and Lin Song, a Hawaiian woman, is afraid she will be erased from history altogether if her father's obsessive search for a map to take him back to Hawaii before Lin died, so he can rescue her, is successful. In much YA these days, one of the most common tropes is what is now called the love triangle. This is not new. I remember rival guys in stories back when I was a teen reader. They seem to be part of the expected landscape now, but I liked what the author did here: Nix does not want to get involved. Having grown up with her father's obsession, she is skeptical at best about the addiction of love. Very refreshing! And I liked the guys: artistic Blake, who loves Hawaii in spite of his deeply troubled family, and insouciant, clever, funny, compassionate and passionate thief Kashmir. I like Nix's wrestle with normal teen responses to cute guys, and her determination not to be suckered into surrendering her life to those responses. And I really loved the plot. I think if I had one criticism, it would be That Nix unaccountably never tells her father her quite understandable fear though they had several very raw and real conversations toward the end but that was small, as the overall unfolding of the story was so satisfying. Full of insightful observations and deftly descriptive character moments, I enjoyed this book enough to put it on my keeper shelf, old as I am. And as a kid, I expect it would have been among those I checked out repeatedly.

It is pretty ironic that the title It's Kind of a Funny Story is actually not true. I understand that Craig could say it is a funny story at how he got to Six North, but really it is not. The story does involve comedy but I do not find smoking pot, attempting suicide and not eating in any way funny, those are serious issues that people like that should go to Six North. When I searched online to find the cover I came across movie posters for It's Kind of a Funny Story. At first I thought they might have been fan art but it turns out in 2010 they made a movie based off of It's Kind of a Funny Story. I watched the trailer for the movie and it seems like a decent movie, but not a good book to movie adaptation. With next weekend being Thanksgiving weekend and the beginning of hunting season, I will most likely watch the movie with how much school I have off (yes, that is right my school district lets us off for hunting season, that tells you something about where I live). It was interesting to see that Craig had different words for what he liked and disliked. Tentacles were bad things or things he did not want to do. On the other hand, Anchors were good things that he enjoyed doing. It was also interesting to see his Tentacles and Anchors change throughout the novel. The cover was brilliant. At first when Craig said he enjoyed drawing maps as a kid, I figured it was a map, end of story. But it is not just a map. In Six North he started to draw maps again, but not your normal street map. He started making head maps of fellow Six North patients. I am assuming that this head map on the cover is of Craig's head. Also, It's Kind of a Funny Story is split into 10 parts. Each of the 10 parts have their own piece in Craig's head map. It was a fantastic idea by whoever designed the cover art. Six North is an adult psychiatric ward on the sixth floor of the Argenon Hospital. Both teenagers and adult patients have to stay there due to renovations on the kids floor. At Six North, Craig meets many people. Almost none of them are normal, but in this book normal is over rated. Craig meets Noelle, Bobby, Muqtada, Jennifer/Charles, Humble, President Armelio and so many more odd characters. For about the first 100-150 pages of the book it was very slow paced and I quit reading it for long periods of time because it did not interest me. Not until Craig got into the ER did the plot speed up and become more interesting. I highly doubt I will reread this book because, frankly, I do not have the time to be mad at this book for the first 100-150 pages. In addition to losing my interest, those pages were extremely depressing. The message that Ned Vizzini seemed to be pointing at is that no matter how many issues or problems you have, there will be someone else that has it worse. Overall, It's Kind of a Funny Story was a decent book, I would only recommend this book if you are a very patient person, to wait the first 100-150 pages until the plot picks up. But the message of the story is reflective. If any of you readers have read this, what was your opinion of the book?

Easily the worst (non-Mercy Thompson) book I've read thus far in 2014. A cliched stumble through space adventure written with all the subtlety of a kick to the head. Fortune's Pawn probably would have been unobtrusive in its infodump-ridden banality had the heroine not been so freaking awful. Devi talks up her military/mercenary background and alleged competence but finds it impossible to think ahead or solve issues without trying to punch them away. She whines like a five-year-old about the jobs she's assigned on The Glorious Fool, as though basic ship chores are beneath her. She also finds it very difficult to follow simple orders or spend time around other people without being a judgmental asshole. Unless they happen to be a handsome-but-distant man, of course. The blurb tries to sell Devi as a combination of Starbuck and Ripley, but she has more in common with your average shit tier paranormal romance heroine than any classic space badass. This story is a predictable romance with a few pieces of sci-fi window dressing. While the plot dictates that once every chapter or so Devi must try to investigate various mysteries related to The Glorious Fool and her crew, she otherwise spends every possible free moment swooning after the resident mysterious dreamboat. I mean sure Rupert does things like sneak into her locked room when she's unconscious and leer over her helpless body BUT HE'S HOT SO IT'S OK. Rest assured that when the bare bones story doesn't force Devi to take some vague degree of action, she'll revert to her default state - staring at Ruprt's emotionally unavailable dreaminess. Wait, I lie. That's only her default state for the first half of the book. As the story plods along, Devi becomes increasingly smitten with Rupert's dreary face. So much so that she somehow becomes even less competent than she was at the start of the book and goes into full I WOULD SACRIFICE MYSELF FOR HIM mode. I'm still scraping pieces of vomit off my monitor. Thanks, Fortune's Pawn.

I have given in. But that's different from giving up. I do enjoy reading about little geniuses. They are so adorable with their grandma language and their serious dispositions. I love how even though some adults dismiss these brainiacs others are in awe of them. Willow is a solitary little creature. I was so glad for her when she made friends with the contrary Vietnamese siblings. Mai Nguyen is a wonderful and lively character. She is 14 and a real handful. I loved her big heart and how she tries to take charge of everything. She's so mature and yet so adorable. Willow's life changes irrevocably when she loses her parents. For someone grieving, moving forward is the challenge. Because after extreme loss you want to go back. This trauma causes Willow to dial back and withdraw into herself. She gives up some of her interests and hobbies. She is most certainly not listless, but her curiosity for life is somewhat diminished. I don't make a chart and monitor the percentage of germination, because I don't do that anymore. I really appreciated all the characters. Dell Dell is not a bad person. First, let me stress that up to this point, I have loved everything I've read by Neil Gaiman. Love Coraline. Love The Graveyard Book. Love Odd and the Frost Giants. Now, add in the fact that the film version of Stardust is my most favorite movie, ever. EVER. I really should have known that there was no way I would like this book--there was too much love happening. Something was bound to go wrong. I had actually tried to read this once before and only made it partway into the first chapter before I realized that I really didn't like it. I decided to try it again because I do love Neil Gaiman, and I thought to myself, "Why not?" What I should have answered was, "Because you vehemently disliked it the first time, dummy." And yeah, the movie is better. How? Let me count the ways... 1) The film presents a much tighter story overall. It eliminates unnecessary characters, backstories, and random bits of information without losing anything important to the plot. 2) All of the movie characters win, except maybe Yvaine. Book Tristran (and props on changing that to Tristan, movie) never convinced me that he'd grown up and was deserving of Yvaine. Book Septimus was completely and utterly uninteresting. Book Witch Queen (Lamia in the movie) was nowhere near as deliciously evil as she is in the film. Film Yvaine and Book Yvaine are both annoying, but Film Yvaine because she's a pushover, and Book Yvaine because she's just plain old obnoxious--so we'll call that one a tie. 3) The flying pirate ship is most definitely my favorite part of the movie, so I was really excited to read it. Imagine my disappointment when I realized that it was apparently entirely rewritten for the movie. The setting is different, the characters are different (I wanted to read about my favorite flamboyantly gay pirate, dammit), and the adventure is nonexistent. They're barely on the ship for a chapter, and no lasting friendships are made. 4) The ending of the book is super anti-climatic.The film has a huge final battle with the Witch Queen, featuring voodoo dolls, zombies, swordfights, animals mauling someone, and a guy drowning without actually being in any water. In the book, they just happen to bump into the story's main antagonist, and she basically says, "I would've gotten away with it too, if it weren't for...something. Oh well, better luck next time." 5) When I read the book, I had a hard time swallowing Tristran and Yvaine being in love. It wasn't at all believable. 6) Many of the tiny, clever details that I love in the film (such as Primus' blood being blue) aren't even in the book. 7) The movie doesn't contain awkward and unnecessary descriptions of sex and gore. I mean, it does contain sex and gore, but it fits in the movie. In the book it's just...you get the feeling that when Neil Gaiman decided to write a fairytale for adults, he first wrote a fairytale, and then made it "adult" by sticking in some sex and violence. Who knows, maybe I would've like this better if I hadn't seen the movie first. Or, maybe I would've still disliked it. I am a sucker for a Hollywood ending, and there is none of that to be found here. So, heed my warning: If you like the film Stardust, just please--don't read the book. You'll wish you hadn't.

Alexia Tarabotti may only be a spinster with no soul but when a she is so rudely attacked by a pack of vampires she discovers just how useful being soulless is. With the ability to negate supernatural powers, she is asked by Lord Maccon, who has been sent by Queen Victoria to investigate what is actually happening with London's high society. Soulless is a book on social etiquette with a mixture of steampunk, werewolves, vampires, and tea-drinking. Admittedly, this is not something I would normally read but the mixture of steampunk and Victorian high society did seem to appeal to me. However I was reluctant to try something that sounded very much like paranormal romance. Being a literary explorer, sometimes you just have to suck it up and read something way out of your comfort zone. I know I haven't read many chick lit/romance novels so I thought maybe it was time to give Soulless ago. One thing I did enjoy about this book was the Victorian elements; Gail Carriger is an archaeologist and it feels like she has taken all the elements from Victorian literature and society, mixed it with her love of science fiction and formed what she likes to call Urbane Fantasy. The Victorian and steampunk elements really help drive this book for me; although I'm sure Jane Austin would be shocked to read this book. Then you have the werewolves, vampires and the soulless which I really did hate, I would have much rather read a book like this without paranormal elements and maybe replacing it with a mystery element. That way everything plot wise could still work barring some minor changes. But I have to accept paranormal novels are big sellers and they won't be going anywhere anytime soon. It just doesn't work for me; I don't think I can continue the series. Overall this book felt too predictable with the romance and the rest was just too cutesy. I like that this novel had a strong heroine like Alexia but there was too much of a struggle between what I liked and hated to really enjoy this book in any form. I know there is a lot of love for this series out there and I'm sorry to say I wasn't able to love this book. I was glad it was a quick read. There is a lot of wit and humour in this novel but it wasn't enough. I'm not going to continue this series but I might give one of Gail Carriger's Etiquette and Espionage a go, even if it is set in the same universe, it does look interesting. ***I received an e-galley of this book from NetGalley in exchange for an honest review*** After seeing the cover of this book and reading the summary, I was so glad that I was approved by Little Brown via NetGalley to read an ARC! The cover is so lovely. I really like that the picture is simple, but at the same time pretty. And I love the font used for the title! I really liked this take on Witches. I really found their abilities and how they do magic/charms very interesting. The Story: I really like that the story wasn't only about what was happening to the characters in the story, but also about the history of the island and the Roe witches. I think the author did a great job at including a lot of background and information while not overshadowing the plot and storyline. I really like the setting and the descriptions. There were times where I wished I could be on this island, seeing what the characters would be seeing. I like that there was a mystery feel to the story as well. I was very interested in the mysterious dream that the main character, Avery, kept having. I also really enjoyed the mystery surrounding the other characters. I felt like they all were mysterious in their own ways. I had fun trying to figure out what was going on with those characters individually and how it relates to Avery. For most of the book, I was left guessing what would happen next. But around the middle of the story, I made a guess for what I thought would happen and ended up being close. But it didn't take away from me enjoying the book. And it definitely did not keep me from feeling emotions about the events and the ending. The Characters: I think that the characters are well written with well-developed backstories. I found them to be very fascinating characters and I enjoyed learning more about them as the story progressed. Avery is interesting, determined, and at times stubborn. But I really like that she knew what it was she wanted and that she would do whatever she could to fight to achieve it. Tane is a very mysterious character. While reading the story, I kept thinking about how there was so much more I wanted to know about his character. I was very happy with the development and found his backstory to be captivating. Avery's Mother is a frustrating character for me. We view her from Avery's POV (point of view) and as a reader I could feel the anger and frustration that Avery had for her mother. My Recommendation: If you like reading about witches and like informational stories, then I would recommend giving this book a read. The story was fascinating and mysterious. I liked the characters and the island. This review can also be found on my blog: My Bookish Itinerary This review was first published on my old blog: Her Reviews of Books Movies and Everything.

Stolen Songbird reminded me of Claire B. Dunkle's The Hollow Kingdom. Both protagonists are kidnapped by a magical species for marriage and eventually grow to find love in their consorts. Between the two, however, I much preferred The Hollow Kingdom. Stolen Songbird has poor world building, plot development, and character development. This comes down to an execution of details. Many important pieces of information are either omitted or introduced late. As a result, it takes time to the pieces together into a cohesive story. Furthermore, the story dives into the action close to the beginning without taking the time to set up the world or the main characters, so it takes a while before adequate information is introduced for us to understand what is going on. The characters are also poorly developed. I never really felt like I got to know any of the characters, much less Cecile and Tristan even though they take turns narrating the story. It didn't help that there didn't seem to be a pattern to the narration switches; many scenes seem to be a poor attempt to develop suspense but weren't fleshed out enough to contribute much to plot development. Overall, Stolen Songbird fell flat for me. If you're looking for a cross-species romance, I would recommend The Hollow Kingdom, which also happens to be a trilogy (with each book focusing on a different character and further exploring the world). A book with a great start that unfortunately ends with a fallacious conclusion. At the end of the ninth chapter, the author asserts that there would be twice as many hockey players if we had two cut off dates. This is ridiculous. It would of course mitigate the bias of age (i.e. what month you are born would not have such a big impact on getting selected). At best we would have marginally better players (though it is quite possible that some other arbitrary cutoff would replace the old one). There can be only so many NHL teams and therefore so many professional players. He also asks, what if a million teenagers had access to the same advantages as Bill Gates, how many Microsoft would we have today? Well, it's quite obvious from his own argument that if so many had the same advantages, Bill would simply no longer be an outlier, and there would probably be no Microsoft. (This is not necessarily a bad thing, the combined contributions to society from these teenagers might be greater than those of Microsoft, a company with dubious achievements). Ultimately the biggest let down is that this book frustratingly refuses to address the subject of inequality. If outliers are, basically, those who got lucky among those who were capable, then what implication does this have for social policy? Is it reasonable that these outliers amass extraordinary amounts of wealth when fundamentally their contributions are the result of chance (not exclusively, of course. Outliers are all hard working individuals, my point here is about the difference in renumeration compared to other similar yet not as lucky individuals). Tyrants are outliers as well. And we could do without them.

I think this gets three-and-a-half stars, but it's a rather special 3.5, so I don't want to put up either 3 or 4. It's a faltered-in-the-execution 3.5, but of one of my favourite types of book (of any genre): the really funny book that is also saying something about life, or emotions or relationships. Devine Intervention didn't quite manage to pull off funny - except in spots - and it seemed to make its own job of dealing with the real stuff much harder by the framework built around the funny. Starting with Jerome's story: he's assigned to be Heidi's guardian angel as a last-ditch attempt to save him from one of the 9 layers of Hell, in SRPNT (the Soul Rehabilitation Program for Nefarious Teens (Deceased)). A total screw-up in death as well as life, he never bothered to read the handbook for guardian angels, and muddles along talking to Heidi whenever he feels like it, despite this being absolutely against the rules. There are sections from the handbook, and these are quite funny for their big-business, management style language, and alternate Ten Commandments. SRPNT is very like a comic school for misbehaving teens, and is fun, as far as that goes. But the problem with this is that increasingly we see there's not much reason for Jerome to be viewed as such a nearly lost soul. It becomes clear very quickly that his view of himself as bad news was something he had from earliest childhood, and it was Not. His. Fault. (I still get sad thinking about his father, whose story is full of pathos, for all he failed Jerome as a parent.) He did one really rotten thing (to a cat) as a kid, but is absolutely remorseful about it, and cares about Heidi, even if he can't always give her the best advice - so, why is Hell even a possibility? As well as this, the reader is also clear on the fact that the *truly* bad teen in SRPNT with Jerome, who is out to hurt people (Jerome especiallY), isn't fooling the two angels in charge. But Jerome is convinced that if he goes to them for help, they'll view it as absolute failure and throw him straight into hell, so bumbles on alone. This is where I think the comic structure clashes with the emotional realities of the story being told. Heidi isn't having a great time in life, despite having her own "imaginary friend"/in-dwelling guardian angel, but she's got a great friend, perfectly fine parents, and gets lot of pleasure from drawing, so her rather fatalistic walking out onto unsafe ice to get her dog back made me doubt all the way through that Jerome should have been paying attention every second, in order to prevent her rather predictably falling through the ice. But when he can't get her into Heaven immediately, he assumes it's his fault, his responsibility, and there's the possibility that she will become one of the tiny number of truly lost souls - i.e. souls that simply dissipate. Again, I think the need for the comic set-up rather caused a misstep, as it required everyone to allow Heidi and Jerome to bumble about with the real possibility that Heidi's soul would be lost forever. It simply doesn't make sense that free will would apply to the actions of an angel who might bring about the permanent loss of another dead person's soul. Now obviously this isn't in any way a 'religious' book, and is certainly not meant to be read as an exploration of what an afterlife might be like. But it does express a fundamental understanding that THE important thing is how much people love others, and I thought the way the 10 Commandments for the Living built up in a serious counterpart to the comic ones for the dead was very effective: the 10th is "Thou shalt love, thou shalt love, though shalt love". This formed the heart of the book, and was shown in Jerome's continued care for Heidi's well-being even when he thought he was lost and love for his father, despite believing his father didn't love him, and for Heidi's increased understanding of how important her family and friends (and dog!) were, and how cared about them. The problem was that the edifice around this heart of the book wasn't as solid as it might have been.

I had problems getting into this book because I couldn't stop my mind from wandering. Maybe it's because the dynamics of the love story were slow in the beginning. So I needed to read more till I could really feel the story. I like the premise pretty much. And it's funny because it reminded me of But of course, there is a man in flesh at the other end, so, no worries ;) . This book is different in a way. The MC don't meet each other till the very end. And you could think... Or maybe you wonder "What can you do with only phone calls? So let's see the plot for a second. Cam is a workaholic who has just broken up with his boyfriend after 4 years of no-future relationship. Riley has been 3 years in a forever-alone mood since that day he burnt his face and arms. Destiny comes and their paths cross when Riley in a very low moment calls a sex phone number, and at the receiving end Cam answers in a very rude way. What begins as a misunderstanding turns into a friendship and the very thing that seemed shallow and stupid changes into deep feelings and thoughts. Soon the everyday call is the most shining time of their lives and Riley is fine that way, but Cam is not. Because Riley thinks this chemistry-without-pheromones is an illusion, and that this beautiful relationship will be erased the moment Cam sees his face. So, he prefers Cam as a friend in safe way than the uncertainty of a love story together. And he believes that will be enough, but of course, it's not. It's very romantic. In an old-school way. Like falling in love by letters. Like falling in love centuries ago, when the hand was the most you touched from that person. Falling in love with someone you have never touched. Falling in love with his voice, his wits, his personality, his way of thinking... It's true love. It felt so real I hurt with them both. Because Riley is not ready to come into the light, and Cam is dying for him to do it. The dialogues are superb, it's amazing the topics you can talk about or the things you can do together without knowing the other person's face, right? ;) I loved the humor and the jokes. But that's nothing if we compare those with some beautiful scenes, like the one in the theatre. Like the happy-birthday one. Not much angst but yes about love, cute and sweet and sincere. The end was perfect for me. I've read opinions saying it was very abrupt, but it didn't feel that way for me. It felt natural, epic and true. And it makes you wonder about their future together. So a book finishing in a open way but with no loose ends.

The White Tiger is the story of Balram Halwai, a small town boy living in the ' The Darkness' near the river bank of River Ganges. Belonging to a poor family, he has been raised to think and act as a servant. Man-Booker Prize winner Aravind Adiga takes us on a vivid journey as our protagonist moves from Dhanbad, to Delhi and to Nagpur while essaying the roles of servant, master, philosopher and murderer all in the length of a long letter to the Chinese President. I think I understand the many negative reviews the book has. But I absolutely disagree with them. I loved the book and quite enjoyed reading it. Fast paced, great narration and bizarre yet profound character pushed this book to my favourites list. With the base of a rags-to-riches story, The White Tiger,, brims with originality, humor, relevance and intellect. The writing is easy-flowing, amusing and gripping. On the surface,a simple tale, it is embellished with graphic characters. The book is probably offensive to every person in the world no matter what religion,caste,race or country they are from. So don't pick this book up if you are the kind of person who takes offence. I think the book would be enjoyed more if people stopped worrying about what picture of India is being painted through a novel which boldly tackles the economic inequality and disparity in our country and start appreciating the literary talent we have here. Kudos!

Guys, this book is so sad. I have never read such a tragedy in my life. Oh wait, no. It's not sad-sad, it's sad because it's so awful. When I heard that R.L. Stine was coming out with a new book, I about wet myself. Goosebumps was the second series I was ever involved in (first being Boxcar Children!) at age 8 or so. I still have every single Goosebumps novel ever written packed in my closet - I'm saving them for my own kids. That said, as an adult I recognize that Stine's not the best writer to grace children's fiction. But, you know, nostalgia and stuff. Anyway, this book is just so awful. Did Stine devolve as a writer, is he not cut out for adult fiction, or is it all because I grew up? The writing was just bad. The story itself isn't awful, especially since Stine specifically states in the acknowledgements that his story is based on horror movies (so he's giving credit where it's due.) But the writing itself... Lots of ellipses. Lots of very bad, oddly place ellipses. Like: "the leg...the leg...the leg came off." "And his eyes...his eyes...they were red." What?! That's not writing! There were also lots of unnecessary fragments. "He lost. He lost. He lost his mind." I also felt like there were SEVERAL typos, or missed editing thingies... like Martha, a minor character, mentions her 30 year old son, Ira. Then Ira turns out to be the name of a main character. Why would you use that same name twice? It confused me at first. The main male character also tells a story about a boy named Sammy, and then one of the other main characters is named Samuel. Do not recycle names like that! It's weird and unnecessary! It's also like Stine could only think of one or two adjectives. I wish I had kept count of how many times I read "creamy white [butt/breasts.]" Creamy white. Really? (As a side note, I wish I was creamy white. I'm more of a radioactive, ghostly glowing white.) The only thing that made this an adult horror novel is the addition of gore, extreme language and sex. The F word runs rampant throughout the novel in so many random moments. It reminded me of The Casual Vacancy by J.K. Rowling - Stine's proving he can write for adults by adding as many swear words as possible. The sex wasn't as bad, but it was present and graphic. The gore was very graphic, and not well written. Some people can write gore. Stine can't. I hold out hope that maybe he'll improve as he "grows up." I was just so disappointed by this novel. As one of Stine's biggest fans in childhood, this was a serious letdown. I'm sorry, Mr. Stine. I still hold fond memories of your books, but I'm just going to try and forget this one.

4/5 stars. Another great addition to the Star Harbor Series! This is the third book in this fantastic series. Although it can be read as a stand-alone, to get good background I recommend reading the previous two books. Plus, the other two books are great too! This book focusses on Cole Grayson. After his hell-raising teenage days, (along with the rest of the Grayson brothers) Cole enlists with the Army and spends 7 years in combat all over the world. After a significant injury, Cole returns stateside, becomes a police officer in Boston before returning to become the Sheriff of his childhood home of Star Harbor. Returning home forces him back into the life of Dr. Julie Kensington - the one girl Cole had feelings for in high school, but he never really acted on them. At first, Julie is reluctant to see Cole, and she avoids him at all costs. You see, the truth is that Julie always harbored feelings for Cole, but was too afraid that if she got close to him he would break her heart. Well, nearly 10 years later, the two finally begin to explore their mutual feelings. And wow, do sparks fly. The two have an undeniable chemistry and their relationship just flowed effortlessly. That's one of the things I love about this author's books - the relationships develop naturally and I enjoy watching the characters' feelings develop. Plus, there's always so much passion between the characters - definitely a steamy read! But, as Cole and Julie begin to get closer, and recognize their true feelings for each other, a serious threat to Julie's safety gets in the way, forcing the two apart. Can they each get over their pasts in order to realize their futures - together? As with the other books in the series, there's the whole pirate mystery element that I really like. I cannot wait to find out the full story behind the keys - *hint, hint Ms. Barett - please tell me this story is coming soon? There's also a lot of action as the drug-smuggling investigation continues from the previous book. Although the ending in this one felt a bit rushed - Can't a guy apologize without proposing marriage?? I really did enjoy this book. I love this series and definitely recommend it to those who haven't yet had the pleasure of meeting the Grayson boys!

Originally posted on The Daily Bookmark 4 / 5 Stars Hemlock is not your typical werewolf story. And it's not your typical love triangle either. Kathleen Peacock wove together a great story about a teen murder and how her friends coped (or didn't) with the loss. When we first meet Mac and her friends Jason and Kyle, it's after Amy's funeral. Amy was killed by a werewolf, a known disease called Lupine Syndrome. Once infected with LS, a person loses all of his/her rights as a human being and can be sent off to a rehabilitation camp for the remainder of their days. Amy haunts Mac's nightmares, spurring her to seek help and find out what really happened to her best friend. As it turns out, things aren't what they seem and after much scheming, tricking and general detective work, Mac begins to unravel her friends' lives. Apart of the story of Hemlock revolves around Mac and her so-called love life. Surprise, surprise, but it's a love triangle. Mac is torn between best-friend-since-forever Kyle or secretive-stormy-protective Jason. Throughout the story, their pros and cons are presented. From the outside, it would be an easy choice but, through Mac's perspective, it's understood why it was such a toss up. What bothered me a little was that (a) it was a love triangle to begin with and (b) all three of them bounced back and forth about their feelings on constant repeat. The character in Hemlock were extremely well fleshed out. The grief and pain and inability to cope with the loss of their best friend was heart-felt and raw emotion. I ached every time Mac was suddenly gripped with the loss as if it were brand new. Peacock did an excellent job of portraying these hard emotions. A lot of Hemlock made it such a great story. - What makes this so good is that it's a werewolf story, yes, but that part almost takes a backseat to the murder mystery. Mac is so desperate to find out what happened to Amy and it shows in her willingness to do anything and everything to get the truth, even if it means risking her own neck in the process. That carnal need for the truth reaches into the pit of your stomach and doesn't let go. - Peacock's werewolves were fantastic! They were menacing and angry and scary. And the descriptions of how they turned were bone-crushingly satisfying. The shift scenes were so great because you could actually get a real sense of how it all plays out, rather than a magic trick through smoke and mirrors as is so commonly seen. - The nightmares including Amy were also really gripping. Amy was dark and troubling as a nightmare should be. The pages feverishly turned themselves during these scenes, in part for the great writing and in part to get to the more upbeat scenes. There were a great many twists and turns, most of which proved unexpected and jaw-dropping. Some are relatively predictable but that's splitting hairs. Unfortunately, I did have a couple of hang-ups. - The murder mystery was great and Mac seeking the truth was awesome but it felt like many of the clues dropped themselves into her lap straight out of the sky. "Suddenly, Mac remembered (insert big plot switch-up of your choosing right here)..." I realize this may be unavoidable in places but it got a bit cumbersome. - Lupine Syndrome and the rehabilitation camps were mentioned, brushed on and left to the readers' imaginations to decide what that's all about. Fabulous, but I wanted more! How did LS come to be? How long has this been going on? What really happens at the camps? The questions piled on top of each other one after another without solid answers to follow up. I'm hopeful that book two will delve further into these issues. - The ridiculous cliffhanger at the end. That's all I'm going say about that. All around, I really liked Hemlock. I had a couple of issues, personally but it was a great, fast-paced and invigorating read. I'm greatly looking forward to seeing what's next for these fabulously created characters.

Before I even begin this review, let it be known that I'm rating this book on what was presented and not for the potential it had. Leonie Woodville is a 17 year old college student who had a rather reclusive life with her father, she is deemed anti-social from the start and as such is awkward as well as abrasive. Unbeknownst to her she is a CHOSEN, an individual with abilities of the elements. Except she's special she is the last PULSAR - a fire elemental. While Leonie didn't have a fantastic upbringing or an ideal life - as a rather horrible incident occurs - she is a rather unlikable character from the get go. Snappy, abrasive, overly snarky and fairly mean. We're not meant to forget that she is anti-social, however when KORREN comes onto the seen it seems that isn't so... Korren is an immortal being, a Kytaen which is essentially a creature that is able to take on a humanoid form, they are the protectors of their chosen or what is known as their Keeper to them. Korren has witnessed a lot in his years and has waited 200 years to be uncaged. He is angsty, bitter and distrusfful of everyone for just reason. He's a brooding sort who glares from across the way and doesn't seem likable either, but when you compare him to Leonie he's a ray of sunshine. As far as the plot goes, it's fairly interesting. The last Pulsar is brought back to her "home" and is revered, but her return brings a fair amount of trouble as well, as rebels congregate and plot to take her down or rather unleash her and use her for their own devices. Meanwhile, Korren, Leonie's protector finds himself battling with whether or not he wants to protect her - he really is just looking out for himself. Sounds great, right? Well, it had oodles of potential, but the writing quality just wasn't there. A lot of the times it read like an angsty teen girls diary. I almost DNF @ 30%, but I held out because there were times it seemed promising. However, there were then moments that read like this. "Light Magic?" "The essence of magic." "Oh" "Do you mind?" "No." There are pages where this is all that it consists of. A lot of dialogue that is short, or it will go to the next extreme and be overly informative. There has to be a balance and because of this the reader doesn't get to witness a lot of what actually happens in the world the author is trying to create. What I would ask Simlett is, "What do you want us to feel and what would you like us to walk away with after reading?" because after reading this I'm no wiser than what I was when I began reading, I'm definitely frustrated because I felt like it was just drawn out for the second book - yes it does make you want to read it, if you can look past the imperfections and the room for improvement. So, while I give this book a 1, it had a grand amount of potential and I see that. I see that in the writer, too. ~Blog~Instagram~

Actual Rating 2.5 ***This review has also been posted on The Social Potato I sadly, did not like Sweet Temptation as much as I hoped I would. I did like being with these characters again but over the past year, I have changed as a reader. Things I might not have noticed a year ago, stick out to me and that's exactly what happened with this book. Before I go any further, I would like to warn you that the review will be filled with some spoilers for the Sweet Trilogy but I will refrain from mentioning anything major. My main issue with this series is the way sex is dealt with in this book. Teen sexuality is dealt in a weird way in this series. Characters have sex, which is great but the main couple has to get married before they can have sex because otherwise Anna wouldn't be pure. That sends so many horrible messages about sex. I appreciate that the two don't dance around the idea of sex and know what they want, I'd rather that sex not be painted as impure if had before marriage. That wasn't it though. One couple who did have sex before getting married... they suffered consequences that affected their happily ever afters. What kind of messages do all of those things send about sex? Moreover, have I frightened you by mentioning sex a bazillion times? I have never had too much of a problem with the way Anna was characterized. She annoyed me but I was always able to get past that and focus on all the cooler things that were going on. This time though, I felt like Anna was being painted as an ideal in a way that made me feel comfortable. Anna was considered pure so if you aren't like Anna does that make you impure? Does that make you someone God wouldn't love? Idk. This book deal with religion and while I am not a religious person I wasn't really disturbed by the things that were happening in this book until now. I think a lot of my issues just come down to the concept of purity put forward by this series. Do I sound like a Lit Major? Maybe all the analyzing stuff in classes has gone to my head. Or maybe there are some real issues here that need to be discussed. The real question here is that was Kaidan just as swoonworthy in his own book as he was from Anna's point of view? I DON'T KNOW. I am glad that Kaidan didn't sound exactly like Anna and had his own distinct voice but he was also cheesy sometimes. I seem to have said so much off putting stuff that it might make you wonder, why do I even like this series? Why was this good brain candy? It's because Wendy has done such a good job in creating a world that is set apart from all the other cliches of Angels/Nephilim in YA. There is world building done beyond just someone mentioning the Lucifer fell and a bunch of angels fell with him. It is unique and that's what drew me to this world. On top of that, the way Wendy develops her plot arcs is just great. Romance does play a huge role in the books but there is also so much more going on. Friendships are forged, relationships are explored, etc. So even though I have a lot of issues and found bits of the books to be too cheesy, I still managed to enjoy the books. Note that I received an advanced copy of the book in exchange for an honest review

Pages read: 87 I've never read an Alex Flinn novel before, so that could be a factor here. Still, I liked the cover well enough and I'm all about fairy tales (which has been betraying me today). Thus far, Mirrored feels like being whacked over the head with the messages that changing your looks won't change your looks won't change your personality and that magic can't fix everything. Violet has been bullied all her life because she's ugly. As a child, she saves a bird from a psychopathic boy. She makes a friend, Greg, who she falls "in love" with. Then he goes off to camp one summer, hits his growth spurt and becomes popular, after which he will no longer talk to Violet. He starts dating the hot bitchy girl, Jennifer. Violet, even more of an outcast, is approached by Kendra (who I know from book knowledge is in the other Flinn books) and told that she has magical powers. This did nothing for me but might be better if you've read the others, which is why I generally don't read companions out of order. The writing has some weaknesses, like the fact that the bitchy mean girl says "Anything she does is total poop." That's TOTALLY realistic teen mean girl dialog, right? Isn't that how the cool kids at your high school talk(ed)? Violet uses her magic solely in pursuit of Greg. She can't magic him into having feelings for her, so she makes herself into an impossible ideal, but that's not enough. Even though this guy dumped her friendship proving he's an asshole, she's still determined to win him from her evil rival. I'm quitting because Violet is a fucking monster and I hate her so much she probably can't be redeemed in my eyes. Why? Well, after mean girl puts ants all over Violet's clothes during dance practice, Violet decides to retaliate. By magicking a dog into attacking Jennifer. There is just no fucking way I can ever like anyone who does this to a dog. I wouldn't be surprised if the dog gets away scot free in the book, but irl it would definitely get put down for sinking its teeth into this girl's cheek when there's no way the dog would have done this without Violet's interaction. Violet's clearly meant to be flawed, but I still suspect I'm supposed to feel sympathy for her and dear Gansey do I not. Since I own at least one more Flinn book, I'll probably give her another chance but no to this.

AHHHHHHH, I loved this book! It's been really hard for me to pick through the fantasy genre and find a summary that even interests me enough to comb through reviews, so I was relieved to pick this up due to my friend's recommendation. Actually, she had recommended it to me a while back but another friend of ours also read it and loved it, so I couldn't resist. And I must say, I have found THE fantasy book that just satisfies all these criteria I've built up in my head somewhere (and it most certainly isn't because of reading many well-written fanfics and stuff. Of course not. Nope.) The hardest part, in my opinion, to reading this book was perhaps the first couple of chapters. In no way was it boring or anything especially since it did capture my attention, especially the whole dragons and virgin daughters thing without an actual dragon , but it was a little slow. Not complaining too much considering it was necessary for background information and character introduction along with Agnieszka's initial life in the Tower , but if it weren't for the whole thing that I mentioned in the spoiler tag up there along with the promise of magic, I probably would have taken a lot longer getting through those first chapters instead of reading through them in one sitting. The main character Agnieszka was definitely a likable character who came with her own faults. Perhaps it's because she's younger than me and is a teenager and obviously grew up in a very different environment than my own, I have to admit that I found her to be quite irritating in certain scenes. Not to say that she isn't a lovable character because I found her to be quite humorous and respectable on many occasions, but her immaturity and naivete in certain scenes throughout the book sometimes got on my nerves. Or it might just be because I can relate to the Dragon better than I can to her... It's hard to say. However, I really did love the portrayal of Agnieszka's magic, especially when shown in contrast to Sarkan's magic and when both were used together. It definitely satisfied my magic craving in all the right places! And of course, the Dragon. He was probably the character I enjoyed reading about the most - it helps that he's the character that introduces magic to the readers - and satisfied that secret part of me that likes these types of fictional guy characters, I will admit. I found him to be more relatable probably because he viewed magic sort of like how scientists go about things, only just applied to magic. Not to say that I shared his view towards Agnieszka's magic since both types appealed to me immensely, but his approach was something that I understood and was familiar with due to my own education. There are many different types of characters in this book, but if I had to choose which ones really left an impression on me, aside from Agnieszka and the Dragon, I would have to say Marek and Kasia. Marek definitely left an impression as "the character I wished would die by the end of the book", but that's only covering the surface. He was not a character I immensely liked (in fact, I disliked him), but he had the charisma, the potential, the talent to be something great (one part that really stood out to me is that scene when he's killed and had managed to inspire everyone around him that he was certain that he would win and looked like a king). Funnily enough, that line made me think back to all the times where I felt he wouldn't have made a good king (and I'm sure we can all find them and list them out) and despite Agnieszka's observation that in that moment, he had looked that way, I just couldn't see any other result but his death from all of his actions up to that point. I would have placed Solya as a character that left quite an impression as well, but he sort of ended up fading to the back after a while, so I actually stopped thinking about him (but when he was an active character, I found him to be quite annoying and disliked him as well). Now, Kasia, oh Kasia. She was just an amazing character that balanced out well with Agnieszka. She just seemed to bring out to best in Agnieszka. Despite having gone through so many ordeals, Kasia was such a strong and dependable character. For me, she was a rock because she was constant and powerful in her own way (and in a completely different way from Sarkan yet those words would describe him just as well to me). I loved her and because of that, I could really relate to Agnieszka's love for her as well. However, there was one thing that kind of bugged me when I finished the book and still does even now. It was after the whole"His tower was broken, he'd drunk Spindle-water, and he'd held my hand. So now he was going to run away as quick as he could, and find himself some new stone walls to hide behind. He'd keep himself locked away for ten years this time, until he withered his own roots, and didn't feel the lack of them anymore." Don't get me wrong. I found that part quite interesting and it described him well, but it just bugged me that in the paragraphs afterwards in which we find out what Agnieszka's been up to after quite some time after that scene, she barely mentions anything about that scene aside from her vague summary of her feelings of the ENTIRE day which consisted of being "tired and lonely and angry and sad all at once". Not to say that I was expecting her to spill out her emotions regarding what happened and she did mention her lack of contact with him, but I was sort of expecting a contemplation regarding that day that kind of acknowledged her thoughts in that part I quoted from the book earlier and what her current thoughts were regarding that. Just... something more to build up to the ending where Sarkan returns is what I was looking for, I guess. Not to say that I can't fill in the missing parts myself, but yeah. I did really enjoy the ending with their reunion scene because it just fit them. The two of them are just adorable together. Because really, I ship it! OTP Yes, but seriously, I definitely recommend this book! I haven't read a book that I've enjoyed as much as this one this year and can see myself rereading this again in the near future.

This book was nostalgia done right, it was first love done right, it was even abuse accurately portrayed. If you're looking for diversity, this book is top of the charts. I was just thinking how books never include a full or near-full Asian as the main male protagonist. Yet Rowell's here to break down constructed norms on that front. However, I found myself letting that go for the sake of the stunning lessons and concept of this book. It was innocent and plucky at the same time. Lost Gate had a strong start, but the longer it went, the weaker it got. The main character never really was in any danger or met an obstacle that truly challenged him, despite the fact that he was only 12 to begin with (16 by the end). The intervening 4 years didn't really show him growing or changing at all. He has a magical power that is forbidden by his society, so he is constantly in fear of being killed, except that everyone he meets wants to help him and protect him. No one tries to control him or trap him, and the nature of his power is such that he could escape such traps easily anyway, so it's all moot. Makes for a boring main character and story if there's no struggle. The secondary story interested me even less. It was full of palace intrigue, my least favorite genre, but it read more like a chess match than a novel. The royal characters were all paper-thin and coldly written. I didn't care about any of them, and even the death of the baby Oath didn't have any emotional impact. When the two threads of narrative came together, nothing was explained. Everything happened internally, within the two main men, like a spiritual battle. Reading this battle, I felt a similar confusion, tension, frustration that I did when (oh so long ago) I read Stephen King's IT. The end of that book described a similar battle between the main kid and the giant spider demon in which they each were fighting while biting the other's tongue. I could never quite get my head around what was going on in either of these fights, but we all know how it turns out. So overall I was disappointed after such a promising start. If you would like to read about gods still alive in the modern world, find American Gods. I feel like I read another book with a similar theme too, but it escapes me at the moment.

I'm just going to explain the entire thing, because the book's not worth reading. Ruby longs to escape from the only life she knows, as part of the Congregation ruled by a terrible Overseer who demands the special Water they collect that provides immortality. But only a select few know that it's Ruby's blood that makes the Water special. Also she's 200 years old, falls in love, and her father may be Jesus. This is your typical teenage girl-in-repressive-society-starts-thinking-for-herself thing. Ruby is unique only because it's taken her 200 years to reach the maturity level of a 17-year-old. See, the Congregation was formed in 1812, when Ruby's mother met Otto, who was very kind and had magical blood. Mix the blood with water, give a drop as Communion every week, and viola! The town sees a cult and runs you out! At this point, Otto of the Magical Jesus Blood had disappeared, leaving only four vials of his blood, but alas, an evil villain lusting after Ruby's mom followed them and enslaved them to obtain the Water. Not good at thinking on her feet, Ruby's mother (Sula, because I'm sick of typing her title) said that the Water had to be harvested from plants (or dew) and only by Otto's devoted followers. So for the past 200 years, that's all they've done. It's all Ruby's ever known--that, and that she's Otto's child, giving her blood to keep the Water ready while they wait for Otto's return someday. The Congregation waits, they do not act. Also, only a very few people actually know about the magical blood. Most Congregants and Bad Evil Overseers believe the plant-water thing. Apparently, Darwin harvests the Water all year long for the Visitor who buys it or something. He's never explained. Darwin The Head Evil Overseer hires a new Overseer, Ford. So long as Ford works for him, Darwin pays enough to help Ford's mom's medical bills. Unfortunately, all I could think of was that this is still not a defense in court and yeah, Ford, you're a jerk and complicit in all the abuse. Ruby and Ford fall in love. SHOCKER. Ford finds out about some of the Otto-worship and decides they're a cult and tries to tell Ruby about Jesus. Ruby, in typical YA protag fashion, decides to run away to find Otto, having decided that he's not coming back. Sula and the Elders of the Congregation dislike this. It turns out they only love her for her blood! Who would have guessed? So they kill Ford and scold Ruby. But she heals him with some of the precious harvest Water the night before the Visitor comes. So he gets there and gets angry and kills Darwin. And also apparently knows the secret of Ruby's blood, though it's never explained why, or even how this guy got involved in the Water business since it's portrayed as Darwin's scheme from the beginning. So after 200 years and their main adversary dead, the Congregation decides to figure their life out. JUST KIDDING. They agree to harvest only *two-fifths* a year of what they did before. And they'll get three meals a day! Sheer luxury! Ruby realizes that everyone she's known for her 200 years are idiots and leave with Ford, who still doesn't know what's going on. So you can see it's not a great story anyway. But THEN there are so many things left unanswered or not thought out that it's even worse. We get that Ruby is supposed to be an average 200-year-old teen, but she has literally never been anywhere but this camp. She's grown up with the beatings and abuse and everything--I felt she should have less fazed by all the happenings, like the beatings. Sure, we get that you don't want your mother to be beaten, but this happens ALL THE TIME. Even if you're mentally a teen, you should not be nearly as impulsive as you are. The outside world: how exactly are you supposed to adjust? You didn't even know what electricity was, for pity's sake. Ruby, you're going to get yourself arrested and/or hospitalized for mental problems. THE OTTO ISSUE. Convenient plot device that didn't work because nothing ever came of it. His parents were "taken," but no one will say what that means. He had magical immortality-giving blood, knocked up Sula, then left. His daughter has magical immortality-giving blood, and along with the rest of the Congregation prays to Otto for deliverance. But nothing comes of it. Since we have proof (Water and Ruby) of his existence, something really should have happened. Christianity obviously exists (thanks, Ford), which makes me very uncomfortable. I hate mixing religion with fantasy. I disliked Drought when I began to realize that Otto was a Jesus-allegory, but disliked it even more when apparently they co-exist (or not, since Jesus never shows up/doesn't grant earthly immortality). What was the purpose? Ford essentially tries to convince Ruby she's a heretic once or twice, and then it's never mentioned again. FORD IS AN IDIOT. We've already established that yeah, it sucks your mom's dying but when you're beating people up we don't have sympathy for you, kid. He's sweet-talking Ruby one minute then roaring abuse like the rest of them the next--to survive, of course. He doesn't get the idea that these abused people might not you know, like Overseers, and Ruby's the same. And then there was the whole thing about the blood. "EW RUBY I SAW THAT YOU KNOW THERE'S ONLY ONE GOD RIGHT AND OTTO IS NOT HIM THAT'S DISGUSTING YOU SINNING SINNER." With so much stuff unresolved it's almost like it's setting itself up for a sequel, except it's written in a way that makes me suspect that there will not be one. So it ends with Ruby and Ford leaving everyone else behind while they embark on an Otto-hunt or something. Wheee.

I was pleasantly surprised by how much I enjoyed this read. I'm a list maker, so buckle down for some pros and cons! Pros: This was my first Bracken read, and I must say- I was blow away by how well she crafts character voice in this story. Prosper felt like a *real* person. He absolutely shined in this novel. I love how this normalizes diversity for younger readers. We have a mixed girl, whose parent's races aren't even mention until over half way through. Her mother is also somewhere on the queer spectrum, which again was hardly an issue of notice for the children and treated like a regular part of life. Just how race and sexuality should be handled. The atmosphere was exceptional. From the orange-knit pumpkin sweaters to the deep fried, sugar-and-cinnamon coated Silence Cakes, fall and Halloween are everywhere. Most of the story takes place within a haunted house, but we also get to visit a fall festival, a creepy basement, a graveyard, and scariest of all: middle school. The dynamic relationship between Alastor and Proper was my favorite part of the whole story. Just read and see! The world building was quite good. I enjoyed learning about the town and family history, as well as the multi-demimsions the fiends and other such creatures came from. Cons: I really don't have any serious issues with this book. The only thing that bothered me (again- a minor irritation) was the author's use of anecdotes to start nearly every new scene. Its a fancy little writers tool I enjoy every now and then, but felt it was over used here. Overall, this is a really great, middle grade halloween read!
