She's getting everything she's ever wanted, but is she really happy or was she better off before as her true self. After reading so many books with dark heavy subject matter, Revenge of the Girl With the Great Personality was just what I needed to read. It was a light, easy, and fun read. It wasn't just about beauty, but also about finding acceptance, and it dealt with family problems, as well. I enjoyed watching Lexi's character development. I think anyone could enjoy this book because the moral of the story is an important lesson; never pretend to be someone you're not. How do I review this book??? I don't have the right words... It is just... Magnificent. I have tried to start writing this review several times today. Each time I get frustrated because I simply can't express exactly how I feel about this book...especially if I don't want to spoil it...and I DON'T want to spoil it! So I am just going say what I feel, and this review will be all over the place and probably end up completely incoherent! First things first - this is the final book in a prequel series. If you haven't read The Mortal Instruments you need to start there!! BUT, the prequel books are meant to be read in between books 3-6 of The Mortal Instruments (In the order they were published). At the end of this review you will find a reading order guide - complete with the sequel series which I had forgotten is coming soon!!! YAY for more Shadowhunters!! Now - on to the review... I LOVED this book! It solidified this series' position right at the top of my YA favorites of all time! I want a book to make me FEEL, and boy did this do that! I felt torn apart so many times, I didn't know how my heart could take it!! The Shadowhunters lives burn so brightly, their passion for life is so big, they feel everything so strongly, that it all sets my poor mundane heart and mind spinning out of control. The characters ALL feel so real, they have such depth, there are no "place holders" in this book, even the most minor characters have so much life in them it is hard to look away. The plot is intricate, but not confusing (though I am always up for re-reading before the next book comes out, because I like to have all the details fresh in my mind - and these are ALL available on audiobook and very well done, so they are a JOY to re-read! ), and the action is exciting and perfectly paced throughout the book. And, of course, we get lots of the sarcastic humor we love from both of these series! This is now my favorite love triangle of all time. Yep, I said it. I have never read a triangle that was a REAL triangle before. Tessa, Jem, and Will all love each other...more than themselves...in a truly sacrificial way. They are each forced to choose the other's happiness over their own at different times, and they never fail to rise to the occasion. The bromance is...I don't have the right word...stunningly beautiful. The connection that Jem and Will share is so beyond friendship, more than brotherhood, they are mystically joined in a bond that can't be broken except by death...and sworn to protect the other's life with their own. Their love for each other is never in question, even when each one realizes that the other is in love with the object of his own affection...even when each one realizes that Tessa is in love with the other as well. I am choked up again just writing this...the relationship between the three of them truly is the most beautiful, self-sacrificing love I have ever read about. It is heart-warming, and heart-wrenching, and I fear I may never recover from it all! The ending. Aaaahhh - the ending is controversial...and I do NOT like spoilers, so I am just going to say that I believe it was as perfect as you could hope for given the situation these characters found themselves in. I hated it. I sobbed like a baby. I loved it. I hugged the book and sighed with happiness. I can't stop thinking about it, and crying again. Both of these series are absolutely golden for me. Just completely entertaining from start to finish. They made me giddy with happiness, frustrated beyond belief, scared, and worried, and absolutely gutted at times. They made me FEEL, and I loved every second of it! Who named this book? Seriously, who? It has nothing to do with the storyline. At all. The same goes for the cover. It's like someone just picked it at random. Ignoring the weird title and cover, this book turned out to be rather excellent. It was completely different than I assumed it would be. I can't think of another time that Enoch has created a heroine quite like this. I loved it. Diane was an awesome heroine. I think some readers might not like her because of how cold and manipulative she could seem, but I loved her. She was a woman who had been knocked down in life, only to pull herself up and take control. I loved that we weren't just told how capable she was, we saw it in every page. No matter what was thrown at her, she took it in stride. It drove Oliver mad how rarely he was able to come out on top in their battles. If he tried to embarrass her or manipulate her, she was always ready to turn the tables on him and come out on top in the situation. At times she came off as a little too bitter but I was too caught up in watching Oliver and Diane's relationship power struggle to care. I thought Oliver was a great match for Diane. They were both willing to do whatever it took to win and had no qualms about walking over other people on their way to success. This is not a rare quality in an Enoch hero, but I can't think of when I've ever seen her do such a like pairing with the heroine. The mercenary natures of the characters could have grated if left in less capable hands. The author always keeps us firmly on the side of the protagonists, even when we're fully aware of the wrongs they are committing. Case in point being the way Diane acquired Adam House. Oliver and Diane had a past together that didn't end well. Diane and Oliver have both changed from the people they were at that time, but it's hard for both of them to forgive and forget that time. "I am sorry," he said, trying to keep his voice low and measured. "You were looking for hope, and I was looking for a bit of fun, and when I realized I'd began to care for you far more than I was willing to acknowledge, I ran. Like a scalded dog, I believe you said. I apologize. It's not nearly enough to say the words, or to confess that leaving you in Vienna stands as the greatest regret of my life, but there you have it." That's pretty much their past in a nutshell. Oliver hightailed it out of there with no word and Diane was left to face the financial mess her husband had left her in. Only now she had to deal with a broken heart on top of it. There was no excuse for his actions, but Enoch did an excellent job of showing us his mindset, so it was easy to see why he felt he needed to run. Diane doesn't make it easy for him to prove himself to her, but he's nothing if not determined. Even Diane eventually can't deny how much he's changed. He was right in saying he would have been a crap husband to her if they had married then. He just hadn't grown enough. Despite the different tone to this book, Enoch's characteristic writing style is still there. The dialogue is snappy and you can feel the tension between the two leads. Unlikely situations occasionally crop up but, as with all other Enoch books, the characters approach them straight on and keep the book from veering toward the silly end of things. We were introduced to quite a few intriguing side characters who always managed to steer clear of the dreaded sequel bait role. I'm particularly interested in Greaves and Jenny. If this is what I can expect from the other books in this new series, I'll be on them like white on rice. I can't wait to see what the next book brings. Favorite Quote: "It's not about what I owe you, Diane. It's about what you're worth to me now."

Amir grew up in Afghanistan in the 60-70's. An Afghanistan before the coup, before the Taliban, before it became everything that we know it as today. He was the privileged son of a wealthy, influential and universally liked man. His constant companion was a boy his own age, Hassan. Hassan and Amir's fathers had similarly grown up together but despite this Hassan and his father were servants at least partly because they belonged to a social subclass. This part of the book is interesting, I enjoyed the descriptions of Afghanistan, which are vivid and exceptionally well written. I did NOT enjoy the way one was never allowed to enter into the rhythm of the story without grim little reminders popping up ever page or so that something dire and terrible was about to happen. The something horrible happens and, yes, it is exceptionally nasty. Amir and father flee to USA and become Afghani refugees in San Francisco. This was also interesting, reading about the efforts of the Afghani community to make a place for themselves. what was NOT interesting was the constant angst, guilt and self flagellation without self awareness or moral growth that the lead character exhibits. So! What do I do with this book? I can't give it a single star and commit it to the shelves of badly written, poorly characterised novels which were never edited with any conviction. This book is very well written, the characterisation is vivid, believable... The verbal painting of the background of pre-war Kabul is really brilliant and the sketching of the refugee Afghanistan in America is compelling. It is a very well done book... I didn't like it though! I almost disliked it enough not to keep reading, I put it down half a dozen times and called myself a masochist for picking it up again, so I suppose it has proved itself as 'compelling' as many a review would have it. But how on earth did people enjoy this book? Early on a foundation plot builder is a really nasty event that is never left behind how can anyone 'enjoy' this and the consequent repetitive, furtive angst that makes up the rest of the story? I don't know, but I seem to be in the acute minority for not loving it beyond measure. I didn't like the rape, but I get that it was needed as a plot builder for all the 'I am bad' angst later. It is a foundation after all for the climax of the story. I ABSOLUTELY hated the following section where the main character then proceeds to abuse, victimise and emotionally desert the person who was raped. I hated this part and it seemed completely, randomly meaningless and redundant. It was sickening largely because it seemed unnecessary, why did the boy do it? Not a clue. Why did the author feel it was necessary? never explained. Just... wtf? The end of the book, Amir goes back to Afghanistan to redeem himself by getting really badly hurt in an effort to bring dead Hassan's son back to USA and so that the bad guy who raped him could get his comeuppance. That is so predictable it should not even be a spoiler. The return of Amir to an Afghanistan devastated by war and under Taliban malevolence has interesting portions, I especially liked when a driver tells him that he was always a tourist in his own country, that his privileged life blinded him to the lot of the average Afghani. Despite that the end dragged quite a bit in my opinion, I resorted to skim reading once or twice because I wanted to know the end but I couldn't be bothered reading every word of the misery and self flagellation. I didn't like it, but I see many merits in it. One of the few other people of my acquaintance who, like me failed to get the more common literary orgasm from this book described it as 'Bleak'. Perhaps I too should have been that succinct.

Originally posted on Slow Reader's Blog In Flow, Bristol flies to LA to connect with her estranged twin, but ends up connecting with the last person she'd expect, and in such a way that she'll never forget. Flow follows rap superstar Marlon James, and powerhouse Bristol Gray before they ruled their worlds. In this intimate prequel, Marlon is a poor wannabe with a host of talent, and a spark and passion so intense that Bristol is unable to stay away from him. In this electric and thought-provoking novella, Bristol is on a mission to put her family back together, but ends up finding out that some bonds are stronger than even blood; sometimes you meet people who dig so deep that you feel them in your marrow. Flow, and the full story, Grip, are standalones featuring two characters that are present in Kennedy Ryan's Soul Series. You don't need to read those books before reading Flow as the story arcs don't overlap. But, I imagine a new reader who reads this love story prequel might label it as "insta-love." But, seeing as how the characters themselves are thrown by the quick intensity of their connection, then that might not necessarily be a negative. Sometimes sparks catch and an inferno builds rapidly, and there's nothing we can do about it except watch it and feel the heat. With Flow, that burn is extreme, and by the end, you'll be dying for Grip, unsure of whether you want a soothing relief, or, if you need the total combustion. Here's a spoiler: you'll get both.

DNF Finnie is young, pretty, rich and adventurous. She's discovered that there's a parallel world to Earth, where everyone has a twin. She's paying a witch a million dollars to do a swap with her twin, so that she can go have adventures in a fantasyland. She's got emotional reasons: she lost her parents in a plane crash when she was fifteen, and she just wants to see them again. While the witch points out that this whole doppelganger thing doesn't mean these people are alike in personality, and this is a dangerous venture, Finnie is determined to go. She does. She finds herself dressed in swanky princess gear in a palace in a wintery land. She doesn't have a lot of time to orient herself, because she's immediately dragged off to a temple, and married to a big handsome cranky man. Finnie has great coping skills and takes this in her stride. She also takes it in her stride when Frey, her new husband, dumps her in a cottage in the middle of the woods for 6 weeks. Before he goes, he makes it known that he's really cranky at her for being a lesbian. I had a great time with this book for about the first 30%. Finnie is just so enthusiastic about her surroundings, and it's refreshing. Usually, when a heroine finds herself dumped in a completely alien environment she's really peeved. Not Finnie. Everything is awesome and so cool. A page rarely goes by without Finnie pointing out how cool something is. Finnie's competent enough to get her new home cleaned up, get her horses and herself fed and watered, and get all her princess junk put away. She learns how to cook on a wood fire stove, and how to do laundry with a wringer. She had impressive skills, but this was a really a cosy transition into a far more primitive way of life than a modern woman would be accustomed to, even a modern woman who had lots of adventures and would know survival stuff about fires. She's also really good at making friends, because she's all bouncy and optimistic and people love her. I was prepared to overlook how easily all of this came to her as well, because it's so nice to spend time with a fun person who isn't spending all her time gloomy and terrified. Frey eventually shows up again, and Finnie explains that she's not actually a lesbian. And she would like some sex with Frey, but maybe not right away. Frey's happy, because he really wanted to tap that, and no longer being forced to respect her sexual orientation made him a little less unpleasant. He was still an arrogant sod, but he wasn't a raping arrogant sod, so they start getting along pretty well. Very early into working on their new relationship, Frey's full powers of awesomeness are revealed. He commands elves AND dragons. No one has commanded elves in 700 ~ish years, and no one has commanded elves AND dragons in 1500 years. He's a big deal. It's the elves who tell him that Finnie's a swap. Since Frey likes her better than a lesbian, he orders the elves to make the swap permanent. They're a bit reluctant, but they do so. And now, Finnie understands the language of cats and birds and other small creatures. Mostly her cat, Finnie is charming about her cat. Unlike actual proper cat owners, who know that when their cat wants cuddles, it's basically so the cat can check that you're still alive. Purring is a sign of annoyance that you aren't dead yet, and ready to be eaten. It's cute, in that everything Finnie goes through is clearly fantasy in the style of a Disney princess movie. This book pre-dates Frozen by 2 years, but Finnie's style is pure Elsa. Sure, she doesn't have crazy ice magic, but she's got white-blonde hair and favours swanky pastel blue gowns. If you offered her sparkle, she'd take it. She loves her crown. This chatty animal magical ability, which everyone has, is heavily gendered. Women talk to small domestic animals, men talk to hunting and agricultural animals. It's part of the overall cuteness of the setting and is otherwise irrelevant. I've abandoned this book at 62%. I even tried to reignite my interest by reading the last chapter, but it didn't work. I didn't care. It's so long. I'd spend over an hour slogging through this massive section of nothing. While Finnie doesn't yet know that she's stuck in this world (given that's the only obvious major source of conflict in her romance with Frey) she and Frey are getting along super great. Everyone loves Finnie. Finnie is having a great time sailing around with her handsome raider husband, who is giving her great sexy times and is being super lovely to her all the time. I'm sure this book eventually gets on track, with some genuine suffering, since I'm leaving it at the point where Finnie is meeting the villain, but I can't do it anymore. I really did want to like this book, and I'm disappointed. I did like parts of it. I don't really mind that this is a cosy Disney princess fantasy, where the world building doesn't need to be very thoughtful about technology or politics or culture or how all these things work together. World building doesn't necessarily have to have a rich, complex and detailed logic for me to enjoy a fantasy novel. Especially because a lot of rich complex fantasy worlds operate with a degree of assumed misogyny that is vaguely justified as 'that's what the Middle Ages were like.' That standard is just as false as what we've got here: where culture and technologies are seriously inconsistent, and the focus is more on a smoothed out, cosy version of a pre-industrial lifestyle. I won't criticise the book on this basis, but the inconsistencies in the way the world worked became really noticeable when it became clear that I'd hit a long stretch of no plot. I had nothing to do but dwell on them. From all evidence to the point where I've left the story, Finnie can handle it all flawlessly, which is the most frustrating thing. I like her confidence and her positivity, but since the only thing she ever gets even slightly wrong is managing her touchy and difficult husband, I can't really invest in her problems.

EVERLOST by Neal Shusterman is one of my favorite books, so when I found out it was part of a trilogy, I had to get the second one right away. I never thought the genius of EVERLOST could be outdone or even matched, but I was pleasantly surprised by EVERWILD. It was even BETTER than the original. I should start off by saying that I don't think the impact of EVERWILD will be as powerful if you didn't read EVERLOST first. EVERLOST introduces the world of Everlost and the primary characters (Nick, Allie, and Mary). Seeing them develop from the beginning of EVERLOST to the end of EVERWILD is a journey that you must start from the beginning of the first book if you want the most out of it. Nick has become the Chocolate Ogre, Allie has become Allie the Outcast, and Mary is now deemed Mary the Sky Witch. The way Shusterman follows these three characters and tells each of their stories individually but weaves them all together at the end is genius. There are new characters as well, who fit perfectly into the story. Neal Shusterman's writing is brilliant. I have never read a book by another author who can describe things as well as he can, which is why he's my favorite author. The way he brings the world of Everlost to life is astounding. EVERWILD is engrossing, suspenseful, and grim at parts, but it is also beautiful in so many ways. The different elements Neal Shusterman brings in have such depth and meaning that I can't even explain what I'm talking about in words. The character I feel the most for personally is Mikey McGill, and he very well may be my favorite character. When you read the book, you will understand why. I can't wait for EVERFOUND. The Skinjacker triology is one you mustn't miss.

Miss Match reminds me of those funny romcom movies with a jackass hero and a down on her luck quirky heroine. Blake Donovan, a narcissist, control freak and misogynist pig of a millionaire is looking for a wife. And he hired someone to search the perfect bride for him. Andrea Dawson, a woman with the worst luck in finding a job after leaving her last sleazy boss. I'm fascinated with Andrea's special skills in reading people, which make her such an asset to her last boss and currently to Blake. Andrea hates that she drop so low as to accept the job offer, but what choice does she has? However, even if Andrea scouting for suitable dates was successful, she still had one very huge problem: How would she make Blake Donovan suitable for dating? Because the MAN himself is horrible and he portrayed himself as one of the most boring guy on earth. He said he only listen to NPR, BBC and classical music. He hates pet and he works all the damn time. Though, he can be incredibly sexy as long as his mouth was closed. When I started on Miss Match, I need some time to warm up to the Andrea because her sense of humor is all over the place, like I can't get a read on her character. But once I get to know her better I'm intrigue with her skill and her past employment that lead to her being jobless for months. As for the douche Blake Donovan, what can I say, jackass usually fascinate me. He is so overbearing and a total pig towards woman in general. I can't wait to see Andrea bring him to his knees. I like the little things about him that was reveal later on. I also wanted to know what make him this way and why he wanted to make himself look so stuffy and unreachable. Their initial get-to-know each other was hilarious even though I wanted to punch Blake every single time he talk. However, I'm disappointed that I didn't get to really learn about Blake's history. His childhood was mentioned in a few sentence. For him to be such a pig, I need more information to make me sympathize with him. So although I don't hate his character, I don't feel like I love him all that much. I enjoyed their bickering in the beginning, but towards the end it gets a tad juvenile. The ending was also too abrupt for my liking. It usually works for a 2 hr movie, but for a book that I spent an entire day to read, I need more romance and lovey dovey scene before the final HEA. To me, Blake and Dawson spent an entire book in the hate/lust bubble and then wham-bam HEA.

** spoiler alert ** I'll start off by saying I don't believe a word of this story. Yes, I do believe in ghosts (or at least I'd like to), but there are too many people calling foul on the Lutzes for me to swallow their story. But I like the movie, as entertainment, so I was hoping to like the book. I can't say I did. The prose was dull and as a story, the book just doesn't deliver. It's a hodgepodge of so-called "true" events that never really come together. I got the feeling that the Lutzes read a few books on hauntings and grabbed a little bit from each account, because not only do we have demonic pigs, demons in the fireplace, but also something in the boat house that we never sort out, ghosts in the kitchen that are apparently not connected to anything else, and a ghost boy upstairs...which we might at first think is one of the murdered DeFeos, but apparently he's not connected to anything either. Oh, and then there's body in a well, underneath the red room in the basement. And supposedly a local Native American tribe liked to trap their insane people there and let them die horribly (except that this never happened). It's a Death House. Not just any Death House, mind you. This has got to be THE Death House, if all of this crap really happened there. Then all of this unconnected stuff drove Ronny DeFeo insane and made him kill his family. Oh, and don't forget the green slime oozing out of the walls. After a while, the book just turns into a comedy, as far as I'm concerned. Mildly entertaining, but otherwise....
Great idea, but very annoying characters.

Hundreds of years ago, a town made a pact with Death. In exchange for near perfect health and long life, any person born within the town will rise as a zombie. The only way to avoid this is to inter the bodies within the town borders and constantly appease them with visits, holy water and liquor. This is the job of the Graveminder, and Rebekkah has just unwittingly inherited it. She inherits it at a most perilous time, when the dead are walking in greater numbers than in generations. This sounds exciting, but astoundingly, Marr manages to make it anything but. Instead of trying to stop the zombies, Rebekkah mostly just describes what dresses she wears in the Underworld and angsts about how she kissed Byron (her Fated One True Love) while he was still dating her step-sister. It takes like three seconds to actually solve the plot. The world building is so full of holes that I can't even handle it. If I started detailing all the ways Marr's town doesn't work, I would wear my fingers to the bone. A nonsensical dystopia would be forgivable if I liked the characters, but they are all too stupid to live.

I enjoyed the new casting of Cinderella, now with more slightly-Celtic-flavored magic -- it's an easy read if you'd like some escapism. Lo is skilled at creating atmosphere by leaving a lot of negative space in some of her storylines... much of the way that the mood of a piece or a turn of the plot is created by her is due to the things you thought might happen but didn't. She deftly shapes your expectations and then subverts them, but never in a way that the reader feels betrayed. Just... surprised. (And many of the surprises are happy ones rather than "rocks fall, everyone dies", so if you're looking for a non-depressing read, this book is pretty safe in the end.) Her depiction of GLBT themes is similar, quietly cheerful in their unremarkableness. Most of the relationships or hoped-for relationships we see in the book are het, but when they're not, no one remarks on that or cares. I appreciate books where that's not even a big deal... the plot is being driven by family, greed, and otherworldly magic, and they all have other things to think about. Would totally give to my niece when she's old enough to read it.

Something that 18-year-olds and potheads have in common (if they're not one in the same) is that they think everything they say is so DEEP and PROFOUND. The problem is that I don't belong to either group. The Disenchantments is the story of four friends and bandmates who hit the road after three of them (Colby, Bev, and Meg) graduate from high school. Colby, the lone boy, is our narrator and manager of the Disenchantments. On the eve of the trip, Bev tells Colby that despite their plans to visit Colby's mom in Paris and then backpack around Europe for the year, she's going to college instead. To further complicate matters, Colby has been in love with Bev since they were kids. Nothing like awkward tension and feelings of betrayal to kick off a trip. Needless to say, this wasn't the light, fun road trip book I was expecting. It was my own fault because I saw the cover, read "road trip" in the summary, and assumed it would be FUN in the SUN! Still, throw France in a story in any shape or form and I'm usually appeased. Unfortunately, I didn't feel engaged in the story until page 246 -- of a 307-page book. For the majority of the book, I felt little connection to the characters. Colby's DEEP 18-year-old thoughts just made me roll my eyes. For example: We drive past a lumberyard, full of a forest's worth of felled trees. I slow as we pass it. It's almost too big to comprehend.Okay, homie. He's not the only one emo-ing out, although he does have the best reasons. Alexa, the band member with a year of high school left, gets a splinter in her foot. But to a 17-year-old, a splinter is not just a splinter. She says, "The world is against me. "Inevitably, when you put 18-year-olds in a room or car together, they come to MEANINGFUL and PROFOUND realizations. "It's hard." "What's hard?" I ask. Bev shakes her head, as if the answer is too big to put into words. Finally she says, "Growing up." And there is nothing any of us can say to that. It feels too true for a response.I was mid-eye roll until I thought back to 2am conversations with my roommates freshman year. Let she who is without self-importance cast the first stone, right? As insufferable as some of the Disenchantments' musings were, they are the typical musings of the age group. The story took a Graffiti Moon-esque turn on page 252 and my interest raised tenfold. The 50 pages that end the book are where the story should've started. That story, and the story that begins at the end of the book, is one I would've loved reading. There is an audience for this book and these characters, but unfortunately it wasn't me. Final verdict: 3/5 stars. This review appears on Young Adult Anonymous.

I got this book because it won one of the goodreads book of the year awards; didn't read the description at all, just went in blind. Well, the first four chapters I thought were kind of slow, not really stand-out, but there was talk about sides in some civil war or another, and I held out hope that it'd get exciting. And then chapter five rolled around, and there was suddenly talk about magical... stuff. I could roll with the Middle Eastern-themed western (haha that's really quite funny when you think about it) but... ugh... The book just lost me at "A Buraqi... a desert horse. A First Being..." Yeah... no. It's not so much that there's magical elements in this book, it's more the way it was just thrown in there, almost as an afterthought. I'd be like watching the first hour of Saving Private Ryan, everything's going great, World War Two, weeeeeee, and then all of a sudden, the Ghostbusters appear and start debating Trump's border wall with Abraham Lincoln. It's just like... what the **** is happening? Frankly, it probably didn't lose me so much at a First Being, but more with its lack of an intriguing protagonist. All I know by chapter five is she has blue eyes while everyone else has brown eyes (which is mentioned twice a chapter at least), that she can handle a gun, that she's from a dead-end town and has insta-love with some foreigner. I see a few reviews saying they love her sassiness, which I didn't see at all, which several other reviewers agree with. The kick-ass heroine is just frankly so over-done that just making a kick-ass heroine doesn't mean she kicks ass at all. She's bland. In the first four chapters, she doesn't do anything really heroic or sassy. It's just... I don't know. I never bought into the protagonist, so I didn't really care to go on her journey with her. When it got to the First Beings in chapter five, I was just like yeah.... No... I'm gonna go play PlayStation. Even some books I do-not-finish, I'm still glad I picked it up and gave it a shot. Not this one. But for all the razzing some reviewers are giving the book about being a Middle Eastern Western, I think it's a splendid concept. Like Cowboys vs. Aliens. An idea like that can either be brilliant or terribly atrocious. And the difference comes down to execution. And this one I think just got it wrong. But that's just my opinion.

After a year spent mourning her dead fiance, Drew McGovern is ready to move on - on to stormchasing and making a difference in her and other people's lives. In the midst of the thrill of facing unpredictable weather changes and the tragedy of ruined lives when a bad storm hits, Drew rediscovers herself as well as secrets that were never meant to be spoken about in the very seat that her dead fiance had left empty. There is so much to love about Drew, whose steely instinct for survival and coping won me over immediately. Her calm acceptance of her attraction to Aiden, her lack of fear when it came to treading the treacherous waters of a relationship with her fiance's best friend left me with open-mouthed admiration for a character so well-drawn and I found myself hoping that Aiden O'Neal would be the strong solid man that I'd wrongly initially assumed he was for her. I was wrong, having landed myself in a rare case of liking a particular main character in a pairing, yet disliking the other. Call me stodgy, but I prefer heroes who don't play fast and loose with women, which is what Aiden is - and I'd really rather not read about his sexual encounters with anyone else other than the heroine, which is proving to be a test of a hard limit for me right from the beginning. He's also a bundle of crude and coarse contradictions, claiming to care and want Drew, yet cowardly insisting that he can't be anything but distant and detached with women, consequently treating them without the respect I personally demand of protagonists in the romantic genre. In fact, I liked the version of Aiden only in the first and last chapter, and felt that Drew simply attributed to him - an overestimation in my opinion - certain qualities that I simply couldn't see. Drew and Aiden's bourgeoning relationship could be best described as fitful and unsteady through no fault of the former; Aiden's tendency to diminish Drew's feelings and his inability to accept her affection for him were simultaneously aggravating and off-putting. My long gripe aside however, 'Blown Away' was absorbing for its setting and action, giving a fascinating yet sombre glimpse of those who live in tornado alley and the very specific challenges that they face because of the weather. *ARC by netgalley (always grateful, mind)

If we take out this Prince Charming and his True Love story, then it was very interesting time travel story about love that lasts over the time. All the characters in this book and in previous books have been living on Nantucket some two hundred years ago and now their souls are back and they find each other again. For All Time is just a wonderful summer read.

Natalie's got confidence and then some, and has no reservations about going after a man, even if it's only for a night of fun. But there's something about the quiet, somewhat grumpy, tattooed man at the farmer's market every week that makes her fumble and ramble. She may love the Brie he makes, but she's interested in far more than just Oscar's handcrafted cheese. When her advertising company picks up the small town where Oscar lives for a project, Natalie's all over the job, mixing business trips with pleasure trips. But as much as she enjoys her time with her country man, she's a city girl at heart. Can they find compromise somewhere in between the two extremes? First, I know, I know, the title and cover may be a bit . unusual. But trust me, this book is worth the read! Cream of the Crop was such a delightful read. It's not so light that there's not some angst/emotions popping up, but it's still relatively fluffy and fun - and I mean that in the best possible way. I very much enjoyed Clayton's writing style (and will be reading more of her books in the future), as well as Natalie's spunk and sass. Natalie's a take-no-shit and give-no-fucks kind of woman, and I loved her for that. She fully accepts that yes, she is plus-sized, but she's damn beautiful and she has the confidence to take what she wants out of life. She wasn't always that way; her backstory includes a douchebag POS ex-boyfriend who really did a number on her when she was graduating high school (controlling, verbally and emotionally abusive, made her believe she was never enough, etc., etc.). But after leaving him, she picked herself up and set her mind on a career where she kicks ass and a mindset that dares the world to call her fat and belittle her for her size. I could truly connect to some of Natalie's early struggles about herself, and while I can't say I'm to the give-no-fucks level that Natalie is (yet), I loved seeing such a heroine in print. Because we can't forget that everyone needs to be able to see parts of themselves in books. And no, this is not the story of the fat girl finding herself - and love - after losing weight. Nope, not at all. Natalie is an unapologetic size 18 from start to finish. She's happy with herself. Which I also loved because far too often when there is a "heavier" heroine, much of her character arc revolves around her losing the weight and suddenly being beautiful. Fuck that shit. Lose the weight if you want to be healthier, I have nothing against that. But a person isn't ugly because they're fat and beautiful once they're skinny; that's society's BS talking. Let's see, I laughed and smiled during a lot of this book. I could relate to Natalie and loved her attitude and confidence. What else? Oh! The chemistry between Natalie and Oscar is fantastic; this is quite a hot read, whether they're simply kissing or getting busy on any available surface. The only complaint I have is minor: I do wish we could have gotten Oscar's POV thrown in. I don't mind 1st POV in my romance novels, but I do prefer if it's dual 1st POV so we can get the full picture and experience of the couple. The epilogue was done from Oscar's POV, which was interesting since the rest of the book was entirely from Natalie, but I would have liked to see Oscar's POV mixed in a bit; maybe not every other chapter, but at the very least a few times during the course of the story. This was my first Clayton novel but it will not be my last. Fun and relatable and sexy as hell, Cream of the Crop reads like a good romcom. 4 1/2 STARS! I don't have too much to say about this book, as I am writing this some weeks after finishing the book. All I wanted to record was how surprised I was by how much I liked this book. The characters are really wonderfully complex and interesting, with a particularly intelligent and interesting heroine, and the plot (while slightly flawed - some issues could have easily been glossed over with some good old fashioned communication, but romance seems to rely generally on miscommunication, so I'm not super mad about it) was surprisingly refreshing. Seen at Bookish Antics! Do you devour books like your life depends on it? Do you use frequently refer to your reading pile as your TBR pile? Do you feel as if you love fictional characters more than the majority of people you know? Then, Afterworlds is the book for you; this is the book that booknerds have been waiting for and it definitely delivers. Westerfeld has written such a creative novel and the way he meshes Afterworlds and Darcy's story into one cohesive whole is just amazing. In one month Darcy Patel wrote Afterworlds, a paranormal romance, but what she didn't expect was that a publisher would buy it in such a hurry. Patel receives a huge advance and defers college for a year to move to NYC to work on revisions for Afterworlds. Readers will read Patel's Afterworlds alongside her life story and will be swept into Lizzie's story, one filled with love, death and everything in between. Both stories start off excellently: Darcy is querying her novel to literary agents and the airport Lizzie is in experiences a terrorist attack. As an excellent novel should, Afterworlds hooks readers in immediately and establishes each story clearly. Each story is told in alternating chapters and I really found it interesting seeing all of the parallels between the two stories. Readers will be able to see bits of pieces of Darcy and her life in her debut, which made Afterworlds feel even more special to me. This book is really meant for those who are die-hard book nerds and those who are involved in the publishing industry. I don't think average people will get the same reading experience out of Afterworlds and will really get this novel. Will laymen understand abbreviations like TBR or ARC or even what Book Expo Of America is? Even if they do, I don't know if they will get how big of a deal getting published and how big of a honor it is. Westerfeld does explain the publishing industry in-depth and I even learned a few new insider tidbits. I'm still questioning whether average people will get the publishing aspect of this novel. Darcy's story was really fascinating to me as a reader and as an aspiring author. Westerfeld gives readers an insider's look on the evolution of a book from its completion to revisions to its publication. I loved watching Darcy interact with other authors and the nervousness she felt when reading an author friend's book was a familiar feeling that I've experienced as a book blogger. It was an enlightening experience watching Darcy hit different milestones in her writing career and indirectly, finding herself. I loved Darcy, she was such an intelligent and snarky protagonist that I felt a strong connection to. Darcy chased her dream which takes a lot of guts and I admired her for taking her life by the reins. It's frightening to just leave your home and everything you know and to abandon it for your dream, but Darcy does it and hardly ever looks back. Though Afterworlds is a book about writing and the publishing industry, it's also a coming-of-age story. Darcy finds herself in her work and she learns so much about herself from being exposed to such a different atmosphere. Lizzie's story isn't quite as exciting as Darcy's, but did keep me engaged and interested for the most part. Some of the imagery in Lizzie's story is so chilling and vivid, especially the black oil sections. Westerfeld wrote a refreshing take on ghosts and tackling one's past; I loved meeting the various different ghosts and watching them interact with Lizzie. In addition, few of the twists in Lizzie's story were a bit predictable, but I really enjoyed the world-building of the afterworlds that was included in it. Lizzie's story is well-drawn out, but I expected so much more from Westerfeld because I hold him in such high regard. There are two relationships in Afterworlds: Darcy's relationship with an older, fellow author named Imogen and Lizzie's relationship with Yamaraj, the Hindu god of death. I enjoyed Lizzie's relationship with Yamaraj, but it wasn't all that different from your average paranormal romance and it had a pretty basic structure. Darcy's relationship with Imogen is such a mature, appropriate look at first-love and what it means to make sacrifices for the ones you love. This romance is extremely realistic and I shipped this couple so much even when they were experiencing relationship issues. I know there's a lot of stigmas in the publishing industry that books about GLBT and people of color don't sell well, which made me appreciate Westerfeld's bold decision to write about a lesbian Indian even more. We need greater diversity in our books and this is just one small step in the right direction. Afterworlds is an intelligent, well-thought out coming-of-age tale that is so out-of-the-box and unique. This book is extremely long and drags in a few sections, but for the most part it reads much faster than I expected. Darcy's story outshone Lizzie's story by a long shot and I wasn't totally impressed with the plot progression in Lizzie's story. No matter what, Afterworlds is still one of the most clever novels of the year and it's totally worth reading especially for the trunk research scene.

Levi "Painter" Brooks came from nothing. He was shoved into group homes and juvie until he met the Reapers MC, and fell into the brotherhood. His family. He owes them everything and he has nothing else to lose. When Painter takes a hit for the club and is sent to prison, sweet Melanie Tucker writes to him. Melanie is a girl he needs to stay away from. Melanie is a girl who deserves better. Melanie is a girl that he can't stop thinking about. Even though Melanie lost everything after she graduated high school, she works her way up through the ashes and forms a future for herself. She's taken in by London who lives with Reese, the president of the Reapers MC. Even though the biker club makes her wary, she sticks close to London and betters herself the best she can. When the hot, bad boy biker Painter lends her his car while he's in prison, she writes to thank him and a friendship develops. At least that's what Melanie thinks. She's soon to find out that when Painter gets out, her innocence is in jeopardy. As a book reviewer, it's SO, SO hard to write about books in a series, especially if it isn't the first book. But I'm going to try my best with this one, because I love this author's series so much. I really like Melanie. She may have been blindsided by life, but she works hard to pick herself up and dust herself off. When she's left with literally the clothes on her back, she grips a foothold, gets an education, and works through the grit. She shows her bravery, loyalty, and resilience multiple times through this book, and I felt connected to her the whole time. The only thing I didn't like about Melanie is how long she holds a grudge, even after the people who wronged her bend over backwards to make it up to her. Painter. In the previous books of the series, Painter is a jackass. Pure honesty right here. He was expected to be matched with Em, who is Reese's (Picnic's) daughter, but Painter failed to man up and form a serious relationship with her. He was too flaky and too immature. But you want to know a secret? I still thought he was hot. He has an edginess about him. His art made him mysterious and I wanted to get to know him and his story. In the end, Painter steps up to the plate and takes care of what's his, and he redeems himself majestically. As always with Ms. Wylde's books, I'm left longing for the next story in the series. If you're new to the check out Book #1: Reaper's Property.

Between Shades of Grey begins with NKVD officers banging at the door. 20 minutes they are told. They have 20 minutes to pack for relocation. 15 year old Lina is swept, with her mother and her younger brother and their small suitcases first into the back of a truck, and then onto a train. They do not know what has happened to her father, and they do not know where they are being taken or why. As they languish in a train car for over a month, barely subsisting on the buckets of gruel they are sometimes given, they begin to form bonds with the other Lithuanians they have been jammed into a train car with. Lina and her brother Jonas become especially close to a 15 year old boy named Andrius. His mother has had him pretend he is "simple" so that he will not be wrested from and taken away to be with "the men." They are a group of women, children and the infirm. They do not know where the men have been taken, and they will not all survive the harsh conditions. Lina begins sending out messages only her father will understand if he ever gets them. A handkerchief with drawings and the words "pass it along" are passed to a man at a train station. Lina relies on her skill as an artist to keep her sane. Her drawings must be guarded closely, as they are certainly "anti-Soviet" and may be punishable by death. Sepetys creates a journey through fear, starvation, and despair, and hope. Impossibly harsh conditions become routine for Lina in a Soviet work camp, where a beet stolen and hidden in ones underwear until later is a cherished treat for a family living on small bread rations alone. Throughout this journey the strength and resilience of the human spirit is tested, and sometimes broken. The epilogue and end notes give further information about the NKVD (later to become the KGB) and the Soviet work camps, where thousands of Lithuanian, Latvian, and Estonian citizens died. As I was reading this book I was comparing it to The Book Theif, which I listened to on audio book over a year ago. I was thinking that, while this is a good historical fiction that deals with human suffering, and would be a good companion to The Book Theif for theme, it just not as well written. The characters are more comlex, and better developed in The Book Theif.
Thoughts are cloudy after reading this book. Will post a review later, or maybe not.

In Partials, Dan Wells creates a realistic future in which humans have suffered through a couple more wars before being decimated by the RM virus. Now, the remainder of North America, at least to Kira's knowledge, has retreated to Long Island. Humanity is now divided in their argument for how to fight for the survival of humanity even as they guard themselves against the Partials, super soldiers they believe to be responsible for the release of the RM virus. It is eerie how Dan Wells is able to create such a realistic future in light of the events that have passed in his world. The Senate is made up of older people who survived the attack of both the Partials and the RM virus unleashed upon humanity, and they are unwilling to take risks with the remnants of the human population. Instead, they decide to use statistics and pass the Hope Act, forcing women eighteen and older to have a baby every year in the hopes that one will be immune to RM. Kira and her younger friends believe that something else can be done, and her friends take little convincing to go along with her outrageous plans that follow. The medical focus of the novel interested me the most. Kira first trained to be a medical intern in the maternity ward, because she thought that the dying newborn babies were the ones she needed to observe to find a way to save humanity, before deciding to research Partials. Kira's conflicting scientific and emotional views give her a unique voice. While there is a lot of scientist in her, Kira will let her emotions get in the way when there are lives in danger, and she will jeopardize more lives along with the mission to save a single person. The events in the novel take time to unfold, and more questions are raised than are answered. Partials is the start of what promises to be a thrilling series about a girl's journey to find herself and the reason behind humanity's destruction. Original post at Imaginary Reads

So I decided to take a chance at the YA scifi book (and series) - I've read a few YA scifi ones back in the right age :P - got this on Christmas and started reading some days ago. I finished the book sooner than I thought, impatient to reach the conclusion even after peeking at the end (haha). I'm quite impressed at the story's quality and that the romance was so well balanced with the actual story, with realistic, tragic details. In 2575, our two main characters Kady and Ezra, have freshly broken up when their colony, a place on a remote planet of Kerenza, is destroyed - they must quickly find their way to evacuation, ending up on two different ships. While they eventually make contact with each other again, troubles are rising again - and not being able to reach their destination Jump Station Heimdall as fast as hoped is just one small thing among them. It is a tale of interrupted life, price of truth, and of great courage against insane, manipulating ship computer capable of blowing up not only the ship wanting the destroy the fleet but thereatening the ship itself, but also the deadly 'anger' virus spreading that might end the people being saved as well as the crew . Kady is a great heroine for this story: a determinator with a power of sarcasm who doesn't just sit there but does stuff (but does have moments of vulnerability). The petite 'secret digger' with fearlessness of youth and a natural computer whiz. We see less of Ezra, but I grew fond of him, his humor, loyalty and growth - I'm glad this pair could patch things up and realise what they meant to each other. Nothing too mushy or sweet, just a right amount at the end, deserving it. The book is written as a dossier of hacked documents, sent a year after to a certain person (I was able to guess who) - cursing censored for them by blacking them out. There's emails, schematics, military files, IMs, medical reports, interviews etc. This spreads a little to the cover art too. Some small commentary marks are also added. It sounds complicated, but it actually makes the reading easier and quicker - another reason why I marathoned the ending *lol* The thickness doesn't matter (500+ pages). I also ended up liking AIDAN eventually, especially after he had a certain important change of mind , and saying this: "The universe owes you nothing, Kady. It has already given you everything. After all, it was here long before you, and it will go on long after you. The only way it will remember you is if you do something worthy of remembrance." -plus then learning afterwards that part of him survived as a 'seed' *grins* The receiver of the documents will not be pleased. Good. :) :P So, I was entertained, pulled in, and came out of reading happy. Slightly surprising but great reading experience, that's for sure 8) <3<3

This is the first time I've finished a book in ages. Between reading Very Long Things and being ill, I haven't been doing a good job of getting through titles, but I listened to Lost Stars while driving and cooking. I went into this one without high expectations. Generally speaking, my experiences with novel-only Star Wars characters has been incredibly hit or miss, and the ~will this heterosexual romance survive~ theme isn't one that gets me excited about young adult novels. But I'm basically vibrating with excitement for Bloodline: New Republic, and I thought listening to Lost Stars would be a good way to temper my expectations. If Claudia Gray's writing was lousy, I reasoned, I wanted to know before I started in on The Book I Have Been Waiting For Since Before TFA Came Out. It was a pleasant surprise to find that this book reads like the Star Wars equivalent of one of the only TNG episodes I enjoy, Lower Decks. Gray could easily have turned this story into a rote retelling of the original trilogy. Instead, she does world- and character-building that fleshes out a handful of Imperial Academy randos into some really satisfying characters. Ciena's roommates feel less developed than Thane's (well, than Nash Windrider, specifically), but the overall effect is still of a cast of characters who could easily feature in their own dramas while the Skywalker family implodes offscreen. The writing is pretty average, but by Star Wars novelization standards, that's pretty darned good. (Bless you, Timothy Zahn, you write great dialogue and plot like a motherfucker, but did you have to constantly use "grit" as a verb and refer to characters as "the other" in the awkwardest way possible?) Gray didn't have any particularly grating tells, so to speak, and that's always a relief for me in a tie-in novel. The audiobook is fun, with sound effects and background music, as Star Wars audiobooks always are. The narrator, Pierce Cravens, was pretty good, but his Ciena and Thane voices were sometimes a little too close for me--I couldn't always tell who was who when there weren't dialogue tags. It might have been fun to have two narrators, a man and a woman, to better differentiate POV sections throughout the book. Long story short, I'm still fucking pumped for Bloodline, and now I'm hoping they'll get around to publishing a sequel to this one, too. It's set up for one, imo, and I'd be delighted to see more from Ciena, Thane, and Nash in the future.

"You might not remember me, but --" "Travis Stephenson," she interrupts, her words like a roadblock. "Welcome home. Now leave me alone." It's always nice to come across a book that has a little bit of everything. Something Like Normal definitely covered its bases in the emotion department. If there was an emotion left to be discovered, I couldn't tell you what it was. Everything from fear, anger, joy, sorrow, caution and anticipation was explored. This particular (male) narrative was somewhat different because his story revolves around living life while continuing to suffer from Post Traumatic Stress Disorder due to his lingering pain and recollections of what happened during his time spent on tour in Afghanistan. "I left everything the way it was," she says as I drop my bag on the floor. "So it would feel familiar. Like home." I don't tell her that it doesn't feel like home at all. The voice of Travis sounds like the voice of a guy you might know. When he's not suffering from reliving the harsh reality of his life through nightmares, he's drinking and fighting and screwing just like any other guy. I appreciated the balance in his tough guy persona as he explored a missed opportunity of being with the girl he'd always had his eye on. Harper comes up alongside me, all green eyes and tousled hair. I could probably look at her forever and not get tired of that face. She's a good kisser. So good I want to beat the hell out of whoever taught her. She beams at me and it's almost enough to make up for the fact that I'm harder than trigonometry right now. Okay, so maybe those lines bordered on cheesy but they made me smile. It's always nice to see a bit of sweetness or humor interjected into a serious subject. There was a diner scene which happened to be quite funny. It's not quite as good as another famous diner scene from another book but I still had a big grin on my face while reading it. It was also nice to see the bond between male friends who have been to hell and back through war, yet can still joke around with each other. "I still have my half of the necklace, and last night I wrote in my diary, 'Dear Diary, Kenneth is my BFF. I hope he gets laid, because it's a special night when a man loses his virginity and contracts a sexually transmitted disease at the same time.'" I thought I was safe from the crying thing because for whatever reason, the flashback scenes sort of played out in my head as an old black and white movie and didn't seem to completely move me. Then the last couple of chapters happened and a lone tear fell from my eye (cue sad music). Don't worry though. The book has plenty of hope to go around. I thought the author did a great job of showing the rough road of healing that was ahead for our main character. If I had to mention one of my favorite things about Travis it's that he was not without flaws, yet he still managed to recognize and take responsibility for the bad things he had done to the one girl who had every right not to forgive him. Watching the relationship develop between Travis and Harper was sweet to witness. Neither one was able to guarantee the other much more than what they could give in the moment and I liked that. Realistic relationships for young people = my stamp of approval. I can't make that kind of promise when I'm only nineteen and owe the Marine Corps three more years of active duty. Anything could happen. If I had to come up with any complaint it would be that there were a few moments which made me feel uncomfortable as Travis described the enemy. I do understand though that this is the "trained" mentality of war. War forces you into an us vs. them, regardless of who you're fighting. This was a sweet book with a realistic love story. War is not pretty, nor are the aftereffects, but it was nice to see that hope does have a chance of winning out with the right support system around you, whether it be friends, family, or a special loved one. I don't know if my life will ever be completely normal again, but something like normal is a good start.

2.5 stars I've been meaning to read this book for quite a long time and am so glad I finally got to it. The reviews seem to waver between either loving it or... not so much, with little in between and I hoped I'd fall into the 'love it' category. Unfortunately that wasn't the case. The story is told through alternating chapters of 'Before'- which is basically the beginning of Reena and Sawyer's relationship all the way up until he leaves her behind, and the 'After'- when Sawyer finally shows up after being gone for two years and discovers he had left a pregnant Reena and now has a little girl. I absolutely loved the setup and the bare bones of the plot. I was very intrigued by this sort of angsty 'love' story and hoped to feel all the swoony longing of a new relationship to the heartbreak when it came to an end, the anger when he returns and perhaps a seed of hope of forgiveness and love again towards the end. And perhaps that's exactly what those who loved this book did indeed find. But for me it was missing so much, mostly characters to root for. I have no problem reading characters that are flawed but I need some sort of redeemable quality to surface before the novel ends. I kept hoping and hoping to find that here. I really wanted to love Reena and Sawyer, I truly did, but it just didn't happen. Reena was kind of bland to me. And I disliked her a great deal in the 'After'. She let Sawyer waltz back in entirely too easily, in my opinion. And that was evident from the first chapter. And Sawyer was far from swoony. He was constantly brushing off big issues and honestly didn't seem to love Reena at all. I didn't feel any real connection between them. Though I loved the setup and I loved the back and forth chapters that really did hold my interest and kept me turning the pages, I almost wonder if we spent too long in the 'Before' because I don't think the overall story was resolved enough by the end. I needed more. I'm disappointed when there was so much potential.

This was a family car trip book -- worried it would be "too young," but some very intense concepts here -- not the least of which is nature vs. nurture. When I was a tween, I read a book called The Grounding of Group 6 and the main idea still sticks with me today: it was a group of teens sent away to your average camp in the woods, only Group 6 was slated not to return -- parents' orders. Chilling. This book reminded me of that -- the fundamental things you think you know that get upended. The town of Serenity, NM is an idyllic place to be a kid -- it's small, remote, but has everything a kid could want: pools, trampolines, tree houses and it's small enough that everyone knows everyone and pretty much everyone is friends. Truly, no meanness or leaving anyone out. 14-yr old Eli Friedan is the son of the town mayor/school principal, so he is literally at the center of the action. He and his best friend Randy do typical boy stuff -- secret codes, challenges, etc. but typically stay in the parameters of the town's rules and the town itself. When the two decide to take a forbidden bike ride outside the town limits, Eli gets violently ill, they both get picked up by the Surety a.k.a. Purple People Eaters (the town's security/police force) and Randy gets sent off to boarding school. This sets a chain of events in motion that leads 5 young people to question everything they thought they knew. Randy leaves a secret coded message that alerts Eli that he is "special" along with about 10 others, 4 of whom figure prominently in unraveling this mystery: Malik, Hector, Torey and Amber. Their last names are all significant, though I don't recall them all! Without giving too much away, Serenity is a "planned" community in the extreme and the kids are human guinea pigs. The only criticism is the ending -- clearly a set-up for a sequel or series! Some humor here too makes this palatable/relatable for ages 12+ Without that, I'd use it with an older audience.

"The Invention of Hugo Cabret" by Brian Selznick is the perfect union of art and literature. It represents an entirely new way of reading, and therefore an entirely new way of understanding a story. This is something I've never seen before - and something I'll never see again. I'm not quite sure of what I love most about this book. I can't really decide whether it's the form that keeps fascinating me, or perhaps the beautifully intertwined storylines that left me breathless. Maybe it is both. It probably is. The form of the book, the use of illustrations as a replacement for words, is truly brilliant. It's what makes this books so special and groundbreaking for me. That the author is actually capable of stopping in the middle of a sentence and replace the letters with drawings, without slowing or ruining the plot, and keep moving the story forward, is really something worth a little admiration. However the plot itself is also worthy of some admiring words. The story has so many layers and angles, and so many possibilities for interpretation. On one side it is a story of a lonely boy, who finds consolation, friendship and love. On the other hand it is a story which praises art and inspiration in its many and various forms. But it is also a way of looking at life, a beautiful idea of life itself as a mechanic system - a clockwork waiting for the time to run out, like minutes and seconds ticking away with every heartbeat. I wish I could turn back my clock, and read this book again for the very first time. However that is not possible - which is the lesson we all have to learn.

Time. Precious time. Never enough but always too much. Running out, either too slow or too fast. Of course there is time for a cup of tea. We have five minutes. That is it. That is all. Or is it? What would time be like if it were not like it currently is? How would we measure life if time, as we know it, did not exist? This book reminded me of another I read a while back. I am pretty sure it was Kurt Vonnegut's Slaughterhouse-Five. If I am not mistaken, there comes a point in that novel when we are told that the past, the present and the future will always exist, and have always existed. The past will forever remain trapped in its present. It is right there, where it always, and as it always, has been. If only we could go back and forth, huh? I can see Henry's face as the thought crosses my mind. I must have said it out loud for he is now shaking his head as he studies his book, freshly brewed coffee in hand, "be careful what you wish for". Both a blessing and a curse, that is Henry's life. And his story? It is a whole new spectrum of emotions that make our ribcage feel way too small at times. And Clare... she found her other half way before they met. And she believed, she believed till her very last breath. This book is a roller coaster. This book is life. Feels like being at a Christmas dinner with the whole family after years apart. Laughs, tears, awkward stories, embarrassing silences... This book is everything. I found myself losing track of time as I read this. Quite ironic, wouldn't you say? Audrey Niffenegger takes us on this journey that does not apologize for its high ups and low downs. This book is not a paper tissue being given to you so that you can wipe away your tears. Instead, it is a strong hand squeezing yours as you cry your heart out. It is a reminder that you are not alone. You have yourself. And that self, that self you call yours, is made of all the people, all the moments, all the time. And it is breathtaking. I am truly in awe after this experience. Must get myself a copy in English. I have a feeling it will be interesting to reread. For now, if you will excuse me, I must find a way of fighting the insomnia. All this time has fed it and bathed it in water. And yes, it is already past midnight. Sigh.

This point as been building up from the very beginning of the series. Roland. He's been such a constant in Kate's life and now it's time for the showdown. We knew after the events in Magic Rises with Hugh that Kate's time of hiding had run out. Magic Breaks starts a few months after the events in Magic Rises. There's a Roland shaped cloud hovering over Kate, but business has to go forward as usual. Curran has been called away on business so Kate is tasked with sitting in on the Conclave (meeting between the Pack and the People). Ready to get the night over with, Kate goes, only of course things don't quite go as planned and the a Pack member is accused of killing a Master of the Dead. The Pack must pull it's resources to find out if the allegations are true in order to avoid an all out war with the People. When Hugh D'Ambray shows up Kate is certain that nothing is going to be easy about getting out of this one. Magic Breaks resolves the main story arc of the series that's been building for seven books now. It reads very much like the end of the series, but I was happy when Ilona Andrews announced that the series would be extended past Magic Breaks. It's a good thing because along with tying up a few story threads it also starts a few that have quite an impact in the Kate Daniels world and I'm glad that we'll get to explore those developments in future books. Magic Breaks both was a was not what I was expecting. I think this is a good thing in that why would I want to read a book where I knew exactly how everything would play out? Ilona Andrews definitely threw in some major twists and turns, most of which surround the final confrontation with Roland. It's very difficult to say much because I don't want to give anything away. I liked going into this book and being pleasantly surprised by the outcome. I think, rather than writing it the way we all suppose it should be, the way Magic Breaks turns out makes things all the more interesting for the future. I flew through this book. Like Magic Rises, it's left me thinking about things long after closing the back cover and I'm eager to start a re-read. Try as they might I think the series is much more enjoyable if started from the beginning. I think to really appreciate how far Kate has come you need to see where it started. I highly recommend this series to any / everyone. It's a very well written series. I'm now faced with the sadness of waiting another year until Magic Shifts. They are always well worth the wait.

For those of you who haven't yet read Chandler - and I won't question why - I'm here to tell you, the man can write. You read him for the words, for the atmosphere, not for plot. The High Window itself has nothing special to recommend it; it's another instalment, one of many roughly equally as good. (First time around The Lady in the Lake was my favourite; my wife, who read them all this year, liked The Long Goodbye.) But it's the one I re-read last week (cos it's tight, short, cuts to the punch) so it'll do. The Belfont Building was eight stories of nothing in particular that had got itself pinched off between a large green and chromium cut-rate suit emporium and a three-storey and basement garage that made a noise like lion cages at feeding time. The small dark narrow lobby was as dirty as a chicken yard. The building directory had a lot of vacant space on it. [...] There were two open-grille elevators but only one seemed to be running and that not busy. An old man sat inside it slack-jawed and watery-eyed on a piece of folded burlap on top of a wooden stool. He looked as if he had been sitting there since the Civil War and had come out of that badly. Thing is, Chandler (it seems) could churn out this stuff in his sleep. Every building's a Belfont Building, or as vivid; every elevator operator a Civil War veteran, or as colourful; every character - from the "long-limbed languorous" showgirl ("From thirty feet away she looked like a lot of class. From ten feet away she looked like something made up to be seen from thirty feet away.") to the "hard boy" ("A great long gallows of a man with a ravaged face and a haggard frozen right eye that had a clotted iris and the steady look of blindness.") - as realised as can be for as long as their in sight. And here's the clincher: "in sight"? So who's watching? Probably the greatest near-non-entity hero/anti-hero short of Kafka's K., P.I. Philip Marlowe, who puts the "eye" in private eye, whose gaze, thanks to British poet turned Black Mask pulp-magazine workhorse Raymond Chandler's near-impossible deftness, is as sharp and resplendent as they come. How does he do it? Give this hard-bitten hard-boiled hard-drinking tough guy such eloquence? It's something to see. And somehow, though (or because) we know virtually nothing about him, this fragile word-edifice that is Marlowe convinces us utterly. We love the guy. Who cares if the plots barely add up, or by the time they do we're past caring? When he talks tender to the femmes fatales I defy you (women especially - Chandler, against the odds, and despite low-grade ingrained chauvinism indicative of his times, is a ladies' man) not to feel a shiver. It's limited in range, but for the slightest tweaks it never changes, but for what it is it's of a very high order, beyond Hammett (Chandler's inventor), beyond genre, unique (despite the imitators) as few genre writers ever have been. When at the end of The High Window he drives the innocent young woman victim to her parents' home in Wichita and says goodbye, I almost teared up at his laconic summation: I had a funny feeling as I saw the house disappear, as though I had written a poem and it was very good and I had lost it and would never remember it again. Sure, maybe that's all Chandler is, a poem he's forgotten. But what a poem! It could break your heart.

weak 4-stars The beginning was weak. It started out like any other young-adult book, and gave the impression that the author was going to include meek characters like Kaz in Karou's adventures, despite him being boring and unnecessary. Taylor did a wonderful job of letting the audience get to know Karou, and uncover her secrets as the story progressed, but her 'real-world' characters felt like unneeded additions. They lacked something. Zusanna has some depth, but she's in the book so little, and her characters develops so little beyond the-best-friend archetype that she became a stepping stone between one part of the story to the next; she had little significant role in the grand scheme of things. The middle of the story was by far the best. Once Taylor got it going there was no stopping her. Her writing is beautiful, mesmerizing even. The romance that sprung up between Akiva and Karou was, while expected, fiery and something to be desired. Her character are tangible and lovable. Brimstone is my favorite character; he's strict, and mysterious, but despite this exterior Taylor hints at his warmth. Of course, I thought-- this is great. This will be great until the end. I even said that there is nothing stopping her from grabbing gold-- but that was only true until it wasn't. Part three was, in large part, completely unnecessary. A frustrating kind of not-needed, because there was parts that were needed, which made the rest of it feel like it should be there. I don't know how to describe it, but ... large parts were boring and just there to fill space and the blanks. This being said, I am a big girl. I am also an intelligent human being. I do not need for the gaps to be filled in for me. I get it. Thank you. My friend, who loves this series, insists that the second book is her favorite. So, we'll see how the second one goes once I get my hands on the time to read it. Wish me luck~ Happy reading.

That this book is beautifully composed is evident after the first chapter. Morton also has an uncanny ability to move forward and backward in time effortlessly and with no confusion for the reader. And the elements to make this mystery chilling were all there - a damp and decrepit old castle, three equally crumbling old spinster-sisters (one of whom is a formidable old piece of business with a smile that could crack her face), and a self-styled investigator who is keeping secrets of her own. Sadly, it just went on, and on, and *on* too long and trudging through page after page of narrative that built atmosphere as opposed to being there to drive forward the plot created a love-hate relationship with this novel that soured me even on the big reveal - where the character I was suddenly to discover was a true noble martyr was already cemented in my head as someone I didn't give a rat's fuzzy little behind about. The themes of sisters and secrets and the contrasts of love and resentment are gorgeously crafted, though, and the arc of Edie's relationship with Meredith, her mother, was equally beautiful. Verdict? Don't miss this one by Morton but don't make it her first title on your to-read list either.

This is a difficult book to discuss without getting into some spoilers, but here goes. I remember about a year ago hearing that a lot of people reading this book were pretty disappointed with it. I felt that too - the characters aren't especially likeable at the beginning, and the writing in certain points is immature and almost embarrassingly bad, as though the author was trying to make the characters likeable but didn't quite know how. Being an impatient person, I skipped ahead to see if things were going to get better, and discovered that most of the flaws in the early part of the book are quite deliberate - the book does improve, and things do get very interesting. In so doing, I did spoil a pretty big twist in the book for myself. And this is really the most confusing part of the popularity of this book, because I think that twist is supposed to be a surprise, but without knowing that twist was coming, I would in no way have continued reading. Because, deliberate or not, bad is still bad, and without reassurance that things were going to improve, I don't have that kind of time to waste. I totally do have that kind of time, actually, but still - if the twist is what retroactively justifies the beginning of the book, what is the incentive to read to it unless you know it's coming, and if you know it's coming does it really count as a twist? All of that said, this is a pretty good story, once you get all the pieces. For me, it's interesting to read a crime story from the perspective of the suspect & victim, rather than from the point of view of a detective. As for the ending, I understand that it's not real popular among fans of the book, and I understand and disagree with that. It took a couple of cheats to get there, but I think it's the ending the book deserves.
