** spoiler alert ** 3.5 stars I'm torn between a 3 and 4 star rating, because on the one hand it was a fascinating read, but on the other hand it gradually got shoddy. Instead of a dramatic climax, perhaps a showdown between Hilly and the maids (that's what I was hoping for as the chapters left to read got smaller), the book just sort of peters out in a feeble sort-of happily-ever-after. No retribution, no in-your-face victory, nothing. I mean, I was happy with the understanding some of the maids got with their employers, but I didn't really feel any justice done. What with all the worrying of the backlash that could come from publishing, and the jumpy nervousness during the last half of the book, you'd expect a more dramatic outcome. Or maybe it's just a more accurate portrayal of attempts at change back then? Big efforts result in small successes. But the historical accuracy and the touchy topic itself is only one aspect of this book. The book is divided into three narratives, Aibileen, Minny and Skeeter. There was something a little too stereotypical about each one. Aibileen's your average don't ask, don't tell type of maid, who keeps her grief hidden and is generally quiet, polite and sensible, the motherly type. Minny's a back-talking, sassy mother of five, and of course her and Aibileen are best friends because their traits complete each other. Skeeter is a white girl who doesn't really fit in with the other white ladies of the town. Hilly Holbrook is the main antagonist, and good God I have never hated a character with such contempt since Dolores Umbridge. I kept waiting for her moment of demise, and while I guess you could say she got her just deserts (no pun intended), it really didn't feel like justice was served (okay, maybe the puns are a little intentional). I guess you could call Minny my favorite. She's a tough, no-nonsense person who gets things done, with a heart of gold. But there were certain aspects that didn't really seem consistent with her character. The beatings by her husband, for example. I really couldn't understand why she would it take it and not kick his worthless behind in the streets, especially since she never tolerated anything from her employers. Skeeter plays the role I've come to really loathe, the white person who swoops in to save the less fortunate coloured people. She never showed any real conviction or emotion towards the issue of black rights. Her strong relationship with her own maid, and her differentiating traits (being tall, frizzy hair, ambitious, etc.) puts her in a position where she has to find a different sort of life, other than a dainty wife and society woman doing pseudo-charity work. The book she writes was more a means to jump-start her writing career than any real effort to further the civil rights issue. At places the book was heavy-handed when it came to race issues. From Skeeter's point of view, it seems all she could see was skin colour. When she talks about driving through Aibileen's neighbourhood, she uses the word coloured and black so many times I mentally screamed, 'Yes, we get it, you're in a black neighbourhood!' I understand that race was a major issue, but it seems exaggerated here to the point where everyone's thoughts were divided into black and white. The whole Stuart/Patricia side story was utterly pointless and doesn't really add anything of value to the story, except maybe to highlight some of Skeeter's personal beliefs about men and marriage. But the idea of the story was a good one, and it's an unfortunate truth that many novels are successfully purely for the novelty of their premise. I think it could've been written a little better, perhaps be less repetitive, maybe a stronger ending. Just my two cents.

DNF at page 188 I've been pushing myself to finish this book the whole time I've been reading it, but I just realised that I don't care at all about anyone in the novel or about anything that's happening. I'm just not clicking with Legacy of Kings at all. There are too many things I don't like for me to connect to the book so I'm just going to put it down instead of forcing myself through something I'm not enjoying. So here's what I dislike about this book: It's not what I was promised. Admittedly, all I knew going into this book was that it was historical fiction with some fantastical elements about Alexander the Great. I was excited, I haven't read any historical fiction set in Ancient Greece. Needless to say this wasn't a great place to start in that regard. It doesn't even feel like Ancient Greece, I kept forgetting that it was set there, it feels so Roman. Which brings me to... So many historical inaccuracies. Look, I'm not even going to pretend I'm an expert on Ancient History. I'm not. I know very little about Ancient Greece and Alexander the Great. What I do know, though, is that arenas weren't even a thing in Ancient Greece, and they didn't like bloodsports when the Romans tried to introduce them. Then there's Alexander himself, who loved himself so much he named a city after himself when he was still in his teens. LoK's Alexander is selfless, kind, not at all proud or arrogant. I mean ??? Everything I've heard or read about him totally contradicts Eleanor Herman's portrayal of him. The only thing Alexander the Great loved as much as himself was Hephaestion, and I was hoping to see that love portrayed in this novel. It's not. A girl comes between them very early on (surprise) and I just don't understand why Alexander would make a fool of his best friend in front of guards and the public just to invite some random peasant girl back to the palace, or why Hephaestion would let Cynane put doubts in his mind when he felt so strongly for Alexander and knew Alexander felt the same about him. Looking at the historical figure, the Alexander in this novel just doesn't make any sense. It's written in third person, present tense. I generally enjoy third person, and I'm not totally averse to third person, present tense, but in this novel there was a fairly large amount of sentences that didn't work in third person. I'm not a fan of present tense but it's bearable, and if this had been written in first person the writing wouldn't have bothered me as much. At times it felt like I was reading a history textbook. There were bits of information - interesting bits of information, to be fair - dotted throughout the text, which is fine, but it was done in a way that didn't quite flow with the story, or they weren't completely relevant to what was happening, and it just didn't work very well, in my opinion. Other than that it the problems I had with it were minor - little to no character development, big leaps in time that were unexplained, nothing was happening, everyone seemed to be plotting revenge against each other. Also Jacob and Zo seem to just be there for no reason. I just feel like this had the potential to be amazing, and it wasn't.

Luckily, Dee is able to sell her heart to a demon (not a spoiler - this is on the flap) so she can cut her parents loose. I really, really disliked this book. I just renewed my Owlcrate subscription and now I have buyer's remorse.

The songs are just briefly mentioned and then brushed away. It's pointless and yet it's the selling point for the novel. The book also has a sickening view of romance as the reason to live basically. The few girl characters that exist only exist in their relation to males and are horribly written as nearly one-dimensional tropes. The fact that a woman wrote this book is unfathomable to me. It's also riddled with mentions that girls are not geeks and don't enjoy those sorts of things. If they do it's fake or they're some sort of precious gem. There is no satisfying conclusion, huge events are explained away with "I wasn't getting enough sleep,". Characters who deserve to have justice brought to them end up being loved and romanticized because when you're hurt doing anything is okay and completely forgivable. A novel which had a great chance to be a poignant view of suicide ended up being a messed up romantic mystery that had one of the least satisfying conclusions I have ever seen. Despite all this, it at least presents an interesting playlist which it refuses to actually use adequately; http://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=... So enjoy that, it's probably a lot more fun than the book was. Make sure to check out http://betterbooks.tumblr.com/ for new reviews every Tuesday!

Please note there will be minor spoilers for Shift (Shade #2). With Logan now a ghost, Aura can begin to wrap up the mourning process that began almost a year ago - this time for his ghost. Safe in the knowledge that Zach and his family are on a plane home to the UK, Aura is ready for as normal final year of high school as anyone can be when you're able to see ghosts. Then Aura gets a call that changes everything, unwinding a thread that begins explains Aura being the first and Zach being the last over the course of a harrowing adventure. I'd been looking forward to Shine ever since I finished Shift, although I have to say there was a bit of trepidation coming into this one. There were some things in Shift that really didn't sit well with me, the biggest being the blase outlook toward physicality. I know the whole point of, for example, things that happened between Logan and Aura exist to display the conflict that she's going through, but the few interchanges between Aura and Dylan just rubbed me the wrong way. I was slightly nervous that this book would carry that on and that, perhaps, Logan would never fade. Thankfully that wasn't the case with Shine, and to be fair, I enjoyed this installment much more without Logan. In fact, my favorite Logan moment in the series appears at the end, which was a rather nice way to tie everything up. Aura definitely had the opportunity to explore herself more, even if it was in the setting of chasing down information. Aura is an enjoyable MC for me as she has that appealing headstrong quality without being overwhelming, but also the sense to merely observe if the matter calls for it. Not to mention that Smith-Ready has Aura's voice down perfectly; a lot of times it's difficult to get into a character, despite how strong of a character they may be, if the right presentation of words isn't there. It's very easy to fall into Aura's head, which makes the progression of the story much swifter. My favorite thing, though, about the book, is the world building. I know that this is something I discuss quite often (especially with dystopian novels), but this series is a great example of where the premise of the story (Aura's and Zach's history) wonderfully sets the background without beating the reader over the head with it. We know why Aura lives where they do (Maryland), we know even a bit about her lineage (her Italian grandmother lives in Philadelphia) and there are relevant hints back to this as the story unfolds that is a pleasant connection of information. What brought me to this series is the idea of a Shift in the first place and the way it was so seamlessly integrated into a recognisable present-day society. What kept me was that, with this last book, we know why it happened and what, if anything, can be done about it. A well-done tying up of events with an interspersion of characters that take the story and run with it in a good way. Shine is my favorite installation of the trilogy, and was truly a wonderful way to finish the series. If you're looking to read a paranormal without instashipping, partnered with a well-researched and well-integrated premise and story then you'll definitely enjoy this series. Thanks again to Simon & Schuster, and I'm looking forward to what else Smith-Ready will create in the future.

I was a little hesitent when I requested this book. I don't normally like to read books about Rape, but I was hoping this one wouldn't make me too angry. The writting was surperb! I really connected with Val, the main character. I felt so bad for her and everything she endured from the onset of the book. When Val's mother is out of town she throws a party where there is underage drinking. Her and her best friend Mimi are getting ready when the guests start to arrive. Val puts her little sister to bed ( had me cringing at the mention of a smal child there) and then begins to look for Adam, whom she is crushing on. Val drinks two wine coolers, and when Adam finds her he gives her something else. After a bit ( not really long at all). Adam suggests they all play spin the bootle, he flicks the bottle so that it lands on Val and they go off together. Val get sick and ends up puking on Adam's shoes. She passes out and I guess the party ends shortly after that. The chapters in the beginning go from Before to After and switch a few times, so you get the Rape in sections. Val wakes up with a major hangover, and her little sister goes out to play. Adam ends up coming back over and while Val is passed out on the couch he removes most of her clothes. When she awakens, you can imagine what happens. Val ends up telling her mother, who then calls the cops. So the rape charge is made. The whole school ends up hearing about it and while a few believe Val, most of the school, her now ex best friend included, think that she made it up. I know how fast and vicious rumors can spread and be in High school, so that wasn't really surprising, what really got me going and had me so mad I almost walked away, was the Principal of the school. I won't go into details about it and ruin anythign, just know that if that was my daughter, I would have his head on a stick! Val ends up in a support group, and while listening to the other girls talk, she starts to think that maybe she wasn't really raped. I will say that I am happy about the support that the other girls gave her, and the message in the book was really glear and one of support for all young/old girls going through this. I love the book, and will be purchasing my own copy as soon as I can. I feel that this is one book that really needs to be read by everyone, you may not be a victim yourself, but you may know someone who is. In the acknowledgements of the book, the author states that she herself was a 16 year old rape survivor, and that a portion of the proceeds from Rape Girl will go to Pandora's Project and RAINN. I LOVE when authors take a portion of the money they make and donate to a cause.
Got about halfway and the book still isn't grabbing me. Maybe I'll revisit it later, but probably not.

You can find this review and others on my blog http://www.shades0fpaper.wordpress.com "But there is one part of this that hurts. The carefree, normal part. The part of me that was lost when we first moved and that I'll never get back." I have to say I've heard nothing about this book before I decided to pick it up, and I honestly don't know why. This was my second Ashley Elston's novel I've read, and after loving This is Our Story, I wanted to pick up another book by her, so this was one I was intrigued by. And even though I didn't adore it as much as I liked her other novel, I have to say it was still a pretty good book and I enjoyed reading that type of plot. I believe I have never read a book where our main character was in a witness protection program (there was one episode in Criminal Minds and I found it so interesting but no books), so reading through the eyes of someone who is in one was quite unique and intriguing (even though it probably wasn't 100% accurate but still). There was also this whole mystery surrounding the main character Meg and her family and the reason why they were in that program. I really loved that atmosphere, it made me want to keep reading to discover what happened and why they were running away from, so that was pretty cool! "He hugs me tight while I look behind him, scanning faces like I did a few seconds ago. And like I will do for the rest of my life." I have to say sometimes I wanted to strangle Meg, but I think she was a very real character other times. I loved the relationship with her sister (she was super adorable) and even though there was a lot of drama with the family, I have to say her interactions with her little sister were pretty nice. You could see how they cared about each other and I love to read stories about sisterhood (even though it wasn't the main focus on the novel). I also really enjoyed the romance and her love interest. Usually ships are a hit or miss to me (mostly hits but there were other times where I hate the couples!) but I really like Ethan! There's a bit insta love-ish at first, but I really enjoyed how the author made them friends before turning them into lovers (I'M LIVING FOR THOSE STORIES WHEN THEY'RE DONE RIGHT) and also Ethan was a really cute guy who worried so much about Meg and honestly, he wasn't mean or anything. "Don't forget who is a friend and who is a foe. And don't forget, sometimes a person can be both." What I have to add is that it was a bit predictable to me. Now me being me I knew I had 90% chances to discover the whole plot twist before it actually happened, and I was right. I knew most of those things, so they didn't surprise me as much as if I probably wouldn't know (duh). There were a couple of things that felt quite obvious and so I was like "well... okay", BUT there was something I didn't know that had to do with the things I guessed, so that's why I didn't lower my rating that much, because I still enjoyed the story. And after that ending... I really want to continue reading the second installment because I've already had a few theories and I'm super pumped to figure everything out!

The Tipping Point: How Little Things Can Make a Big Difference is a standalone nonfiction/educational business book written by journalist Malcolm Gladwell. As noted in the synopsis, "the tipping point is that magic moment when an idea, trend, or social behavior crosses a threshold, tips, and spreads like wildfire." Mr. Gladwell offers multiple examples of this phenomenon in various domains including business, education, religion, health, and crime. My husband ONLY reads business books (how boring right?) and he has suggested this book to me on multiple occasions. When he shared with me the definition of a tipping point, I thought it was pretty much common sense and wasn't overly motivated to read this. But, my husband doesn't get excited over much in the reading world so I gave in. I have to admit though that Mr. Gladwell's thoroughness provided a valuable learning experience. I anticipate viewing business advertisements and public policy/protocol with new eyes now that I have a bit more insight into the psychology, sociology, and epidemiology behind them. Check it out! If interested, take a look at a Q&A with the author HERE.

I'm a huge Julia Quinn fan, so much that I willingly forgive her for things I castigate other writers about, such as historical anachronisms and 21st characters plopped into historical settings. I was, however, disappointed in her last book (The Secrets of Sir Richard Kenworthy) and I deliberately delayed reading this one in fear of being disappointed once again. Well, I was not disappointed. Billie (Sybilla) Bridgerton is the oldest child of Viscount and Vicountess Bridgerton of Aubrey Hall in Kent. She has two younger brothers, Edmund (who later fathers Anthony, Benedict, Colin, etc.) and Hugo. Billie has taken over much of the estate's business, particularly the farming aspects, which she finds fascinating. (JQ doesn't explain why Lord Bridgerton has relinquished these tasks to Billie. I confess some irritation over this omission and hope it's explained in following books.) George Rokesby, Lord Kennard, and the future Earl of Manston, lives with his family at Crake House, also in Kent, just three miles from Aubrey Hall. He has two younger brothers, Edward and Andrew, and a sister, Mary. Edward, Andrew, Mary and Billie are all very close in age and always have been great friends. Billie and George, though, have always been rather at odds. So each one finds it definitely disconcerting when their relationship evolves into something different. Let me say that I just loved George. He is strong and dependable and everything a girl could want, including a lovely sense of humor. And I liked Billie as well. She is smart and kind and funny and confident in her normal sphere. She has a sensible attitude about life - she strains against the bonds of social convention (she wears breeches around the estate and rides astride) but complies, more or less gracefully, when circumstances dictate. I loved that JQ gave us some background for some of the things in the Bridgerton series, like the Pall Mall game and the Mallet of Death. I can see bits of Billie in her nieces Daphne, Hyacinth and Francesca. I really look forward to the other books in this series.

The Burning Sky is a creative fantasy novel with an appealing heroine. Iolanthe is smart, brave, loyal, and resourceful. She may be prophesied to be this great mage but she has to work really hard to master her abilities. I enjoyed the parts of the book where she was at Eton passing as a boy for safety reasons. She is something of a tomboy and has had an unusual upbringing which made it plausible. I enjoyed the relationship between Iolanthe and Titus. While Titus is attracted to her right away, the romance develops at a slower pace because of more pressing concerns (and the fact that she has to pretend to be Archer Fairfax, a fellow student at Eton). I also liked the friendships that Iolanthe developed with the other boys at Eton, especially with Kashkari. I look forward to seeing more of the secondary characters. They added much needed humor at times. As much fun as her life at Eton was, I really found myself intrigued by the magical world too. To help her learn to harness the elements she hasn't mastered yet, Titus trains her in The Crucible, a place that reminded me of the Holodeck from Star Trek. The entrance is through a book of fairy tales and you have to proceed through various levels, fighting dragons and wyverns and other challenges. I also found their mode of transportation to be interesting. People "vault" from place to place but they can only vault certain distances and so many times in a day. It reminded me of apparating and disapparating from the Harry Potter books. While the book has excellent world building, I thought it read like a page turner and didn't get bogged down in detail. It was easy to catch on to the rules of the magical world and it also helped that part of the book was set in historical London too. I definitely had some questions that were not answered at the end of the book though I have some suspicions about the Bane. He is really a mysterious figure for most of the story and doesn't get as much page time as the creepy Inquisitor. I found her to be very menacing and she added suspense to the story whenever she appeared. I don't know why I bother reviewing these anymore. They are almost always 5 stars for me. When I read one, I can't put it down. The plots are great, I love the characters, the action is exciting. The books always culminate in an amazing showdown that is seat-of-your-pants gripping. (I don't even know if that last clause works but I like it so I'm keeping it.) I love Harry. I know a lot of you don't (though really, don't listen to the audiobooks, I hear the narrator is annoying) but I do. I actually like that he's kind of chivalrous (NOT a chauvinistic) which is usually sexist but it's cute in him. His chivalry isn't about opening doors or covering mud puddles with his coat; it's that he is always trying to protect women even though he absolutely acknowledges and is impressed by the power of women. It tears him up when he thinks of women getting hurt and it moves him to violence against the perpetrators, which is funny because most of the women are perfectly capable of taking care of themselves. He even acknowledges this about himself in a self-deprecating way. Murphy is always calling him on his crap and is always in the thick of things with him, equally powerful in her own human way. The supernatural people, both good and bad, are both male and female and are equally powerful. Leadership positions are help by both men and women, including the current leader of the wizard guard who is female. I get the impression that Butcher isn't sexist but he likes this gallant side of Harry. There isn't any "she was in power even though she was a woman" or even acknowledging that someone might find it odd to find a woman doing that particular job. (Well, I can't remember the beginning books that well and he might have mentioned that it was hard for Murphy as a female cop. But when he met her she was already head of her division.) The de facto leader of the White House, who is the best White House vampire leader he's seen, is a woman who is very attractive and very dangerous to him. I'm always annoyed that Butcher says people speak "quietly" way too often. I always love Bob the skull and wish he were in it more. I always wish he and Murphy would just do the nasty and get it over with. I'm really glad he's gotten rid of weak love interests. Thomas is so sexy and I love that he doesn't care about a person's gender in his sexual conquests. Ramirez is very hot, too. But Mouse is my favorite character. Okay, specifics about this book. I liked how adamant/rigid/angry Harry was with his apprentice when she broke the rules and I like how the situation was resolved. I love the boat action sequence. Finally, a little more about Mouse is revealed. I even like the cat and was only mildly annoyed when someone referred to him as the master of the house. Very mild spoiler (one tiny part of the book) that won't ruin the book at all: In one scene, Harry has to pretend to be gay and I laughed so hard I snorted. The mini-city is ridiculous as it would be impossible to have created let alone maintain. The scale alone meant that it wouldn't have fit in his subbasement. It's an easy gimmick that I don't like. I'm mad at Murphy for being a commitment-phobe and love that Harry doesn't want short-term relationships (revealed in last book). They are meant to be together God damn it! One of the mini-plots was awkward and there were so many characters in the book, some with similar names (Anne and Anye in similar roles) that it was hard to keep them straight. I love the ex love interest who comes back from his past and if Harry can't have Murphy, a woman like that is perfect for him: she's smart, sexy, sarcastic, imperfect and extremely powerful, much like he is. My favorite part of the book was the last three pages and I'll leave it at that. What I love best of all though is that morality isn't always black and white and choosing the right path isn't always easy for Harry. He's still struggling with the demon in his head. (He mentions that it's been three years! I don't feel like it's been that long. Does anyone know what book she first appeared in?) As I've come to expect from Butcher, this was another tight, focused novel with tons of action and drama and the usual snarky humor that I love, even when Harry is being an idiot. (The scenes between him and Ramirez are classic Butcher.) If you like this series, don't miss this one.

She does this to come at peace with her feelings and to finish a chapter in her life, so to speak. One day, her letters get sent out by someone anonymous, and Lara Jean has to figure out what to do with the embarrassing secrets that wash ashore. Lara Jean seems really childish at times. The story itself is sweet but pretty predictable, it feels as if I've read a book or seen a movie similar to it so many times, even though that is probably proper nonsense. My biggest problem however was the ending.. because it literally had none. It made the book feel very.. pointless. Yet.. this book helped me to get back into reading. It was sweet, cute and light. Four and a half rock stars! This had absolutely everything my little heart could wish for. Sarcasm, double-entendres, humour, a sassy heroine and an aloof hero. They travel the world with a rock band. Nuff said. Sophie is a social media liaison consultant and travelling to London for a job interview. Somehow she has been bumped from cattle class (sorry, economy) to first class where she is sat next to the most beautiful man on the planet. Unfortunately, it appears that he didn't get the personality to match and starts creating a fuss because he paid for two first class seats. Now when I read the first few chapters of this book at the end of the first book in the series Idol, I carped about how this just wouldn't be possible - they would have told Sophie that the flight was full rather than give a first class seat that had been paid for (and they cost in the $000's) to someone from economy who paid a couple of hundred dollars for a seat. Well Kristen Callihan explains it beautifully. The beautiful man is Gabriel "Scottie" Scott and he is the manager of probably the biggest rock band in the world, Kill John. Since he was such an ass and made such a fuss, Sophie decides to have some fun at his expense. But it seems as though the uptight guy in a suit actually has a sense of humour under his cashmere vest-top and in a weird way they hit it off. Until Sophie explains why she is travelling to London and the guy reveals that he is Gabriel Scott and they could very easily be working together. I don't want to reveal anything more of the plot, suffice it to say there are rock star shenanigans, tour buses, opulence and cuddles. And Kristen Callihan nails the Britishisms, well-played it's hard to get it right but she does it. Just two things. First, Pret a Manger doesn't sell egg salad and rocket (arugula) sandwiches in the UK, that's an American sandwich filling (and yes I checked because I get my lunch sandwich there every day). Second, my fully paid for copy from Amazon had lots (between 10 and 20) of silly typos in it: "he" instead of "the", the occasional misspelling etc. I found that surprising, I'm used to it in ARCs but not in a published book. Other than that? Perfection. I loved every second of reading it. Kristen Callihan can do no wrong in my eyes.

I'm really confused about what I can write and what I can't write here on Goodreads. One of my recent reviews was deleted for being not about the book. Your review of Logic: A Very Short Introduction was recently flagged by Goodreads members as potentially off-topic. As the review is not about the book, it has been removed from the site. I can't complain about that, they were quite right - I had actually shelved that book on my TO READ site, so by definition, I hadn't read it yet. So the logic is, I think, that ANY remark about a book you haven't read yet is "potentially off-topic". This means that ANY comments you have made about a book on your TO READ shelves should be deleted by the unhappy staff members who are tasked with zapping this stuff. (Do they read George Orwell essays in their lunch breaks? I would like to think so.) They don't need to wait for the non-review to be flagged, they can just go ahead and zap any review they find on anyone's TO READ shelf. But, you know, they aren't doing that... so far. Well, not to me, anyway. So until we get a little more clarity about this, I would like to present a short entertainment which I freely admit cannot possibly be a review of Tampa because I haven't read it yet, and therefore is "potentially off-topic". Okay, enough with the mealymouth, I'll make it simple : it's COMPLETELY off-topic. There you go, I'm trying to help here. HOW TO CHOOSE YOUR NEXT NOVEL When I'm three quarters through my current novel I get the urge to pick the next one. It's a horrible urge - next, next, next. O the disease of novel-reading - one ailment I hope I'm never cured of. So anyway, which one to choose out of the dozens on the groaning shelf? The one with the sexiest cover? The one with the waggly tail? No, that's how you choose which dog to buy. How about the serious one which has been sitting glowering at me for about a decade and which will make me a better person? So I thought I'd approach the problem scientifically this time, and base my decision on First Lines. I mean, if I was a novelist, I'd want to spear the reader like a fish with a really strong first line. So I'm the fish, spear me. Here are ten contenders, taken from the groaning shelf at random. 1) Tampa by Alissa Nutting I spent the night before my first day of teaching in an excited loop of hushed masturbation on my side of the mattress, never falling asleep. Wow, like not sleeping for the whole night? Wouldn't you be totally zombified on your first day at the new job? Anyway, yeah, I want to know what kind of nutcase we're dealing with here, so I'm hooked. 2) Platform by Michel Houellebecq Father died last year. Oh that's so tiny I will allow him another sentence. I don't subscribe to the theory by which we only become truly adult when our parents die; we never become truly adult. Mmm, so so. I can't say I'm bothered one way or the other. 3) The Lowland by Jhumpa Lahri East of the Tolly Club, after Deshapran Sashmal Road splits in two, there is a small mosque. I read a book about literary devices and one chapter was about first lines of novels and the guy was saying that you really need a strong first line, obviously, and he was reeling off all these great ones, you know, Call me Fishmeal and The clocks were striking 13 and all of those. Well, it seems most novelists do not subscribe to this idea at all and are happy to write very dull first sentences. 4) The Mosquito Coast by Paul Theroux We drove past Tiny Polski's mansion house to the main road, and then the five miles into Northampton, Father talking the whole way about savages and the awfulness of America - how it got turned into a dope-taking, door-locking, ulcerated danger-zone of rabid scavengers and criminal millionaires and moral sneaks. Yes, that's more like it. I'm interested. Let's go. 5) Continental Drift by Russell Banks It's not memory you need for telling this story, the sad story of Robert Raymond Dubois, the story that ends along the back streets and alleys of Miami, Florida, on a February morning in 1981... Hold on there, Russell ! I finally found a full stop towards the end of page one, it's one of those clausally incontinent whoppers. But yeah, I like that. 6) Burr by Gore Vidal Shortly before midnight, July 1, 1833, Colonel Aaron Burr, aged seventy-seven, married Eliza Jumel, born Bowen fifty-eight years ago (more likely sixty-five but remember : she is prone to litigation! Well, this is lighthearted enough. He's trying to put me at ease - this will be history with its tie loosened. Gets its jauntiness in immediately. Nice. 7) A Fire Upon the Deep by Vernor Vinge How to explain? How to describe? Even the omniscient viewpoint quails. Oh deario. This is a much-praised space-opera but is that not one of the clunkient, least appetising first lines you've ever seen? Quails? Who says quails? is this going to be a novel where they use verily and quoth? Back on the shelf. 0 out of 10. 8) Omensetter's Luck by William H Gass Now folks today we're going to auction off Missuss Pimber's things. I love this, I instantly want to read on. There's no quotation marks, this being The Gassman, a notorious modernist, so I'm expecting it to be all streamily conscious and that. 9) Crystal Vision by Gilbert Sorrentino I will call this drink the Flowers of Summer, the Magician says, I would call a drink the Flowers of Summer too, but I hate magicians. 10) Blonde by Joyce Carol Oates There came Death hurtling along the Boulevard in waning sepia light. Ooh, that's a bit pulpy and lurid. It's not all going to be like that is it? This is supposed to be about Marilyn Monroe, and she did die. Must be one of those stories that start at the end and then flashback (for 738 pages). So, we have a winner. Alissa, it's you, you saucy minx. Well, this year was not very prolific, in terms of reading. I blame James Joyce, largely, for his excellent Ulysses. While not my favorite read of the year, it was mostly engaging and brilliant in long stretches. I think I'm good for one big, difficult read a year, and that's about it. I need to tackle Proust sometime in the near future, probably next year. Probably. As far as "best of", I don't have a lot to choose from, but here goes: Best Novel: Experimental Film by Gemma Files. Best Graphic Novel: Space Riders, Volumen Uno: Vengeful Universe by Fabian Rangel and Alexis Ziritt. Best Non-fiction: Spring Chicken: Stay Young Forever. Best Short Fiction (collection or anthology): Burnt Black Suns by Simon Strantzas. Now, I must admit that my interactions on Goodreads have been minimal this past year. I've been working on a non-fiction book and self-published a role-playing game supplement, so that's curtailed some of my social media time, not to mention my reading time. Again, though, I can't overemphasize how much of my time was taken up by Joyce. When I pick up a book I know nothing about, I give it between 75-100 pages of "fair chance" reading. It doesn't take up too much of my time and if after that, it's not really grabbing me, I just put it down (as an aside, that why almost all of the books on my Goodreads are typically three stars or above; if I don't think it's going to be at least slightly better than average, I don't bother finishing it, and I don't rate anything I didn't finish out of fairness. If it's not my cup of tea, it might be someone else's). I couldn't even make it 50 pages into this. I know I said in that parenthetical that I usually never give less than three star reviews, but I'm really using my willpower not to give this two, or even one. If I had to rate it, I'd probably give it two out of kindness to the concept: the idea is good. It's strong and it's there. But the author has no voice. ** spoiler alert ** My Sister's Keeper is what I like to call a "cheap book." It lures you in with its controversial topic, keeps you reading with endless mini-cliff hangers and moves you to tears with passages calculated to stir your emotions. Of course, that's exactly what one should expect when they pick up a book by Jodi Picoult, a writer who is probably making money angels right now in the piles of cash she's earned from capitalizing on the tender hearts of women. I don't even mean that in a bad way. It's what everyone knows they're getting when they open a book like this- a book where the author's name is printed bigger than the title. A script for a chick flick. Truthfully, if you're looking for a fast-paced, interesting, easy read, you could do worse than this book. It's just that a book like this has a ceiling on how good it can be. This book centers around a 13 year old girl named Anna Fitzgerald. She was conceived using in-vitro fertilization as a perfect donor match for her sister Kate, who was diagnosed with a rare and tricky form of leukemia. The original intention of her parents was for Anna to donate only cord blood to her sister, but when Kate's cancer returns, she is expected to donate more and more genetic material (like blood and bone marrow) in the hopes of curing her. When she is asked to donate a kidney, she decides that enough is enough and hires a lawyer to sue her parents for the right to make her own medical decisions. First, the good: No matter your feelings on books like these, this is an interesting plot. I read this one quickly to see how the story would unfold. It asks a lot of interesting questions about parental responsibilities, maturity, and self-sacrifice vs. self-preservation. The characters in the story are put into an impossible situation with no true good choices. They all seemed like good people who were trying their best to survive under extraordinary circumstances, and it put me into the mindset of constantly wondering what I would do if I were in their shoes. So it had a promising storyline. Now for the bad. I have a few points to make here. The storyline with Campbell, Anna's lawyer and Julia, Anna's guardian ad litem was boring and completely unnecessary. I found myself feeling very irritated when I would get to a section dealing with them. Honestly, what are the odds that these two would have been old flames back in high school with a rocky past? It was a coincidence that felt very forced. Their inclusion in this novel seemed like a ploy to make the book longer or to draw out fake suspense by getting away from the Fitzgerald family every so often. While I'm on these two, are seizure dogs really a great mystery to anyone anymore? I knew that's what Judge was for when I realized that Campbell wasn't blind. Also, is epilepsy something that a normal person would consider to be a deal-breaker in a relationship? The idea that you would have to abandon a relationship because you have epilepsy and don't want to tie someone down is ridiculous. Their story didn't make sense all the way around. So boring. Anna was written inconsistently. She was too smart and sassy in her internal monologue and too childish in her external actions. Her inside and her outside just didn't match up and that continually bothered me. It's like Picoult made her smart and rational when it was convenient to the story and made her scared and weak when she needed to create tension. The ending was a betrayal to the reader. That sounds awfully dramatic, but it's how I feel. Throughout the story all of these great, interesting questions are raised. Anna wins her medical emancipation case and is finally in charge of her own body. She had to make a hard decision in the story, one with difficult consequences. It would have been nice to see the natural outcome of those decisions. t would have been nice to see how Anna and Kate and the rest of the family came to terms with what happened. Instead, here comes the surprise ending! Picoult destroys the moment she has been building up to by killing Anna in a car wreck on her way home from the courthouse. Good thing her kidney is still okay. After all that, Kate winds up with the kidney anyway and she miraculously gets better. Obviously, an organ transplant is not a cure for leukemia, so the cure really is a miracle. Kate closes the book by saying that Anna took her place in heaven. I think I just threw up in my mouth a little. This could have easily been a 3 or 4 star book without the ludicrous manufactured drama of the ending. Why bother to ask the hard questions and explore such difficult topics if you're just going to throw it all away with a "shocking" ending? It's a trap designed by Picoult to trick her readers into thinking she's done something profound and edgy. All she's done is throw away anything that was good about her story. What a waste. Not a favorite of mine, especially due to the ending. It wasn't bad for a quick read when you aren't in the mood to think too much.

Sixteen year old Ever (yes, so sorry that's not a typo) lost her family, her dog, her home and her popularity in a tragic accident. When she awakens she has the ability to read thoughts and see auras. This is not a good thing for Ever and it turns her into a "freak". Now living with her wealthy, absent aunt, she shuns people and hides her beauty behind ugly hoodies and big sunglasses. One gloomy day a new boy arrives at the school where she is now one of the misfit freaky kids. For some reason she's chosen to befriend a gothy bitch and a disinterested in anything but himself boy named Miles instead of the bitchy, self-involved popular kids she used to consider her BFF's. This new kid, Damen, is all smoldering good looks and is interested in MissHoodie and she can't read his thoughts! Ahhh, blessed silence replaces the voices in her head whenever he is near. Here I stop to let the feelings of Deja freaking Vu wash over me and lament the loss of originality in the YA world. The rest of the book follows Ever and Damen around as he keeps her in the dark about his dark and mysterious past and generally acts all dark and mysterious but because he's sexysuperhot they fall into an obsessive dysfunctional crazy sort of love. He must really know how to work the smolder because I couldn't for the life of me figure out when or why they were in love or how he jumped straight from wooing to almost getting her out of her panties in a blink. He was a BORING character and no amount of movie star looks is fixing that when I can't see him! She ain't no prize either, for that matter. She's moody and spoiled and acts like a real nut when he finally tells her the truth about himself. I could forgive the moody, hell her family was dead, but the author didn't work that angle to any real emotional effect. The deaths were used as means to get her to where she is, living with an aunt who conveniently works 168 hours a week so she can hook up with Damen. I should know, I lost a parent at thirteen and life was an emotional hell for a very long time. In this book, I felt none of the pain and torment that invades every pore of your being when something so earth shattering happens. Thus, many of Ever's thoughts were distasteful and shallow to me. All she did was whine about unimportant shit and fret about Damen. Sure she could still talk to her little ghostie sister so I guess that made all the pain go away? To me it was all a bit lazy and not at all clever. So yeah I admit I'm biased but I did finish the book and it didn't get better for me. I don't care how much woo-woo or adventure or paranormal twisties an author throws in, if I find the characters tedious and completely lacking in emotion it's a fail. Ever is a fail.

I do not say this lightly: this is now my very favorite book I have ever read. I am a World War II historian. Since middle school, I have read more WWII books, fiction and nonfiction, than I can count. As a result, I normally separate out my emotion when reading WWII books. That's the only way you can really seriously studying the subject, without becoming depressed. But "The Book Thief" was one of the few WWII books I have read where I could not compartmentalize my emotion. Markuz Zusak's brilliant prose is just too strong, too heart-wrenching. Liesel, Hans, Rudy, are some of the most beautifully imagined characters I have read. His imagining of Hitler and his emphasis on Hitler's words represent some of the most insightful discussion of Hitler and the rise of Nazi Germany I have encountered in fiction. Death as narrator was moving, especially as Death discussed how busy WWII kept him, and how he caught the souls of Jews rising from chimneys. Zusak does things with words I have never seen another writer do. Which is appropriate, considering the emphasis on words in this book. "The Word Shaker" - the book Max, the Jew hidden in the basement, writes, is a powerful testament to how friendship and good acts can reverberate. This is a WWII book, but it is really much more than that. It's about the importance of love, warmth, loyalty, patience, and words.

Intricately laid out and beautifully written, this was a story about lost connections, love and friendship, difficult choices and unexpected coincidences. It was one of those books that leaves you wondering; about love, about life, about ordinary everyday blessings that most of us take for granted and about the power of chance. There were stories within stories, like a literary puzzle where you need to keep account of the characters and events as they turn up later and start getting entwined. Most of the narration varied from the reflections of an eighty year old retired locksmith Leo Gursky, to the ramblings of an adolescent fourteen year old girl Alma Singer. A few chapters in between, were from the point of view of a young author Zvi Litvinoff and his wife Rosa and some towards the end were narrated by Alma's younger brother, Bird. The whole plot revolved around a book called "The History of Love". Every character had some sort of connection to this book, but the relation they all shared was not evident until the story unfolded quite a bit. What I really liked, was how delicately the author weaved the complex connections between the lives of seemingly unconnected people. How the mere existence of one book, changed the choices these people made, in ways they were unaware of themselves. However, what made me take a star out was the climax. I did not understand as to why the author would want to depict Bird's point of view towards the end, since he was hardly there in the story. I also found his character the least believable of all. I wish those last few pages had either Alma's or Leo's narration. What also left me frustrated was the feeling of, "Okay, so what happens next?" because the ending was seriously abrupt, and a lot of questions were left unanswered. For a book that started out beautifully and kept me engaged throughout, the ending was certainly disappointing. That being said, it was still an elegantly written, thought-provoking tale that would leave one amazed.

3.5 rating On a snowy Christmas morning, Holly Judge awakens, the fragments of a nightmare-something she must write down-floating on the edge of her consciousness. Something followed them from Russia. On another Christmas morning thirteen years ago, she and her husband Eric were in Siberia to meet the sweet, dark-haired Rapunzel they desperately wanted. How they laughed at the nurses of Pokrovka Orphanage #2 with their garlic and their superstitions, and ignored their gentle warnings. After all, their fairy princess Tatiana-baby Tatty-was perfect. As the snow falls, enveloping the world in its white silence, Holly senses that something is not right, has not been right in the years since they brought their daughter-now a dangerously beautiful, petulant, sometimes erratic teenager-home. There is something evil inside this house. Inside themselves. How else to explain the accidents, the seemingly random and banal misfortunes. Trixie, the cat. The growth on Eric's hand. Sally the hen, their favorite, how the other chickens turned on her. The housekeeper, that ice, a bad fall. The CDs scratched, every one. But Holly must not think of these things. She and Tatiana are all alone. Eric is stuck on the roads and none of their guests will be able to make it through the snow. With each passing hour, the blizzard rages and Tatiana's mood darkens, her behavior becoming increasingly disturbing and frightening. Until, in every mother's worst nightmare, Holly finds she no longer recognizes her daughter. For once, I'm sticking with the synopsis provided by the publisher. It's written very well and I don't want to butcher it. But more importantly, it provides a glimpse at the writing style within the novel. For me, this took some getting used to. There aren't chapters and the writing can seem all over the place. For the majority of the novel I felt that the author was rambling, though the writing was very poetic at the same time. The latter is what kept me engaged. There were some lovely passages. Although, there was some frustration while reading. I wasn't sure if this was a book I was going to finish. I'm glad to have made it to the end. To be honest, this book stressed me out. The incoherent narrative really helped set the scene. The author really did a great job at developing the world that the characters were set it. I felt stretched thin and worn out while reading this, which is exactly what the characters were experiencing. I am personally glad that Christmas Day is months away so I don't have to worry about the possibility of dealing this kind of mental pressure. This book takes places over the period of a day. But the author takes us through 'flashback' scenes to give the reader the background and insight to the characters. There were times when I felt that this might turn into a supernatural twist. I thought that the child might be a changeling. However, I was very wrong. I didn't realize until I got to the last few pages that I was dealing with an unreliable narrator. Which was perfect, and really tied the book together for me. A surprising psychological thriller. And while this book was under 300 pages, I felt it ended on the right note. *Won in a Goodreads First Reads Giveaway

A little over a month ago, I stopped eating meat - not out of some deep, ethical compulsion but for simple health reasons. I immediately noticed that I felt better - physically and especially emotionally. In the midst of my temporary vegetarianism, I also found myself finally relieved of the cognitive dissonance inherent in an animal lover regularly eating animals. I took the opportunity to do research on the subject that previously I had been too timid to undertake. Eating Animals was the first book I had the courage to read. Foer presented a personal, emotional, rational, and straightforward defense of animal welfare and vegan/vegetarianism. I have been so totally moved by this book that I no longer find it difficult to forego the steak dinners I once craved. Furthermore, I have decided - quite easily - that I do not ever want to return to my former diet. I suspect I will look back on this book many years in the future and still feel as sure of my decision as I do now. Truly, this book has changed my life.

Five stars doesn't begin to cover it. I wish I could've given it more because I did not want this book to end. Daniel James Brown is a master of narrative non-fiction. His story starts by telling the tale of Joe Rantz who grew up during the Depression quite on his own after the death of his mother and the abandonment of his father and step-mother while he was still a child. His gritty spirit carried him through incredibly tough times until he ended up at the University of Washington where he took up rowing. The rest is history. Underdogs no matter when or where they competed, the boys who manned the boat grew under the tutelage of their coach and the incredible builder of the boats, George Yeoman Pocock, to be one of the greatest teams in history. It was "the shared experience---a singular thing that had unfolded...when nine good-hearted men strove together, pulled together as one, gave everything they had for one another, bound together forever forever by pride and respect and love." The writing is absolutely incredible and when you add in heart-pounding races, the trials of the Great Depression and the rise of Hitler, well, it just doesn't get much better. Very highly recommended.

***ARC provided by author for an honest review*** Forgive me if I get over emotional with this review, once in a blue moon I read a novel that affects me in the most tremendous ways. A novel that tugs at every emotion and consumes me. A novel that causes me to bawl like a baby one minute and then has me laughing the next. It's been a while since I've read a novel that sends all my emotions scattering about. I've recently became a huge Fan of A.L. Jackson's after reading her Bleeding Stars series. I've come to learn that you have to expect the unexpected when it comes to her novels. Show Me The Way is a deeply emotional and endearing novel. This is a story of what it is truly like getting over heartbreak and pushing aside the fear that stands in the way of moving on. Rex Gunner is a single father to an adorable little girl (Frankie Leigh). After his wife up and left with no word as to why, Rex decides to shut his heart down, the only exception being his mama and his daughter. So Rex lives day-to-day doting on his beautiful daughter and running his very successful construction business. Rynna Dayne ran away from home 12 years ago. She swore to herself she would never return to Gingham Lakes no matter what. But when she receives a call from an attorney in regards to her grandma's passing she has no choice but the return home and live out her grandma's final wishes of continuing on with the family business. Pepper's Pies. When Rynna moves back into the house she once called home everything falls into place for her and she truly realizes at that moment Gingham Lakes is where she is supposed to be. That is until she sets her sights on her brooding next door neighbor Rex. She instantly feels unwelcome a feeling that has taken her years to overcome. Rynna and Rex's relationship starts off rocky. They both are struggling with the fear of opening their hearts back up and letting others in. Rex is fighting the guilt caused by the chemistry that is continuously building between the two and Rynna is trying her damnedest to show Rex it's okay to let someone in. "In a Wonderland they lie, Dreaming as the days go by, Dreaming as the summers die: Ever drifting down the stream- Lingering in the golden gleam- Life, what is it but a dream?" - Through the Looking Glass, Lewis Carroll Over the years tones of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland adaptations appeared, the Disney's animation is the most popular of those. It also inspired the music industry such as Blink 182, Marilyn Manson and Aerosmith; Vladimir Nabokov's work or even famous manga Pandora Hearts. But I've never get along with retellings since Lewis Carroll's novel is one of my life time favourite, well until Splintered. From the moment I physically held the book I knew they were a difference thanks to a long and deep research from the author. The cover happens to be colorful and wild, very close to the spirit of the story. Also a title which, and finally, isn't a pun not even a wink to Alice but very original. Original as the story embellished around Carroll's legendary work. Alyssa Gardner is secretly a relative of Alice Liddle, the real life inspiration of Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. Never fitted in the real world, Alyssa can hear the whispers of bugs and flowers. Her mother Alison has been in an asylum since she ever remember but when her mental health turns to the worst, Alyssa learns that her family is cursed since the "Alice incident" in Wonderland. She needs to go there and alongside her comes Jeb, her best friend but more complicated since they grew up. During a trip in Wonderland a series of test is waiting Alyssa such as the ocean of tears or the tea party. She will also meet the deadly gorgeous Morpheus, none else than the Caterpillar who happens to be the one she sees in her dreams... "Little blossom in peach and red, trapping boys with your pretty head; tease and play, be coy and smart, for you will one day break his heart." The protagonist Alyssa is a goth-punk modern version of the young and naive Alice. Her favourite place is a skate park named Underland, she could be the girl from McFly's 5 colours in her hair and has a crush on pseudo bad-boy Jebediah. With these characters A.G. Howard breaks the "fairytale" feeling of Wonderland, the reality is darker and through a retrospective of the human misery you can observe facts as child abuse or mental health in a 21th century America. (illustation that could be close to reality) Alyssa's physical and spirit aspects bring to the story a hint of the 2010 version of Tim Burton's Alice in Wonerland. I adore Burton's work over the years but never get into his remake which is lack in emotions. Although the cinematography, techno-colored and vivid, is definitely what inspired the author. Even more the tea party moment reminds me of Kerli's Tea Party music video promoted by the same movie (probably because Kerli style is so close to Alyssa). The author achieved an enormous work of reinterpretation by including a new version of Wonderland, very far from Alice's point of view. But with audacity Howard adds new details to Carroll's work as it looks like an apocalyptic scenery because of Alice's trip. (possible illustation) "He is glory and deprecation -sunlight and shadows- the scuttle of a scorpion and the melody of a nightingale. The breath of the sea and the cannonade of a storm." My favourite and by far is the Caterpillar, or should I say Morpheus. I like him not because he is helluvasexydiosmioiwantyourchildren but the proof Splintered is more than just a retelling. It also brings a romantic plot that is brand new in the Alice's context, although it involves in triangle love but for once it's worth it. And the twist shows how much potential has this book. For my personnal pleasure: "Intense familiarity lures me closer. Jeweled bark covers the entire tree, from the gnarled trunk to the branches that twist hundreds of feet into the air. It glimmers in the sun like a million white diamonds. At the end of each branch, rubie well up like liquid and dribble to the ground, as if the tree is bleeding jewels, the way elves do when their skin is pierced." Full of originality and well written, Splintered gives me hope to read more retelling novels as wonderfully handle as it and by far the most refreshing and new book I've could read in the past months.

Restless Waters (Left Drowning #2) by Jessica Park 5 stars! "Trauma - the gift that keeps on giving." Two years ago I read a book that literally decimated me, I even created a tag line for it, "you've hit 69% now cry like a bitch." Left Drowning hit me hard and it is a book that is at the top of my all time favourite reads. You can read my review here http://www.theromancecover.com/2013/0... You can imagine my jubilation when Jessica Park announced that she was working on a secret project and only giving us a few days notice announces that Restless Waters has gone live and it is Left Drowning 2, to say I was excited was an understatement, especially knowing that this was essentially Sabin's story. "Because the girl I trust most in this world is taken." Sometimes an author really delivers on character connection and Jessica Park nailed this with Left Drowning, I had taken this bunch of misfits into my heart and soul and they have stayed there for the past two years. I was hesitant to start because I just knew that this book was going to kill me, if it was anything like Left Drowning I was going to be an emotional mess, but then knowing that this book was hot property and to avoid any spoilers, I put on my big girl panties and dived straight in, dropping my current read and I hardly ever do that. "You draw me in, and we're completely in sync. I'm fucking complete." This book is not as bad as Left Drowning you will be pleased to hear but it still is one book that packs an emotional punch and has its fair share of angst. Jessica Park always manages to hit me hard with her quirky characters, they are so different that you cannot forget them and diving into this book brought all those feelings and emotions flooding back. Even though Blythe is still the narrator effectively, there is no doubt that this is Sabin's story but we are still treated to catching up with everyone in this "family." "I have two hands, Sabin. Grab one." This book was a voyage of discovery for our three main characters, Blythe, Chris and most importantly Sabin. All three are broken, all three have their fears, but most importantly they have each other and when the past comes back to haunt Sabin all three have to dig deep to get through it. I love this "family" and while what some people on the outside would see as a bunch of misfits, they are as tight as any biological family, if not more so. These characters are bonded by pain and circumstances, by love, by their pasts but most importantly their futures and the relationship that they have can only bring tears to your eyes. "And we have us. We don't follow rules." While Restless Waters was no comparison on the "tear scale" I will admit that quite a few fell while reading this book. Jessica Park nails the emotion and as I said above the character connection. When they hurt, I hurt and that is something that I love in a book. It takes talent to draw out those intense, overwhelming feelings in relation to characters and every single time Jessica Park hits me hard. Whether it be her Flat Out series, Left Drowning series or even Clear, each book brings that emotion out on so many different levels, while compensating your tears with her ever present wit. Sabin has always been an integral character and while on the outside he portrays that charismatic, hilarious, deep, loyal, loving facade, underneath all his pretences is a man that is overcome with guilt however misguided. He is drowning in his thoughts, he is drowning in jealousy and there is only so much one person can take before the water finally pulls them under for good. Sabin feels he only has one choice and that is to get the hell out of there. He needs to find Sabin, the real Sabin and he can only do that if he is not surrounded by constant reminders of his past. "It's like you're in my blood...I can't get you out." For a tight knit family like this Sabin's departure is not only shocking but also creates major separation anxiety with Blythe. Sabin has always been her constant, her companion, her confidante, her best friend and while she still has the love and guidance of Chris, losing Sabin is like chopping off an appendage and she doesn't cope very well. The trouble is, with so many miles between them will Sabin be able to surface from the sea, or will he just drown anyway? "It's hard to float in a storm." Jessica Park, I seriously take my hat off to you, once again you have delivered an emotional, heartfelt story that rocked me to my core once again. A book that delivered everything, a book that was perfectly balanced, that ebbed and flowed with your emotions, while leaving that life buoy just a finger tip away. I seriously cannot recommend this series enough; it is one that I will never forget and one that I have re-read several times. As always, I am greedy and would love to hear more from them, but as I wasn't expecting this one, I will wait patiently for the next secret project and just hope it pertains to this one. The description says that you'll remember your own first love, and while it did have moments that reminded me of what it's like to fall in love for the first time, I just couldn't connect with Eleanor. Was she in a bad situation? Yes, but in times like those, you either let it make you or break and I feel like she let it break her. Again, yes, she's 16 and "helpless" but all I'm saying is that 16 is old enough to call the police and not give a second thought to "Oh, is my mom going to be mad that I'm doing something that she as 40 something year old can't?" The saving grace for me in this book is Park - not only the character but his POV (the book is alternating POVs). Without Park, this book would have probably been a Did Not Finish. Park - my sweet, sweet boy - WHY do you even like Eleanor? She's an Avon lady who loves makeup, nails, and hair - AND she always wants to make other people over. I will say that I really enjoyed Rainbow Rowell's writing style and I'm reading her next book, Fangirl, right now and absolutely loving it. So it's just this particular book that didn't do it for me. Also, the narrator for Eleanor on the audiobook was not the best so that probably played into things a bit. I put this book on my Everyone Loved But Me shelf as there are no less than TWENTY 5 star reviews from my friends on GoodReads. Maybe I'm the misfit in this story.

It seems as if every fantasy I pick up these days features some gleaming redhead as their protagonist... (Well, Name of the Wind, Eye of the World, and now this... So, three. That's still a lot, hey?) Cashore has obviously learnt from Graceling's crawling beginning - Fire hits off with some action and is all go-go from there. The eventual climax is much more exciting, too. Whereas as the former sort of fizzled out, Fire ends with all-out war! Having said that, overall, the story follows a similar structure to its predecessor. Here's the condensed version: Super-powered girl (who will never get married EVER) lives an unfulfilled life, and people want to use for her powers; she goes on an adventure of sorts; falls in love; vows to never have children. During all this, the antagonists lurk mainly in the shadows, only to be introduced properly towards the end before being quickly bumped off. It's not particularly unpredictable or shocking, and I saw many of the twists coming... But hey, it works - and I think I may prefer it this time around. Fire is set in The Dells, the previously-mysterious lands over the mountains from Graceling's Seven Kingdoms. But here, there are no Gracelings (I presume the mountains have special anti-graceling powers?). Instead, there be monsters. Which are actually really cool. Beings known as 'monsters' are especially vibrant and beautiful versions of everyday animals. They come in impossible colours (expect green kittens to make an appearance) and have special mind powers to control their lesser contemporaries. Although I sometimes felt the monsters thing went a bit overboard - I swear there are more monsters than normal animals in the book. Our heroine, Fire, is the last human monster, blessed with impossible good looks and a prism of red/gold/pink hair. You may groan at such a description, but despite fitting all the criteria, Fire escapes the dreaded Mary Sue label she could have so easily fallen into. The characterisation overall is good, and I was invested in the characters. Many agree that Cashore's books have a feminist agenda. And they do, but I thought the social commentary was interesting. She delves into sexual politics - In how beauty and sexuality are treated differently between the sexes. A beautiful man inspires respect and allegiance; his sexuality gives him power. But a beautiful woman inspires jealousy, hatred and certain baser instincts among men. In other words, a woman's sexuality renders her more powerless in comparison. It's certainly an idea to reflect upon in our own society. But, after two books of it, Cashore's no marriage, no children, shave off your hair and tear up your dresses thing comes across as more than a little heavy handed. Maybe it'd be more effective with some subtlety. I think one of the weaker points of the book is tacking it onto Graceling's story-verse. Trying to reconcile the two mythologies just adds confusion and unanswered questions - why does one have gracelings and the other monsters? And we're given Leck in the prologue, but then he's largely ignored for a lot of the story. It didn't need the connection to work. I can't help but wonder if Cashore has daddy issues? I think literally every character has some sort of revelation about their paternity. It actually became quite comical. Expect someone to discover their long lost father every other chapter.

"President Obama came on the scene right as so many people in my community began to believe that the modern American meritocracy was not built for them." The feeling that the white working class has fallen behind, and can no longer identify with the present-day nation, is a central theme in this raw, eye-opening book that attempts to provide a view in to the white middle- and working-class Appalachian mindset. "Barack Obama strikes at the heart of our deepest insecurities. He is a good father while many of us aren't. He wears suits to his job while we wear overalls, if we're lucky enough to have a job at all. His wife tells us that we shouldn't be feeding our children certain foods, and we hate her for it -- not because we think she's wrong but because we know she's right." The two central questions this book talks about are: What is the nature of Appalachia, and what problems is it facing? And how did Vance escape the same fate as others around him? This book pulls no punches and offers a deep view of Vance's life, talking frankly about addiction, being forced to lie to authority figures, and violence. A few takeaways: Vance escaped because he had uncommonly good support structures that gave him a sense of control. Mamaw (his grandmother) was always there for him, and implored him to focus on his studies. Papaw taught him math and made him excel in that area. He was able to gain control over his life, and escape the learned helplessness of the people around him and turned it into learned hopefulness. Gaining control and confidence, and having the right role models around him who sometimes implemented their rules with force--Mamaw threatened violence if she saw J.D. with his drug-smoking friends--led to him being able to succeed. Economics leads to fragile communities. When factories close, like the factory that used to be in Vance's town, the community becomes fragile. People always relied on these jobs to be there, but after the Good Times where the steel mill always could offer a job, people no longer had the safety net that they thought they had. That's economics and larger society's effect. The steel mill always being available was an anomaly, I would personally say--but people took it for granted. Vance thinks the problems facing Appalachia are mostly on the people, not the structure and society around them. Instead of government being able to enact policy to save these people, they have to save themselves, since, for the most part, he thinks these are problems that the people must solve. Being better parents, being better with money, all that--they have to be solved internally. That's hard because if it were a policy issue, it would be relatively easier than hoping people would solve the problems themselves. One example he gives is the cultural idea that it's "feminine" to be good at school. I think it's a mix of both, and much more on the policy side--the failure to re-train people whose jobs went away before, during, and after the recession, due to automation and export of factory jobs, was a trigger or at least a catalyst for the state it is in today. Policy caused that, to some extent. It's harder for policy to undo that, but I still think there are structural things that make it hard for people, when they do have the motivation and effort to make their lives better, to do so easily. There are obstructions that can be removed, and I think this is more promising than he does. He does say, and I would agree, that there are certain things that are less receptive to a thumb on a scale than others. Yes, culture is harder to change. But I think there are structural things that can be more easily changed, and those things can lead to potential follow-on effects. At the same time, he is also right to say that people shouldn't blame the government for all their problems. There are some things that they should be blamed for, but they also have to take responsibility for themselves. So this is a complex topic. Honor was important--it was sometimes the only thing they had. People who didn't have much sometimes saw the only thing they had control over was their honor. So if someone did something that insulted their family, for example, that was one of the few situations where they could show their honor. In a sense, those were the times where they felt like independent, free-willed people, and sometimes that fueled the need for extremeness in their response, like violence. Stress begets stress, distrust begets distrust. "Mamaw's life had been a constant struggle. From the poverty of the holler, to Papaw's abuse, from Aunt Wee's teenage marriage to mom's rap sheet, Mamaw had spent the better part of her seven decades managing crises. His community was very high-strung and stressed, and because they had a lot of life trauma, they found it difficult to trust people. Being on guard means being less likely to associate with people, and more likely to distrust, and also leads to more stress. This also means that people are hardwired for conflict. This leads to many follow-on effects: children are raised in a less encouraging environment, which can lead to childhood trauma. Stress can increase the risk of miscarriages. Uncertainty exacerbated these kinds of issues. As a result, people just focus on self-preservation. There's a culture of blaming your condition on society. People on welfare will criticize welfare. People who never went to work and got fired will criticize Obama for not protecting their jobs. There are people like this out there. Trump told these people they were right--Vance is telling them they're wrong. Strong communities are truly more resilient, and religion is one of the few fallbacks for fragile communities. He brings up the example of Mormons in Utah, who were more resilient in the face of the recession and the difficult state for the white working class. He repeatedly talks about the importance of the church and religion as community--perhaps even more important as community becomes more fragile. The feeling of persecution can make people ignore facts. When he started taking up Evangelical Christianity, partly as a refuge from his home life, he started believing in creationism and separating him from normal society. Other peoples became heretics. When he saw people waging war on Christmas, and hearing about Christian discrimination, made him feel stronger about his views and reject what science said, seeing those as "ideologies to confront, not theories to understand". Patriotism--love of country--was so strong that it was part of people's identity, even though government was ignored or hated. People's identities were based strongly on one's love of country. The history of his town was based in WWII veteran pride, and that people and their families "did their part during WWII." But they felt like it was being lost. The modern American meritocracy, they feel like, is not made for him, whereas they did see it as being made for people like them. Eternal hope. Even though life was tough, and continued to be, people still had eternal hope. Maybe this is a component of the idea that they see themselves as 'temporarily embarrassed millionaires.' This is a complex, enlightening book, and an important read. It's hard to summarize it, and probably requires multiple reads to get everything out of it. Absolutely worth a read.
